O Lord of Knowledge, I desire to hear the secret essence of all tantras, characterized by the emergence from the *sampuṭa*. 1.1.2.
The Blessed One said:
"O Vajragarbha, excellent, excellent! O you of great compassion, excellent!"
Excellent, O Mahābodhisattva! Excellent, excellent, O Guṇākara!
Whatever secret is found in all the tantras, all of that is being asked by you.

Then those great bodhisattvas, headed by Vajragarbha, their eyes blossoming with joy, asked here out of their own uncertainty: ap1.6 <SU 7a→> Then those great bodhisattvas, headed by Vajragarbha, their eyes blossoming with joy, asked here out of their own uncertainty. (1.1.5)
Having prostrated again and again, [he asks: "What is called the 'entire tantra' (sarvatantra)? How does the 'nidāna' come to be? And what is said here regarding the 'secret' (rahasya)? (1.1.6)
How indeed does the emergence from the *sampuṭa* occur, and what would be its characteristic mark therein? (1.1.7)

The Blessed One said: "All those tantras are 'all-tantras' (*sarvatantra*). By the term 'all-tantras,' [it refers to] the *Samāja* and so forth; the meaning is that this [work] is determined to be their source (*nidāna*). It is a 'secret' (*rahasya*) because it is not within the domain of Harihara, Hiraṇyagarbha, Śrāvakas, or Pratyekabuddhas. It is a 'union' (*sampuṭa*), consisting of wisdom and means (*prajñopāya*). That very [union] is the 'arising' (*udbhava*); the meaning is that it is the union-attainment (*sampuṭa-samāpatti*). 'Arising' (*udbhava*) means origination. By the phrase 'characterized by the nature of such stable and moving entities,' its definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is indicated. (1.1.8)

Alternatively, by the term "the compendium of the nidāna of all tantras," Vajrasattva is designated. By the word "secret" (rahasya), the extraction of mantras based on oral instruction (*aupadeśika*) and the characteristics of the initiation of the deities of the maṇḍala and so forth are indicated. 1.1.9 ||
Listen as I proclaim that Tantra whose essence is wisdom and skillful means:
first, having contemplated emptiness, one should wash away the impurities of embodied beings.
One should cause the sound "the realm of form is empty" to be uttered for that very [object]. || 1.1.10 ||
For those who are empty of the sound element, one should cause them to perceive smell;
for those who are empty of the smell element, one should cause them to perceive taste. || 1.1.11 ||
One should cause the emptinesses to perform the function of the taste element;
one should cause the emptinesses to perform the function of the mind for that very [taste element]. || 1.1.12 ||
Vajragarbha said:
"If the eye is the self, how can consciousness exist among things that are empty?"
If the self were the auditory faculty, how could consciousness exist among things that are empty? || 1.1.13 ||
How could consciousness exist within the emptiness of the nose-self? How could consciousness exist within the emptiness of the tongue-self? (1.1.14)
How can consciousness exist among those things that are empty of a body-self?
How can consciousness exist among those things that are empty of anything external to the mind? 1.1.15.
Therefore, there is no form and no seer; no sound and no hearer; no smell and no smeller; no taste and no taster. 1.1.16.
There is neither touch nor toucher, neither mind nor mental factors. 1.1.17.
The Blessed One said:
Listen to the reality of the path, which is non-dual and free from duality.
It is beyond reasoning, unknowable, and likewise difficult to be understood by logicians.
The secret of all Buddhas is equal to space; the Śrāvakas do not understand it, being shrouded by the darkness of ignorance. 1.1.19
Even those who possess the knowledge that follows the path of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*), which is fashioned by the Pratyekabuddhas—
they too do not know the secret that is the domain of the Buddhas. (1.20)
For those whose minds have already crossed over the terrors of the ocean of saṃsāra,
yet who still maintain a body in its midst, he is called one who has "crossed over" (uttīrṇa). 1.1.21.
One should discern the characteristics of the objects of perception through the consciousness of the knowing mind;
having perceived the knowable by means of knowledge, one should observe the course of those knowables.
By the path of the mind that perceives past lives, the yogi may reach them at will; having attained such power, he goes to the state of his many thousands of previous births. (1.1.23)

Having contemplated the equality within the void according to the previously stated characteristics, the wise one should indeed perform the sowing of the seed for the body that begins with the void-field. 1.1.24.
Emerging from the hollow of the channels, that stainless [essence] is proclaimed as the luminous *bodhicitta*, resembling pure crystal. (1.1.25)
The reality consisting of the five knowledges is the size of a mustard seed;
within its center resides the deity, unmanifest yet possessing a manifest form.
The supreme, subtle half-measure, in the form of a point (*bindu*), consisting of mind,
dwells eternally in the center of the heart; it is the color of light, possessed of great splendor.
A single thread, extending from the twelve-finger space and the nine-finger space, down to the soles of the feet and up to the crown of the head, emerges and is situated in the center of the navel.
But that [light], measuring only a fifth part, expanded into the form of the Lord of Nagas;
and that part, having pierced through, emerged from the center of the vajra.
The seed-syllable situated in the center of the womb, liquefied by the *dharmadhātu*,
moves sequentially through all nine gates in every way.
"Agnibrahma" is likewise [to be recited].
One should apply the earth element as the seed-syllable for the two eyes;
the blazing [fire] at the place of the head is for the seed-syllables of wind, space, and so forth, by means of the mind directed toward the nose, ears, and other [senses]. (1.1.31)
The Lord is the master of the sense-organ of the tongue, which has the seed-syllable of nectar-water (*amṛtāmbu-bīja*);
likewise, the neck is formed from the seeds of delusion (*moha-bīja*), and from the arms, as well as from affliction (*kleśa*). (1.1.32)
Having moved from the region of the heart to the navel and the root [perineum] by means of the two animals,
one who possesses the method should maintain the eightfold practice of the seeds with the eightfold limb. 1.1.33.
Pervasive, it encompasses the entire world, including all things stationary and moving; Brahmā and the others, along with the gods and asuras, constitute its support. (1.1.34)
They say that *bhaga* is the place of becoming (*bhavana*), where the Lord moves;
as long as He remains established in the body, there may be both action and inaction for Him. (1.1.35)
The "all-doer" performs all actions, whatever they may be, whether auspicious or inauspicious;
yoga, however, is said to be equanimity, which becomes a state of cultivation for one who is practicing.
When the body of karma is destroyed, one becomes such a deity;
then his own power pervades all that is stable and moving. (1.1.37)
"Therefore, one should understand its color to be like space;
the Hero, established in nirvāṇa, is unstained and free from impurity. (1.1.38)
One's mother, sister, daughter, and female relative,
as well as a Brāhmaṇa woman, a Kṣatriya woman, a Vaiśya woman, and likewise a Śūdra woman. (ApDhS 1.41)
One who is devoted to reality should worship the actress, the washerwoman, the *ḍombī*, and likewise the outcaste woman (*caṇḍālinī*), according to the ritual procedure of wisdom and means. 1.1.40.
One should practice with great effort so that no separation occurs; for if one is unprotected, suffering is caused by beasts of prey, thieves, and other creatures that roam the earth. 1.1.41.
The mudrās are said to be of five kinds, distinguished according to the divisions of the families (kula).
The Brāhmaṇī is born of the twice-born family, and she is considered to be Tathāgatī.
She who belongs to the Kṣatriya caste and the royal lineage, born of families such as Mārīci and Candra,
is called Amṛtavajrā. (1.1.43)
The Vaiśyā is indeed Gopālikā, and she is considered Karmakulikā;
the Śūdrī and Vṛṣalī are both considered Mahāvairocanī.
The actress belongs to the Lotus family, the washerwoman likewise to the Action family;
the *ḍombī* is known as belonging to the Vajra family, and the *caṇḍālinī* should be understood as the Jewel.
The five mudrās have been definitively established; thus, the family of the Tathāgatas is described in brief. (1.1.46)
The glorious one has gone into suchness and has come forth from it in exactly the same way; by virtue of this wisdom and reasoning, he is designated as the Tathāgata. 1.1.47
The Kula is said to be fivefold; the infinite Kula becomes a hundredfold.
Afterwards, it attains a threefold state through the divisions of body, speech, and mind. (1.1.48)
The families of the five elements, which consist of the nature of the five aggregates,
are the source-families of those who hold the vajra, wheel, jewel, lotus, and sword. || 1.1.49 ||
There is no meditator, nor is there an object of meditation; there is no mantra and no deity.
Yet those two—the mantra and the deity—abide by virtue of their nature being free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*).
Vairocana, Akṣobhya, Amogha, Ratna, and Arali are [the Buddhas] associated with the sattva quality;
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Sarva are said to be the awakened reality (tattva). (1.1.51)

Brahmā is so called because of his being the source; he is called Buddha because of his awakening; Viṣṇu is spoken of because of his pervading; Śiva because of his eternal auspiciousness; and Sarva because he abides within his own self.
Because it is realized as true reality through the awakening of bliss, and because it arises within the body through the experience of delight, it is therefore called "the deity" (devatā). 1.1.53
He is called "Bhagavān" because he possesses *bhaga*. They say that *bhaga* consists of six kinds, comprising all qualities such as sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) and the rest. (1.1.54)
Alternatively, he is called Bhagavān because he has destroyed the afflictions and so forth.
Wisdom is called "mother," because it gives birth to the people of the world. (1.1.55)
Because wisdom (prajñā) shows such a distinction as "sister," wisdom is called the washerwoman, since she cleanses all sentient beings.
Likewise, it is traditionally known as "rajaki."
Wisdom is called a daughter because she milks out all virtues; wisdom is called a dancer because of her great compassion and her flickering nature. (1.59)
Because the Blessed Lady is untouchable, she is therefore proclaimed as Ḍombī.
Recitation is said to be chatter, arising from the continuous muttering of the vowels and consonants. (1.1.58)
A circle (maṇḍala) is a footprint; it is called a maṇḍala because of its circular shape. A hand-clap constitutes a mudrā, as does the snapping of fingers. || 1.1.59 ||
That which is to be meditated upon is that which has been contemplated, and from that contemplation arises the object of meditation;
just as the happiness obtained from a father is experienced by oneself, so too is that bliss enjoyed personally. (1.1.60)
That happiness by which death occurs here is called the bliss of meditative absorption (dhyāna). || 1.1.61 ||
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Reality of the Cultivation of the Designation, the Designated, the Arousing of the Mind of Enlightenment, and so forth.
Part 2.
Now, I shall explain the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*).

One dwells contemplating the body in the internal body, in the external body, and in the internal-external body—mindful, clearly comprehending, and having subdued worldly ignorance and dejection. 1.2.1.

He dwells contemplating feelings as feelings—whether internal feelings, external feelings, or both internal and external feelings—mindful, clearly comprehending, and having removed worldly ignorance and dejection. 1.2.2.

He dwells contemplating phenomena in internal phenomena, in external phenomena, and in both internal and external phenomena—mindful, clearly comprehending, and having removed ignorance and dejection regarding the world. 1.2.3.

He dwells contemplating the mind internally, contemplating the mind externally, and contemplating the mind both internally and externally—mindful, clearly comprehending, and having removed worldly ignorance and dejection. 1.2.4.
These are the four foundations of mindfulness. 1.2.5.
For the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states, he generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, takes hold of the mind, and applies right effort. (1.2.6)
He generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, takes hold of the mind, and applies right effort for the abandoning of evil, unwholesome states that have already arisen. 1.2.7.
For the arising of wholesome states that have not yet arisen, one generates desire, exerts effort, arouses energy, takes hold of the mind, and applies right resolve. 1.2.8.

In this way, for the sake of the stability of wholesome states that have arisen, for the fulfillment of the cultivation of immeasurable means, and for the completion of what is not yet complete, he generates desire, exerts himself, arouses vigor, sustains the mind, and applies right resolve toward their further cultivation, increase, and expansion. 1.2.9.
These are the four right efforts. 1.2.10.

He cultivates the basis of psychic power endowed with the concentration of desire and the formative forces of abandonment; it is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment, [thinking]: "May my desire not become too lax, nor too over-exerted."

He cultivates the basis of psychic power endowed with the formative forces of exertion and concentration, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment, [thinking]: "May my energy not be too slack, nor too over-exerted. || 1.2.12 ||

He cultivates the basis of psychic power endowed with the formative forces of investigation and concentration, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment, [thinking]: "May my investigation not be too lax, nor too over-exerted. 1.2.13.

He cultivates the basis of psychic power endowed with the mental formations of concentration and abandonment, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment, [thinking]: "May my mind not become too slack, nor too over-exerted. || 1.2.14 ||
These are the four bases of psychic power. 1.2.15.

One has faith in the mundane right view pertaining to the realm of desire. One takes refuge in the ripening of one's own karma, thinking: "Whatever action I shall perform, whether wholesome or unwholesome, I shall experience the ripening of that very action. Thus, even for the sake of life, one does not perform an unwholesome deed. This is called the faculty of faith.
Those phenomena which one has faith in by means of the faculty of faith, those very phenomena one brings to fulfillment by means of the faculty of vigor. This is called the faculty of vigor. 1.2.17

Those phenomena which one brings to fulfillment through the faculty of energy, those same phenomena one does not allow to be lost through the faculty of mindfulness. This is called the faculty of mindfulness. 1.2.18

Those phenomena which one does not cause to be lost through the faculty of mindfulness, those very phenomena one makes one-pointed by means of the faculty of concentration. This is called the faculty of concentration. 1.2.19

Those phenomena which one makes one-pointed by means of the faculty of concentration, those phenomena one penetrates by means of the faculty of wisdom. One becomes inclined toward the discernment of each and every such phenomenon; this is called the faculty of wisdom. 1.2.20
These five faculties become the five powers: the power of faith, the power of energy, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom. These are the five powers. 1.2.21

In that regard, what are the seven factors of enlightenment? They are as follows: the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness, the factor of enlightenment of the investigation of phenomena, the factor of enlightenment of energy, the factor of enlightenment of rapture, the factor of enlightenment of tranquility, the factor of enlightenment of concentration, and the factor of enlightenment of equanimity. One cultivates these seven factors of enlightenment, beginning with the investigation of phenomena, which are based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and result in relinquishment. || 1.2.22 ||

1.78 What is the noble eightfold path therein? It is right view, which is supramundane; it does not arise from the view of a self, nor does it arise from the views of a sentient being, a living soul, a nourisher, a person, a human, a man, an agent, or an experiencer; it does not arise from the views of annihilationism or eternalism; it does not arise from the views of existence or non-existence; it does not arise from the views of the wholesome, the unwholesome, or the indeterminate; and so on, up to: it does not arise from the views of saṃsāra or parinirvāṇa. This is called right view. 1.2.23

Those volitions through which the afflictions of attachment, aversion, and delusion arise—those volitions he does not form. Those volitions through which the aggregates of ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation arise—those volitions he does form. This is called right intention. (1.2.24)

With that speech by which one does not cause suffering to oneself or others, nor causes affliction to oneself or others, nor mocks oneself or others—one is endowed with such speech that is composed and disciplined. That speech by which one correctly enters the Noble Path is called right speech. 1.2.25

One does not perform that action which is black and has a black ripening; one performs that action which is white and has a white ripening; one does not perform that action which is both white and black with a white-and-black ripening; one performs that action which is neither black nor white with a ripening that leads to the destruction of the black. This reliance on wholesome action is right action. This is called right action. 1.2.26

When there is non-abandonment of the noble lineages, vows, virtues, and ascetic refinement; when there is no hypocrisy, no flattery, and no seeking of praise through talk; when there is good conduct and character; when there is no envy toward the gains of others; when there is contentment with one's own gains and blamelessness; and when there is a livelihood authorized by the Noble Ones—this is called right livelihood. 1.2.27

That exertion which is false and not authorized by the Noble Ones, being underlain by the latent tendencies of the afflictions of passion, hatred, and delusion—that exertion he does not desire. That exertion which is the entry into the truth of the Noble Path and leads to the practice that goes toward Nirvāṇa—that exertion he pursues. This is called right exertion. 1.2.28

That mindfulness which is well-established, unshakable, straight, and not crooked; which clearly reveals the faults of saṃsāra and leads one along the path to nirvāṇa; that mindfulness, that recollection, which is the correct application of the Noble Path—this is called right mindfulness. 1.2.29.

Right concentration is that concentration established in which one, for the sake of the liberation of all sentient beings, enters into the perfect stability of nirvāṇa; this is called right concentration. 1.2.30
These very stages, beginning with *muditā* (joy), are fully described as the *ālaya* (receptacle) of the Bodhisattvas, who possess the nature of the faculties and so forth. (1.2.31)
The *ālaya* is the foundation of all Buddhas, specifically of the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth;
it is the supreme bringer of Buddhahood for both Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. (1.2.32)

When the thirty-two aspects of bodhicitta reach fullness here, immediately thereafter, the state of Buddhahood is attained for those consisting of the sense faculties, aggregates, and elements. (1.2.33)
Buddhahood resides only within one's own body and nowhere else;
those obscured by ignorance believe that Buddhahood exists apart from the body. (1.2.34)
The great knowledge residing within one's own body is free from all conceptual constructions;
though it pervades all things and dwells in the body, it is not born of the body. (1.2.35)
Vajragarbha said:
"Which are the channels within the body? (1.2.36)
The Blessed One said:
"One hundred and twenty-four [channels] arise from the differentiation of the four wheels. By way of the nature of the *bodhicitta*, thirty-two channels are considered supreme. They are as follows:
Abhedyā, Sūkṣmarūpā, Divyā, Vāmā, Vāminī, Kūrmajā, Bhāvakī, Sekā, Doṣā, Viṣṭā, and Mātari—[these are the Mothers]. || 1.2.37 ||
Śarvarī, Śītadā, Uṣmā, Lalanā, Rasana, Avadhūtī, Pravaṇā, Hṛṣṭā, Varṇā, Surūpiṇī, Sāmānyā, and Hetudāyikā. (1.2.38)
Viyojā, Premāṇī, Siddhā, Pāvakī, Sumanas, Trivṛttā, Kāminī, Gehā, Caṇḍikā, and Māradārikā. || 1.2.39 ||
"O Blessed One, what are these channels like?"
"All things transformed within the three realms of existence are devoid of the grasped and the grasper. (1.2.41)

Chapter Two, titled "Entering the Bodhicitta," which is an exposition on the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and culminating in the noble eightfold path, etc. (Ap 1.93).
Part 3,
ap1.94: Then all the Tathāgatas, having performed worship to the Blessed One and prostrated themselves, spoke as follows:
"O Blessed One, please speak the essence, the secret, the unsurpassed knowledge."

Then the Blessed One, having understood the exhortation of all the Tathāgatas, entered the samādhi called the Vajra Lamp of Knowledge of the Heart of All Tantras and proclaimed this secret of all tantras. 1.3.2
Abiding eternally within the supreme, most delightful secret, which is the self of all,
the being who consists of all Buddhas is Vajrasattva, the ultimate bliss.
For that Blessed One is Yoga, firm, eternal, and supreme; yet the god of love has arisen, and his nature is always difficult to overcome. (1.3.4)
Through the application of diverse karma, for those who desire various ritual methods,
the Buddhas, Vajradharas, and others are known as being created for the sake of discipline. (1.3.5)
He becomes all things, both stable and moving, beginning with all the Buddhas;
he is the *Sarvabuddhasamāyoga-Ḍākinījālasaṃvara*.
By means of this application of illusion, the supreme universe is everywhere accomplished by the Buddhas and other disciples for the highest benefit of all sentient beings. (1.3.7)
All women are accomplished in the art of illusion through the transformation of their own forms; even those of immoral conduct attain success through all gains, pleasures, and festivals. 1.3.8.
This mudrā of manifold illusion is called *ḍākinī* by the Mlecchas;
here, the verbal root *ḍai*, meaning "to move through the air," has been conceptualized. (1.3.9)
"The accomplishment that moves through all space is established as the Ḍākinī;
she is the Universal Seal (Viśvamudrā) in every respect, through all the universal vows. Thus [ends verse 1.3.10].
The Vajra and the Vajradhara, likewise the Padma and the Padmadhara,
and the Maṇi and the Maṇidhara— these constitute their families.
Then, having entered the samādhi called the Stainless State that Overcomes All Tathāgatas, he uttered this thought of awakening:
Neither empty nor non-empty, the Middle Way is not apprehended; for the yoga of the perfection of wisdom is indeed the means whose essence is compassion. 1.3.13
Then, through the perfection of wisdom and skillful means of great compassion,
it is clearly manifest that among non-conceptual phenomena there is neither existence nor cultivation.
Even while resolving upon the non-conceptual, one should conceive of all conceptualization;
even within phenomena that are non-conceptual, one should conceive of the welfare of sentient beings.
The Dharma whose essence is the Tathāgata is neither a possessor of attributes (dharmin) nor a nature (dharmatā).
Therefore, that speech of the Dharma was like the sound of an echo.
Then, through the expansion of qualities consisting of the cultivation of the origin of the Mahāyāna,
all the Tathāgatas of the three times praised [the Buddha] with this King of Praises.
Homage be to you, O Lord of Yoga, the liberator of beings!
Homage be to you, the son of all, who possesses a single nature!
Homage be to the one who cuts through the delusion of the ocean of saṃsāra!
Homage be to you, the sole seer of the knowledge of all reality!
I always pay homage. || 1.3.18 ||
Once again, having performed worship and prostrated themselves, they spoke thus:
"Speak, O Blessed One, the essence that is the single compendium of all dharmas. (1.3.19)
The Blessed One said:
Whatever sense faculty enters the path, that very thing [is so] by its own nature.
By means of non-concentrated yoga, he is always indeed concentrated. || 1.3.20 ||
Since consciousness, which is the self in its entirety, is dependent upon the aggregates (skandhas), those of lowest birth with deluded minds do not awaken at all. 1.3.21.
Mind, consciousness, and the nature of consciousness are cognition whose very form is the object of knowledge;
the causality within effects and the cultivation of the nature of phenomena belong to the dharmas. (1.3.22)

1.3.23 Since liberation would become manifold through the multiplicity of dharmas— like the ocean [receiving] the streams of rivers— liberation would indeed be only one; multiplicity is not perceived.
That is obtained from the mouth of the Guru, exactly as it is established in the inner self.
Thus ends the third chapter, the Section on the Enumeration of Reality.
Part 4, ap1.117:
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the definitive conclusion regarding all tantras.
Because all sentient beings are equal, [it is] triangular and of noble form.
But their support shall be Brahmā and the others, including the gods and asuras;
that very [support] is the Perfection of Wisdom, possessing the form of conventional appearance. (1.4.2)
That very [Self] transcends all objects and abides in the hearts of all living beings.
What is the use of elaboration for you? That state of awakening is [evident] from this summary. 1.4.3.
Buddhahood, the supreme state, which is attained only after tens of millions of incalculable eons—
you have reached it even in this very life through true happiness alone.
Then, one may attain the state of a Vajradhara, or else universal sovereignty by this very means; or the eight great siddhis, or whatever other [attainment] is desired by the mind.
Delusion, hatred, passion, pride, and envy are the five afflictions;
beings who are firmly bound by them destroy themselves by their very own limbs. 1.4.6
Bound by these, sentient beings are born wandering within the saṃsāra of the six realms; deluded by the afflictions, they commit manifold evils. (1.4.7)
Therefore, having seen the suffering of separation from those fallen into the ocean of saṃsāra, this reasoning was devised by one of clever intellect in order to dispel it. (1.4.8)
The afflictions, having become conditions, are well-fashioned by means of wisdom and skillful methods as the cause;
that very characteristic, which has become the fruit, is the stainless light within the three realms.
By whatever means those beings are to be bathed, they take on that very form; like the analogy of fire and fuel, the divine drama of the Jina is beautiful. 1.4.10
This very one is pure in character; these are the aggregates, sense-bases, and elements.
Yet a capable enemy destroys that [purity], just as a capable [enemy] destroys another enemy.

Delusion through the purification of delusion, hatred likewise through the purification of hatred, passion through the purification of passion, and great pride through the purification of pride. (1.4.12)
Through the purification of envy by means of envy, the Lord Vajradhṛk is indeed all-purified;
through the purification of that form, the five afflictions come to pacification. (1.4.13)
These five families are the five gnoses and the five Buddhas.
From these are born sentient beings, the Vajragarbha wrathful deities, and the three realms. (1.4.14)
This very internal distinction is obtained with extreme clarity from the mouth of the Guru;
those beings who are devoid of a Guru do not obtain even the mantra and the mudrā.
In this Jambūdvīpa, inhabited by the Buddha, which is triangular and pure, in the center of which is the form of the letter *E*, there is the syllable *Vaṃ* exactly as it is. (1.4.16)
In the beautiful triangular mandala, which issues forth from the Vajrāralli,
there is that which is renowned as the Dharmodaya and is also called the *bhaga* of women. (1.4.17)
In its center is an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp;
there, the vowels and consonants are intermingled, arranged according to their eight groups.
They perform the aggregate of actions for embodied beings in the form of mantras;
these Vedas themselves are established as consisting of exactly fifty syllables.
The mantras, the tantras, and the external treatises—
all these have Vajragarbha as their true nature; there is nothing else whatsoever apart from them.
The fifty letters of the groups beginning with *a*, *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*, *ya*,
and *sa* are likewise fashioned as equal, situated upon lotuses within the Vajrāralla. 1.4.21.
On each petal, [the deities] are known in the eight directions;
however, in the center of these, within the filaments, resides the Supreme Lord.
The supreme syllable is encircled by eight groups; the letter *a* is the foremost of all phonemes, of great significance, and the leader of the groups. (1.4.23)
From that very source indeed have all the mantras of embodied beings arisen.

Those supernatural powers— such as the sword, collyrium, foot-ointment, pills, the underworld, and yakṣa women— which follow the course of alchemy (sūtaka) existing within the belly of the three worlds; || 1.4.25 ||
All those goddesses of great supernatural power, who reside in their own abodes endowed with the five objects of desire,
emerge from the excellent vowels situated within the midst of the eight classes of consonants, which are themselves composed of those classes. (1.4.26)
Whatever flow of speech people employ, all of that is indeed of the nature of mantra; for it is born from Him alone. (1.4.27)
For it has been said that sound is indeed the mantra for all embodied beings; from the great seat of the universal knot, the rosary of dharma shall emerge. (1.4.28)
No mantra whatsoever is fixed as a cause for accomplishment or supernatural power;
for the supreme Lord of the Classes is a mantra whose intrinsic nature is unarisen. (1.4.29)
Henceforth, I shall explain the characteristics arising from the *sampuṭa* (the union).
The letter *e* is to be known as earth; Locanā is indeed the *karmamudrā*.
Great compassion, possessing the universal form of great skillful means, and having the universe as its sphere of activity,
she indeed resides in the emanation wheel at the navel in the universal lotus.
The syllable *vaṃ* should be known as water; Dharmamudrā is Māmakī.
She is the goddess whose form is the vow of loving-kindness, the foremost of the Vajra family. (1.4.32)
She is situated at the wheel of dharma within the heart, in the eight-petalled lotus;
she is designated as the letter Ma, fire, the Great Seal (Mahāmudrā), and Pāṇḍarā.
Through the application of the power of sympathetic joy (muditā), the Goddess, born from the Lotus Family,
resides in the enjoyment wheel (saṃbhogacakra) at the throat, within the eight-petaled lotus.
The letter *yā* is the form of wind, which shatters all afflictions;
it is indeed the Mahāsamaya-mudrā, the principal goddess of the Karma-kula.
Through the union of equanimity and primordial wisdom, Tārā is the one who carries beings across the ocean of saṃsāra;
she abides in the wheel of great bliss, within the thirty-two-petalled lotus.
The letter *e* is known as wisdom (*prajñā*), and the syllable *vaṃ* is likewise the means (*upāya*).
Adorned with the syllable *vaṃ*, this letter *e* certainly shines with splendor. (1.4.37)
Furthermore, through the meditative attainment of the upward and downward [movements], by virtue of the nature of wisdom and means,
the letter *e* and the letter *vaṃ* are each declared to be a dyad. (1.4.38)

By the indeclinable *evam* (thus), the entire collection of the tantra up to the word *avocat* (said) is indicated; or [it indicates] that he will say: "Thus indeed have I heard: here the Great Passion always abides. *Śru* is specified as hearing—that which is the Lord of Great Bliss (*mahāsukha*). "By me alone it was heard," "by me it was heard"—it was heard by means of the ear and by means of gnosis (*jñāna*), but it was not realized (*adhigata*). For if it were realized, what fault would there be for the Blessed One? {C10v} ap1.156

The Blessed One said: There would be no distinction between the compiler and the teacher; or rather, it is precisely the teacher who is the compiler, depending on the needs of those to be trained. 1.4.40
"I am the teacher, I am the Dharma, and I am the listener, accompanied by my own retinue;
how then is this known? (1.4.41)

"Wherein the Lord of Great Bliss dances—dances as one and with manifold moods," according to the scriptural statement. "Whatever has been taught by the Blessed One, O sons of noble family, all that was heard by me at one time, in a single moment"—by this, he indicates his attainment of the samādhi of inconceivable resolute conviction. (1.4.42)
It is said that "samaya" means time; for time is considered to be of three kinds:
good time, bad time, and inconceivable time. (1.4.43)
When it enters through the nostril cavity like a stream of milk, it is called "good time" (*sukāla*);
when it exits in the form of fire, it is "bad time" (*duḥkāla*). One of these two is proclaimed [as the primary]. (1.4.44)
One would be solitary and alone; time has become inconceivable.
There is neither passion nor dispassion, and the Middle Way is not perceived. (1.4.45)
In that regard, passion is characterized by attachment, while dispassion is considered to be cessation.
Apart from these two, a middle state is not perceived; thus, this triad is not apprehended. (1.4.46)
Passion and dispassion, when blended together and undisturbed,
likewise become a single moment of equal flavor through passion and dispassion. (1.4.47)
The Blessed One, who is the equal flavor (*samarasa*) of all phenomena, is called the single *samaya*. For example:
Of complete sovereignty, beauty, fame, and splendor—
Furthermore, the Vedic revelation states that "bhaga" refers to knowledge, effort, and the six [perfections].
He possesses these [qualities], thus he is the Blessed One (bhagavān). || 1.4.48 ||

Alternatively, he is called the Blessed One (*bhagavān*) because he has conquered (*bhagna*) those factors that belong to the opposing side. Those very bodies, speech, and minds of all the Tathāgatas are the heart; that itself is the vajra; she herself is the consort; her *bhaga* is the place where he dwelt. O Blessed One, what is meant by the statement "he dwelt"? 1.4.49

The Blessed One said: "The meaning is that he has captivated the minds of those to be trained through the diverse skillful means of all the Tathāgatas who are of equal flavor (*samarasa*). When the Blessed One dwelt within the *dharmodayā*, which is by nature the Vajra Consort of the heart of the body, speech, and mind of all the Tathāgatas, then this was heard by me. It is as follows: 'By which even affliction (*kleśa*) is destroyed, and those afflictions are dependent upon wisdom (*prajñā*); therefore, wisdom is called the *bhaga*. Within that *bhaga*, all the Tathāgatas together with the Consort reside. (1.4.50)
"Oh, how supreme is the omniscient wisdom of all the Buddhas, that for the sake of the Tathāgata’s happiness, they even assist by taking on the state of being his wife! (1.4.51)

O sons of noble family, thus have I heard: the syllables are eternally established at the beginning of the Dharma; they are pure, the generators of the accomplishment of the Perfect Buddha, and though they are ineffable, O Vajrapāṇi, they have been declared by me. By means of these syllables, sentient beings go to the far shore of saṃsāra. Having made them the objective focus, with a mind repeatedly absorbed therein, one attains in this very life either Buddhahood or the state of Vajrasattva. (1.4.52)

They indeed go to the inconceivable state which was not attained even by the Sugatas; yet beings become Buddhas when they have correctly spoken regarding the characterized and the characterizable. By merely practicing [with] a defiled mind, one goes to the Avīci hell; therefore, one should abandon that which is defiled. But the glorious practitioner, having transcended the fear of existence, meditates with a pure mind. Through the application of wisdom and means, he attains that pure truth which is characterized by the nature of direct experience, the transformation of wisdom and means, equal to space, the light of the three worlds, difficult to perceive, all-pervading, dependent on causes and conditions, like a wish-fulfilling gem in the world, accomplishing the welfare of self and others—the supreme siddhi. (1.4.53)
Thus ends the first chapter, the King of Ritual Manuals arising from the Glorious Sampuṭa, from the Secret Source of All Tantras (Sarvatantranidānarahasya).
Ap2.
Chapter A2,
Part 1
Now, therefore, for the benefit of practitioners,
I shall fully explain that by which the disciple is consecrated, and the ritual procedure is also described.
First, the yogi, whose nature is that of the deity, should purify the earth; then, with the effort of making it vajra-like through the syllable *HŪṂ*, he should subsequently draw the maṇḍala. (2.1.2)
In a garden, in a secluded place, in the dwellings of Bodhisattvas, or in the midst of an empty pavilion or house, one should draw the excellent maṇḍala. (2.1.3)
One should draw [the mandala] with divine powder, or else with that of middle quality;
or with powders consisting of the five jewels, or with rice and so forth.
A mandala three cubits in size, increased by three thumb-breadths, should be prepared;
there, the four Vidyās— divine and born of the five families— should be introduced.
When a wise person has been consecrated according to the path of mantra within the maṇḍala, the abode of the Sugatas, they are directly perceived by all the Buddhas. (2.1.6)

Nevertheless, the wise one, having attained the state of self-consecration and fearing any violation of the commitments, should accept [the consort] who is the sovereign of infinite world-realms. (2.1.7)
Furthermore, it is stated in the Mantra Path by the Perfect Buddhas from the perspective of ultimate reality:
"The commitment (samaya) of the deities, such as Vajrasattva and others, is difficult to transgress. (2.1.8)
Therefore, for this purpose, the son of the Victor should, with all effort and as is appropriate, approach an ocean of qualities, a Vajrācārya, for consecration. (2.1.9)
Alternatively, it may be his own eldest sister, daughter, or niece;
among these, he should employ whichever one is available as an excellent means for accomplishment. (2.1.10)
If these vidyās explicitly described by the Omniscient One did not exist,
then other [vidyās] specifically distinguished by the Buddhas would have to be compiled. (2.1.11)

2.12 Whether she be the wife of a twice-born, or a washerwoman, or a Caṇḍāla woman, or a Dombī of noble birth; whether she be the wife of a king, an actress, or an artisan; or a deer-eyed woman, slender-waisted, broad-hipped, with uplifted breasts, fortunate, well-versed in the traditional conduct, established in reality, and knowledgeable in mantra and tantra—these maidens are said to be priceless in the three worlds for the lords of practitioners. Through them, all accomplishment (*siddhi*) is attained according to the Kula lineage alone.
Alternatively, having obtained such a consort (mudrā) as she may be found— a sixteen-year-old endowed with fresh youth and beautiful eyes— just so [should one proceed]. || 2.1.13 ||
Having grasped that knowledge and purified it through the sequence of going for the three refuges,
one should explain the secret of reality and the entire sequence of mantra and tantra.
Sound, the lower path, the reality of the tongue, as well as upward projection—
all these are thoroughly burnt away, along with the sequence of various differentiations.
Adorned with earrings, waist-bands, and so forth, as well as necklaces, anklets, and bracelets—
the Vidyā that has been purified in this manner bestows the supreme accomplishment. (2.1.16)
In a place free from all disturbances, the Vidyādhara and his companions,
having adorned themselves with garlands, sandalwood paste, garments, and other ornaments, should then present [the offering]. (2.1.17)

Having diligently worshipped with devotion through offerings such as perfumes and garlands, and through extensive rites such as the milk-offering, the practitioner, together with the mudrā, [should proceed]. (2.1.18)
2.19 The disciple, having placed his kneecaps upon the ground with faith and joining his palms, should entreat the Teacher with this hymn of praise:
Homage to you, whose essence is emptiness, who are free from all conceptual constructions;
homage be to you, the embodiment of wisdom, the mass of the omniscient one’s knowledge.
O Vajrasattva, who has arisen from the selflessness of phenomena, you who teach the pure reality that severs the ignorance of the world— homage be to you! 2.21
The perfectly awakened Buddhas and the Bodhisattvas, as well as the qualities of the perfections, always arise from you, O Protector; homage be to you, the mind of awakening! (2.1.22)
O Hero, the Three Jewels, the Mahāyāna, all that is moving and stationary,
and this entire triple world— homage be to you! (2.1.23)
Like a wish-fulfilling gem arisen for the sake of accomplishing the desired aims of the world,
O glorious son of the Buddha who carries out the command of the Sugata— homage, homage to you! (2.1.24)
O Omniscient One, through your power and your excellence, may I know the unsurpassed reality; now, by means of the vajra-consecration, grant me your grace. (2.1.25)
The secret of all the Buddhas has been revealed to Vajradharmin;
just as it was by Śrī Cittavajra, so too, O Lord, be gracious to me. 2.1.26
Apart from your lotus feet, no other refuge exists for me.
Therefore, O Lord, conqueror of the course of saṃsāra, show me compassion. (2.1.27)
Then the glorious Vajrācārya, compassionate and intent on the welfare [of others], having aroused pity for the disciple, summoned him into the maṇḍala of the assembly.
[It was] strewn with the five strands of sensual pleasure, radiant and spread with canopies,
joined by the yoga of yoginīs, and filled with the resonant sound of ringing bells.
In the most wonderful mandala of Vajrasattva and the other deities, delightful with flowers, incense, and ointments, and filled with the fragrance of garlands and wine. (2.1.30)
Then, having performed the mudrā-yoga, the preceptor, the most excellent of the fortunate ones,
places the *bodhicitta* born from the Conqueror into a lotus vessel.
With uplifted yak-tail whisks and parasols, and with auspicious songs in verse,
the Lord of the World should consecrate that disciple together with the ritual mudrās.
Having bestowed the consecration with the supreme jewel, the preceptor, who is the Supreme Lord, should indeed grant the beautiful, divine, and primordial sacrament (samaya). 2.1.33.
Great red [saffron], together with camphor and mixed with red sandalwood,
combined with the water of the thunderbolt (vajra-water), is the fifth, which arises from the mind.
This commitment of yours has been correctly proclaimed by all the Buddhas; O auspicious one, always observe it, and now listen to the vow.
One must not commit the taking of life, nor should one abandon a jewel of a woman; one must not forsake one’s teacher, for the vow is difficult to transgress. (2.1.36)
Of the aforementioned vidyās, or that which is the consort of the Self—
take that pure, emanated vidyā, permeated with *sihlaka* and camphor. (2.1.37)
The yogin should practice with the mudrā only so long as she remains possessed of semen; likewise, he should seal the mouth of the mudrā and the mouth of the means (upāya). 2.1.38.
That which has arisen through service should be poured into the mouth of the disciple;
and therein, within the sphere of the disciple, the state of equal flavor (samarasa) must be brought about.
Knowledge should be self-cognized, devoid of the perception of self or other;
it is equal to space, stainless, empty, and supreme, consisting of both being and non-being. (2.1.40)
Intermingled with wisdom and skillful means, and blended with passion and dispassion,
that alone is the life-breath of living beings; that alone is the supreme syllable.
All-pervading is he alone; he alone possesses the wisdom of a Buddha.
He is declared to be Śrī Heruka, in whom existence and non-existence have become one.
And those others which are [mentioned] there. || 2.1.42 ||
The hero experiences the first bliss, while the yoginī experiences supreme bliss; indeed,
he who knows all the means to that happiness experiences the entirety of the bliss of union.

The first is mere bliss (*ānandamātra*), while supreme bliss (*paramānanda*) is the second; the third is called the bliss of cessation (*viramākhya*), and the fourth is known as the innate (*sahaja*). (2.1.44)
And that consecration is fourfold:
first is the consecration of the vessel (kalaśa), and second is from the secret consecration (guhyābhiṣeka).
The third, however, is the knowledge of wisdom (prajñājñāna), and the fourth is likewise again. || 2.1.45 ||
When the disciple’s defilements have been removed by the consecration of the thought of awakening (bodhicitta),
one should then grant permission regarding that excellent city of the Buddhas.
Until you reach the seat of enlightenment, throughout the entire circle of the directions,
turn everywhere the unsurpassed, supreme wheel of Dharma.
Your very self, whose nature is wisdom and skillful means, like a supreme wish-fulfilling jewel—
tireless and free from attachment, act now for the benefit of sentient beings.
Having received the consecration and permission, fulfilled in purpose and filled with joy, he should speak very sweet words that bring delight to the world. (2.1.49)
Today my birth has become fruitful, and my life as well;
today I am born into the family of the Buddhas and have now become a son of the Buddha.
O Protector, I have been rescued by you from the great and terrible ocean of kalpas, which is as turbulent as the Avīci hell and exceedingly difficult to cross because of the mire of afflictions.
Through your grace, I know myself as if fully accomplished;
I have no further longing for enlightenment, and all latent predispositions have been abandoned.
Having prostrated at his feet with devotion, his eyes wide with joy,
he should offer whatever object is most dear to him. (2.1.53)

Even by a compassionate teacher whose mind is free from restraint, that [instruction] should indeed be imparted for the sake of removing the student's grasping and for their ultimate benefit. (2.1.54)
Then, having prostrated, performed worship, and given the teacher’s fee—
one hundred thousand pieces of gold and various kinds of jewels— (2.1.55).
And a pair of garments for each of the hundred [brahmins], as well as elephants, horses, and a kingdom;
earrings, bracelets, necklaces, and excellent finger-rings.
Having prostrated before him, he should offer a golden sacred thread, or his own wife, or even his daughter, a male slave, a female slave, or his sister. (2.1.57)
Having prostrated with one's whole being, one should offer oneself:
"From this day forward, I am your slave; I have surrendered myself to you. (2.1.58)
Having thus attained the desired state, he should further inform [the deities]:
"Now, the supreme grace of all the Buddhas is present before me. (2.1.59)
Just as I shall accomplish unsurpassed enlightenment through my power,
I shall bring to completion the state of perfect awakening, which is honored above all.
Right there I shall establish all beings who dwell within the three realms of existence.
The consecration should be bestowed according to the ritual by the Sage himself,
having ascertained in his mind the disciple’s inclination.
Or, for one who has faith in the noble and profound method, one should bestow the jewel of consecration with words alone. (2.1.61)
He who has received the consecration, the bearer of the preeminent vajra, possessing rare and incomparable prosperity,
and who has received the consecration of the great bodhicitta for the purpose of grasping the glory of the field of enjoyment.
Having obtained permission, with an intellect prepared for the undertaking of victory over the enemy that is the evil of the three worlds,
the stainless yogi of reality should place the mind upon vast awakening and practice here. (2.1.63)
Thus ends the first section of the second [chapter], the empowerment of the awakening mind (bodhicitta).
Part 2, ap2.65:
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the cultivation of the meaning of wisdom and skillful means.
Truly for the benefit of practitioners who have initiated vigor for the sake of others. || 2.2.1 ||
Having contemplated which, yogins neither remain in cyclic existence— that terrible and difficult-to-cross ocean— nor abide in a nirvana consisting of mere self-interest. (2.2.2)
At the ultimate limit of the excellence of which, for the Buddhas, there arises the stainless,
supramundane, unsurpassed awakening, free from both decrease and increase.
One should not transcend the phenomena such as the five aggregates, nor the three vehicles;
one perceives them as being equal to the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), like a plantain tree. (2.2.4)
One should not practice the meditation on emptiness, nor should one practice the meditation on non-emptiness.
The yogi should not abandon the empty, nor should he reject the non-empty. (2.2.5)
When there is grasping at the non-empty and the empty, a vast conceptualization arises; when there is no intentionality toward their abandonment, one should therefore relinquish this dyad. (2.2.6)
When both forms of grasping have been abandoned, one is liberated and devoid of a basis.
Therefore, one should completely relinquish even this conceptual construction of "I. (2.2.7)
Changeless, free from apprehension, devoid of doubt, and cleansed of impurity,
the wise one should meditate like space, liberated from the conceptualization of beginning and end.
Furthermore, one who possesses compassion should not turn away from sentient beings;
nor should one conceptualize whether a so-called "sentient being" exists or does not exist. (2.2.9)
Wisdom is proclaimed as having the nature of being free from conceptual proliferation; compassion is that which effects the welfare of all sentient beings, like a wish-fulfilling gem. (2.2.10)
In the state that is without support, great compassion is said to be without support;
it becomes one with the intellect, like space merging with space in the sky.
Where there is no one who cultivates, nor indeed any cultivation,
and nothing whatsoever to be cultivated— that is called the cultivation of reality.
And there is no action whatsoever here, nor is there anything to be experienced;
the realization of the ultimate truth is entirely free from both agent and experiencer. (2.2.13)
And here there is no agent of proof, nor is there anyone who presents [the object];
therefore, there is nothing at all to be avoided, nor is there anything to be grasped here. (2.2.14)
It appears like a city of the Gandharvas, resembling an illusion or a mirage;
it is like the city of Hariścandra and like play in a dream.
Just as an illusion is seen and touched from every side, yet no such thing is apprehended, so too is the existence of the entire world. (2.2.16)
In a gathering of inconceivable contact, as in the transition from sleep to waking,
there is a union of both sense-faculties, like that of one possessing the form of a youth. 2.2.17.
Having established the *liṅga* in the *bhaga*, one cultivates the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*).
A certain gnosis arises, stainless in its beginning, middle, and end. (2.2.18)
For that cognition is self-cognizable; it cannot be described in any other way, just as for those who see all forms and hear sounds. (2.2.19)
Even for those who are talking, laughing, or tasting various flavors,
or performing all manner of activities, [the breath does not depart] as long as their minds are not directed elsewhere.
For those yogins who know reality, an unceasing yoga arises.
This is called non-duality; this is the supreme *bodhicitta*. (2.2.21)
The Vajra, Śrīvajrasattva, the Perfectly Awakened One, and Awakening itself—
this is the Perfection of Wisdom, consisting of all the perfections.
And this very equanimity is said to be the supreme cultivation of all Buddhas;
herein alone has arisen the entire world, consisting of both the stable and the moving. (2.2.23)
The infinite Bodhisattvas, the Perfect Buddhas, the Śrāvakas, and the rest—
these very ones the yogi should meditate upon, through being free from both existence and non-existence. (2.2.24)
Freed from both existence and non-existence, one who meditates will quickly attain accomplishment;
he is certainly an adversary to all faults and turns away from affliction.
For him, infinite, glorious, and auspicious qualities are born.
Overwhelmed by the darkness of manifold conceptualizations,
and as flickering as lightning driven by a tempestuous wind;
For the Vajra-holder declared that the mind, when smeared with the difficult-to-restrain impurities of passion and the like, is indeed saṃsāra. (2.2.27)
Luminous, free from conceptual construction, and with the stains of passion and other defilements eliminated.
That very [reality], O Supreme Being, is neither the object of apprehension nor the subject; it is that which he declared to be the supreme nirvāṇa.
And therefore, there is nothing beyond this that serves as the cause for the great mass of suffering.
It is the cause for the arising of infinite happiness; for those seeking liberation, there is nothing beyond this.
By those who have girded their loins for the destruction of all suffering without exception,
and who desire to attain the true bliss of perfect enlightenment;
Having steadied the mind and investigated with effort,
let its nature be made non-existent.
As long as the mind of living beings is obstructed by the heavy veil of ignorance,
so long will there be endless suffering; once it is freed from that, [suffering] shall cease.
Therefore, since there is such noble, incomparable, and supreme happiness for the Noble Ones [in this state],
they themselves will see that vast convergence [of conditions] in order to bring about its cessation. (2.2.32)

Thus, the practitioner of reality (*tattvayogī*), having reached certainty regarding yoga and being authorized, remains established in his own discipline (*svasamaya*) and performs meditation. What would be the use of the common accomplishments produced by ritual gestures (*mudrā*), mantras, images, the cultivation of the divine identity (*ahaṃkāra*), and conventional pledges? For one whose goal is the state of Buddhahood, the objective must be directly realized; the yoga of one’s chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) must be performed. When that objective has arisen, the three worlds become like space. Therefore, having abandoned everything else, the adept—intent on that meditation and yoga which has attained the state—practices throughout day and night, focusing solely on pure awareness (*saṃvedanamātraka*). (2.2.33)

On a mountain peak, in the abode of Śiva, in a lotus garden, or on the shore of the ocean, in a royal garden, in a secluded place, in any location whatsoever, or in one’s own home—wherever the mind finds delight—the knower of mantras, remaining there with enthusiasm, performs the meditation praised by the Omniscient Ones. Without wisdom and means, Buddhahood is certainly not attained directly. Therefore, having abandoned wisdom which bestows perfect enlightenment, one will never grant even a single divine [attainment]; for without this union of the mudrās, there is no accomplishment. Thus, from the arising of primordial wisdom, the mudrās should be employed. (2.2.34)

Delusion is the pledge-seal (samayamudrā); hatred is said to be the great seal (mahāmudrā); envy is the action-seal (karmamudrā); and passion consists of the dharma-seal (dharmamudrā). The yogin should accomplish and worship these various seals, having clearly contemplated the form of both deities as being manifest therein. (2.2.35)

From delusion one becomes tranquilized; from anger one becomes enraged; from rage one becomes impassioned; through passion one performs actions for that purpose. By these five, one becomes a Victor (Jina). 2.2.36.

The yoga of the mudrā should be performed correctly at dawn, at the end of the day, at midday, and at the time of midnight; otherwise, there is no accomplishment. For that yogi who, fearing the disparagement of the teaching, remains among wicked people, he should meditate on his own mind alone through mental resolve, directly. Furthermore, the diligent yogi who here strives properly for yoga should practice constantly even toward animals until direct wisdom is attained. Indeed, if the yogi does not perform the touch of the excellent lotus daily, monthly, or yearly, there occurs a violation of the pledge (*samaya*). From the violation of the pledge, negligence arises regarding the yoga. Having performed the restoration of the Bodhisattva’s pledge, he should again undertake the vow of non-repetition. Therefore, one who abides by the pledge, is endowed with the vow, and is intent upon reality, should perform the secret yoga of the mudrā with substances or with mantras and tantras. Having understood this, sitting always in the yoga of the perfect union (*sampuṭa*), he meditates with one-pointed form upon the inconceivable state of the three worlds. (2.2.37)

Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the miraculous manifestation of all wheels.
The supreme universal manifestation of all the deities, beginning with Śrī Vajrasattva. || 2.3.1 ||
In this supreme and delightful secret, which is the self of all, one should practice accomplishment— either in a secluded place,
or in one’s own garden, and so forth.
But by means of the Viśvamudrā in every respect, through the universal vows (saṃvara) in every respect, one should accomplish all universal activities at will. 2.3.3.
The mandala of all the Tathāgatas is indeed the gnosis of emptiness;
it is the complete means for accomplishing all the wrathful deities as well as the peaceful deities.
What shall I say regarding the inconceivable drama of the Buddha—the sequence of the ritual procedures for the deity-yoga, recitation, and mantras of meditative cultivation? 2.3.5.
Whether it be a cloth painting or an image, everything is a manifestation of the mind;
I have taught this in the tantras out of a desire for the welfare of sentient beings.
The family is said to be fivefold, for all are indeed one in the case of the Śūnyavajrin.
Vajragarbha said:
"O Great Lord of the Radiance of Supreme Rapture, please speak out of your grace."
And [he taught] the color and form of their origin, as well as the sequence of the rules for the arrangement of the arms.
And the ritual procedure for the recitation of mantras, by which practitioners achieve success.
The Blessed One said:
"One should first cultivate loving-kindness, and likewise compassion in the second."
Third, meditating on sympathetic joy, one should finally cultivate equanimity toward all remaining beings. || 2.3.10 ||
Furthermore, in the first [stage] there is the awakening to emptiness; in the second, the gathering of the seed-syllable;
in the third, the accomplishment of the universal image; and in the fourth, the placement of the syllable.
Having visualized the sun in front by means of the syllable *repha*, one should visualize a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*) born from the syllable *hūṃ* within that sun.
And with that very same vajra, one should visualize a rampart and the binding of a cage.
First, the wise one should meditate on the corpse as being of the nature of the *dharmadhātu*; the yogin, standing upon it, should visualize himself as Heruka. (2.3.13)
Within one’s own heart, one should visualize the syllable *repha* (ra), from which arises the solar disk;
right there, one should also visualize the syllable *hūṃ*, whose nature is wisdom and means.

One should again meditate on the reality of the syllable *hūṃ*, black in color and most terrible, arisen from the *vajra* [of the seed-syllable] *hūṃ*, situated in the center of the *vajra*-pericarp. (2.3.15)
Having seen that [seed-syllable] transformed, one should visualize the Great Hero born from the Vajra, who is of the nature of hatred and resembles a blue lotus. (2.3.16)
Alternatively, one should indeed meditate with faith upon the Lord who has the luster of blue and red,
having beheld him in the sky— the Great Compassionate One born from the vajra.
One should worship [the deity] with the eight goddesses, all of whom bear every kind of ornament:
Gaurī, who holds the moon, and Caurī, who holds the vessel of the sun.
Vetālī with a water-pot in her hand, Bhaiṣajyā who holds medicine, Ghasmarī,
Pukkasī with a vajra in her hand, and likewise Śavarī who holds mercury.
The Caṇḍālī sounds the hand-drum, while the Ḍombī embraces his neck;
by these, through the extensive rites of worship, the Lord is fully honored.
Then, it becomes free from syllables and consists of the nature of all phenomena (sarvadharma).
The seed-syllable of Kālī, the Sun, situated in the midst of the row of Moons, shall be present.
They call that very state "sattva," whose nature is supreme bliss;
the radiance of one's own body flashes forth, covering the entire circle of the sky.
The yogi should bring those who are susceptible to being led astray into his heart; he should become one whose nature is characterized by aversion toward them. Thus [ends the section]. 2.3.23.
One should contemplate a solar disc situated in the midst of the space-element (nabhodhātu).
Then, [one should visualize] that which is born from the syllable HŪṂ, possessing a blue and reddish luster, and adorned with all ornaments.
Two-armed, with one face, three eyes, and tawny hair standing erect;
with a wrathful gaze, having the appearance of a sixteen-year-old, and trampled upon by Bhairava. (2.3.25)
In the left [hand] is a vajra-khaṭvāṅga and also a skull-cup;
in the right is a black vajra, consisting of the utterance of the syllable HŪṂ.
The Lord sports in the cremation ground, surrounded by the eight goddesses;
thus the yogi should contemplate this, the supreme nectar of all yoga.
He alone is the Blessed One, Yoga, Vajrasattva, the Tathāgata. (2.3.28)
Assuming a form of wrath, resplendent with four arms,
he is indeed the nature of the four joys through the purification of the four Māras.
Situated within the previously described maṇḍala-cakra, born from the seed-syllable *hūṃ*,
he holds in his left hand a skull-cup filled with the blood of gods and asuras.
In his right [hand] he holds a vajra like a cresting peacock, which strikes fear even into fear itself;
with his other two arms, his body is embraced by Prajñā.
One should meditate on Prajñā as Vajravārāhī, who has the form of the Blessed One. Thus [ends the section]. 2.3.32.
First, one should meditate on the void, partless within the pericarp;
there, one should meditate upon the syllable *hūṃ* situated in the center of the moon-maṇḍala. (2.3.33)

the first face is black, while the right face is white and peaceful.
The left [face], however, is red in color, three-eyed, and of divine form;
it is complete with all ornaments and seated upon a skull-throne.
And holding in his hand a skull containing feces, urine, semen, and blood,
as well as a bow and arrow, and likewise a vajra and a bell.
In the first [hand] is a flame-vajra, and likewise a trident in the third;
glorious, embraced by Prajñā, and adorned with a crown of matted locks.
There, in the center of the bhaga, the practitioner should meditate upon himself as clouds consisting of radiant Buddhas, emitting manifold rays of light and flames. (2.3.38)
Then one should visualize the mudrā conjoined with the deity; moreover,
one should draw the goddesses upon the petals, seated upon skull-thrones.
First, one should draw the auspicious Vidyā, who is beautiful with her manifold forms, having one face and four arms, and holding a bow and arrows. (2.3.40)
In the second [circle],
she holds a skull-cup filled with semen in her hand and grasps a goad; moreover,
she has a trident in her hand and a skull-cup filled with blood.
Likewise, one should draw a vajra-noose in the right compartment;
and one should draw the third goddess in the north, holding a sword in her hand.
Then, one should likewise draw a skull-cup filled with water and a vajra-bell;
next, one should draw the fourth goddess on the western petal.
In her left [hands], she holds a khaṭvāṅga and likewise a skull-cup;
in her right hands, she holds a musuṇḍī and a triple-bannered staff.
The fifth [deity] has a staff in her hand; holding a skull-cup in her hand,
one should likewise draw an utpala lotus and a *ḍamaru* drum in the northeastern corner.
In the northwest corner, one should draw the sixth [deity] with a lotus in hand,
as well as a skull filled with fat, a mirror, and likewise an axe.
In the seventh [position], one should draw Śaktihastā, who holds a conch and a discus as weapons,
and a skull-bowl filled with blood in the south-west corner.
One should draw the eighth goddess in the corner named Agni;
she holds a *bhadrakalaśa* in her hand, as well as a vajra and a bell.
A skull-cup filled with substances and covered with human skin;
having drawn the goddesses upon the petals, one places Mahāsukha in the pericarp.
One should draw various musical instruments in the secret maṇḍala;
likewise, one should draw the gatekeeper and the goddess Vajrāṅkuśī.
One should visualize the vajra-noose, the vajra-chain, and likewise the vajra-bell in the center of the bhaga; thereafter, one should begin the recitation.
The syllable HŪṂ of Vajrasattva, differentiated by the sound of OṂ,
and the syllable ĀḤ joined with speech, resembling pure crystal. (2.3.52)
Having joined the syllable *hrīḥ* there, as well as the syllable *svāhā*,
this is declared to be the mantra for recitation; however, in meditation, it becomes a single-syllabled mantra.
Then, one should place the syllable *hrīḥ* upon the petals of the goddesses,
conjoined with four seed-syllables according to the nature of the fourfold worship.
Combined with the first vowels and so forth, [the practitioner] should place them everywhere upon the female gatekeepers;
thereafter, the adept should indeed insert the vajra into the bhagas.
In that case, one should utter the syllable *hūṃ* and likewise the syllable *hrīḥ*;
with the mouth, one should consume the semen along with blood during the period of menstruation.
One should worship oneself and the bhaga with perfumes and flowers;
if the practitioner desires accomplishment, the recitation (japa) should be performed right here.
Vajraraudrī is likewise one, and Vajrabimbā is just the same;

Part 4 ap2.163 <Sz 3.2.1a→> Listen, O Vajra, according to the rule, especially regarding that which is to be accomplished by means of the wheel.

one should join the name in the middle and cause the protective formula to be placed at the end. || 2.4.4 ||

one should employ it within the protection wheel at the station of the All-Knowing One of Equality.
The wise person should cultivate protection so that fear exists nowhere except at a great distance;
yet, through the non-existence of sentient beings, one should cultivate the state of yoga.
One should contemplate a lotus seat situated in the center of the lunar disc;

Oṃ tāre svāhā. The head.

who has two arms, sits in the sattva-paryaṅka posture, and is adorned with all ornaments. (2.4.9)
With her right hand in the gesture of granting fearlessness and holding a blue lotus in her left,
she should be accomplished through the King of Mantras, impelled by all the gods. (2.4.10)
Oṃ kurukulle hrīḥ svāhā. This is the mantra for all rites. 2.4.11.
The binding of royal enemies, those who administer terrible poisons and the like,
various fevers of the limbs, untimely death, and [the effects of] poison and so forth. (2.4.12)
Wherever there is a place of danger, there one should employ this; a person of dull wit or lacking intelligence should wear this written protection. 2.4.13.
This divine protection is a safeguard that releases one from fear everywhere;
thus is the unsurpassed protection for all, consisting of the reality of yoga. 2.4.14.
Having visualized the solar disc blazing like a mass of rays,
one should contemplate within its center the syllable *hrīḥ*, possessing a radiance equal to the color red.
Then one should meditate upon oneself as having one face and four arms;
[the male deity] holds an arrow and a bow in his hands, while she holds a blue lotus and a goad.
By the mere cultivation of this [mantra], one may bring the three worlds under control;
by one hundred thousand recitations, a king; and by ten thousand, the world of common people.
By means of ten million [recitations], one subdues the animal-spirits (paśu) and yakṣas; by seven hundred thousand, the asuras;
by two hundred thousand, the gods; and by one hundred, the ministers (mantriṇaḥ).
Having visualized this eight-petalled wheel as white in color and most beautiful, with a form that is equanimous by virtue of its nature as the three realms. (2.4.19)
One should accomplish that which is endowed with the previous characteristics by means of what was previously stated;
one should meditate upon her wheel in the rite of blazing wisdom.
Oṃ, O Prajñā, O Mahāprajñā, hūṃ svāhā. 2.4.21.
One should meditate through the state of being as being upon the manifold flames of light rays,
fashioned as the self of wisdom (prajñātman) situated in the center of the lunar mandala.
One should meditate on her as having two arms, seated in the sattva-paryaṅka posture, adorned with all ornaments, possessing a divine white complexion and radiance, and whose essence is wisdom.
By reciting this seed-syllable, wisdom grows like a branch;
for those who are dull-witted or of poor intellect, it serves as a means for increasing wisdom. (2.4.24)
One should place there the syllable situated in the center of the lunar disc,
seated upon a skull-throne, with one face and four arms.
Holding a wheel and a bell, gentle in appearance, and likewise bearing a skull and a noose; he is radiant on all sides and enveloped by garlands of flames.
By this sequential method, one should meditate upon Ratnasambhava,
yellow in color, of great splendor, with a radiance like molten gold.
Seated in the midst of a skull-throne, with one face and four arms,
the Hero holds a jewel and a goad, as well as a skull-cup and a noose.
By this sequential method, one should meditate upon the Lotus-Vajra-holder,
who has one face, four arms, and a radiance equal to a ruby.
The hero, holding a bow and arrows, seated upon a skull-throne,
bearing a lotus and a noose, and adorned with all ornaments.
By this sequential method, [one visualizes] the one who holds an unfailing sword in his hand,
seated in the midst of a skull-throne, with one face and four arms.
He holds a skull-cup, a vajra-bell, and a raised goad in his right hands;
he resembles green beryl and is adorned with all ornaments.
One should indeed contemplate a moon mandala situated in the center of the space-element;
in its center is the seed-syllable *bhrūṃ*, having the form of Locanā.
Seated in the midst of a skull-throne, adorned with eight arms,
[he holds] a discus, a bow, an arrow, a vajra, and likewise a bell in his hands.
He holds a noose, a sword, and a skull-bowl; he has three eyes and one face.
He is complete with all ornaments and adorned with necklaces and anklets. (2.4.35)
She is white in color and most beautiful, likewise adorned with a skull-crest;
she is situated in the midst of the space-element, within a full moon mandala.
Therein, one should contemplate the syllable HŪṂ situated in the center, having the form of Māmakī,
resting in the middle of a skull-seat, blue in color and blazing with great splendor.
Three-eyed and single-faced, adorned with a garland of skulls,
he likewise holds a bow and arrows, as well as a goad and a sword.
The noose-vajra, and likewise the bell and skull-cup;
the wheel, jewel, lotus, and khaṭvāṅga—these are the twelve. (2.4.39)
One should draw the secret maṇḍala, adorned with all ornaments;
one should meditate upon a full moon disc in the center of the bhaga.
One should contemplate there the syllable Hrīḥ and visualize her who is called Pāṇḍarā,
seated in the middle of a skull-throne, red in color and blazing with great splendor.
Complete with all ornaments and adorned with eight arms,
he holds a bow and arrows, as well as a lotus in his hand and a sword.
A skull-cup and a vajra-bell, as well as a noose and a jewel,
resounding with the tinkling of necklaces and anklets, and adorned with all manner of ornaments.
The yogi should meditate on this; he shall swiftly attain Buddhahood.
He should meditate on a full moon disc in the center of the sky. (2.4.44)
Therein, one should contemplate the syllable *tāṃ*, which has the form of a star, situated in the middle of the skull-throne and adorned with eight arms. (2.4.45)
Furthermore, [he holds] a sword in his hand, as well as a lotus, a goad,
a skull-cup filled with blood, a noose, and likewise a wheel.
One should likewise depict him holding a bow and arrows, with one face,
green in color, possessing three eyes, and adorned with all ornaments. (2.4.47)
By meditating in this way, the yogi shall become equal to Vajrasattva. (2.4.48)
From the Secret Source of All Tantras, this is the second king of manuals, the Śrī Sampuṭodbhava.
