The first has twenty-four eyes, while the remaining faces are like bees;
he likewise holds a vajra and a sword, as well as an arrow and a discus.
Likewise, he holds a wine-cup and a staff, as well as a trident and a goad;
in his left hands, he carries a bell with a lotus, and a raised bow and khaṭvāṅga staff.
The skull-cup, the jewel, and likewise the noose of the forefinger,
[are held] by clouds equal to the radiant Buddhas, with various rays of light on all sides.
In such a manner, one should indeed perform the ritual arrangement for Gaurī and the others, and then install them.
Gaurī is fair-complexioned, intent on drawing her bow and arrow,
and likewise holds a skull filled with blood, as well as a vajra and a chisel.
Caurī is red in color and is known to hold a wheel and a goad;
one should place her of divine form, holding a skull-cup and a *ḍamaru* drum.
Prāmohā is black in color; she holds a skull-cup and a drinking vessel,
and her right hand raises a trident used for lifting up the earth.
Vetālī, possessing a white-yellow luster and beautiful form, should be visualized holding a liquor-filled vessel and a skull-cup in her two hands.
Pukkasī is yellow in color; likewise, there is the Kalpavṛkṣa creeper, a skull-bowl filled with flesh, and the jewel-granting gesture. 3.1.24.
Caṇḍālī is blue in complexion and likewise wears a garment of wind;
with her other two [hands], she holds a skull-cup and a white lotus.
Ghasmarī is greenish-yellow in luster; she holds a vajra, a fire-pit, and an axe in her hands,
and in her right hand she holds a skull filled with fat while granting protection.
Śavarī has a white complexion and holds a khaṭvāṅga and a skull-cup in her hands;
one should likewise visualize her holding a vajra and a noose— these goddesses who possess manifold forms.
Rohita, Varāha, Kūrma, and Uraga,
as well as Siṃha, Vyāghra, Jambuka, and Ṛkṣa.
In this manner, for Gaurī and the others, [the worship] is performed according to rule upon eight sacrificial dishes;
she is adorned with all ornaments and endowed with the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa) and the rest.
Hayāsyā, Śūkarāsyā, Śvānāsyā, and likewise Siṃhinī—
each four-armed and four-faced, adorned with ornaments of serpents.
Vaṃśa, Vīṇā, Mukundā, and likewise Murajā—
each having two arms and one face, and adorned with all ornaments. (3.1.31)
The one with black, white, and yellow lusters likewise has an upward-facing green horse-head;
the one with yellow, black, and white lusters likewise has an upward-facing red boar-head.
Having red, black, and white lusters, with a yellow upper canine-like face;
likewise, having green, black, and white faces, and a blazing upward-facing lion’s head.

All [the goddesses] have blazing hair standing erect, stand in the *pratyālīḍha* posture treading upon corpses, possess three eyes, and should be meditated upon with faces smiling with wrathful passion (*krodha-śṛṅgāra*). Thus [ends section 3.1.34].
Thus ends the first chapter of the third [section], concerning the arising of Heruka.
Part 2, ap3.37: Listen, O Lord Vajra, to the king’s *sādhana* of the Jñānaḍākinī.
It is free from the state of duality for those who possess the knowledge of non-dual phenomena. 3.2.1
Having first recited the three purifications in all yogas and other practices,
All phenomena are pure by nature; I am pure by nature. All phenomena are pure as a vajra; I am pure as a vajra.
All phenomena are pure through yoga; I am pure through yoga. || 3.2.2 ||
Having done this, the yogi should again practice meditation upon that very [object];
then he should begin his meditation in places conducive to the mind. (3.2.3)
A canopy was spread out, with various garments hanging down;
banners and flags were raised on all sides from ten locations.
And with a mass of fragrant flowers and likewise a mandala of perfumes,
one should contemplate one’s own body through the yoga of instantaneous visualization.
The wise one should maintain [the practice] with Jñānaḍākinī preceded by worship;
in this manner, one should indeed contemplate the ocean of knowledge according to the prescribed ritual procedure. 3.2.6.
Having visualized on the summit of Mount Meru the four castes in every direction,
[one should meditate upon] that which has arisen from a golden palace and is variegated with the seven precious gems.
Moreover, one should visualize a garland of networks of tinkling bells extending in every direction at will, as well as a lion throne with five locations. 3.2.8.
Having visualized the solar disk adorned with a white parasol,
one should cause Jñānaḍākinī to emerge from the center by means of one's own breath.
Three-faced and six-armed, seated in the sattvaparyaṅka posture,
adorned with disheveled hair and embellished by the five Buddhas.
Blue in color, Mahāghorī is adorned with ornaments of serpents;
laughing, she possesses the sentiments of wrath and passion, has three eyes, and a divine form.
Aṭṭahāsī is indeed Karālī, beautifully adorned with red garments;
she holds a khaṭvāṅga staff aloft in her first hand and an axe in the second.
In the third [hand] there is a vajra, and likewise in the left one there is a bell;
in the second [right hand] there is a vessel, and in the third there is a sword.
The wise one should meditate on the flame of the rays in manifold ways as being in the center;
it has issued forth from the self-breath by means of Jñānaḍākinī in the east. (3.2.14)
She was white-complexioned and most beautiful, adorned with disheveled hair,
decorated with ornaments of serpents, and imbued with the sentiments of love and the rest.
One should visualize Vajraḍākinī as being most beautiful, adorned with garments and ornaments, radiant with two arms, and holding a khaṭvāṅga staff and a yogic bowl.

In the northern part of Jñāna, one should visualize [the goddess] seated upon a lion in the sattva posture, possessing two arms, with a radiance like molten gold, and absorbed in the breath of the Self.
She holds a skull-topped staff and a yogic bowl, adorned with disheveled hair;
her body is decorated with serpent ornaments and beautifully radiant garments.
One should meditate upon her by the name Ghoradākinī.
In the western part of Jñāna, Vettālī has emerged;
she again has two arms, sits upon a corpse in the sattva posture, is blue in color, and is most beautiful.
She was adorned with a skull-topped staff and a yogic bowl, her hair disheveled,
her body decorated with serpent ornaments, and beautifully arrayed in exquisite garments.
To the right side of Jñāna is Caṇḍālinī, red in hue,
adorned with disheveled hair, and holding a khaṭvāṅga staff and a yogic vessel.
The yogi, possessing a complete and radiant form, should meditate upon her as having two arms and one face, adorned with various ornaments. (3.2.22)
In the northeast, one should visualize the goddess Siṃhinī with a lion’s face;
she has a white and yellow luster and is seated in the ālīḍha posture upon the king of nāgas.
One should meditate upon her, beautifully adorned with the vajra, the goad, the threatening gesture, and the noose as her ornaments,
her body blazing with manifold rays of light.
In the southeast is the one named Vyāghrī, seated upon a throne of the seven supreme jewels;
she has two arms, possesses a blue-white luster, and is adorned with garments and ornaments.
One should visualize her with a blazing vajra-hook and likewise a threatening mudrā with a noose;
her body is ablaze with manifold rays of light.
In the southwest is the goddess Jambukī, who laughs boisterously and is terrifying;
she is seated upon a buffalo and is red and black in color.
With limbs beautifully adorned with garments, he shines with two arms;
he is decorated with ornaments of serpents and holds a goad, a noose, and a threatening gesture.
In the northwest is the goddess Ulūka, yellowish-red in color;
one should provide her with a serpent as a seat upon which she sits, and likewise fashion ornaments for her.
One should visualize her with two arms, seated upon a being (sattva), holding a goad, a noose, and a threatening gesture, her body ablaze with manifold rays of light. (3.2.30)
The eight ḍākinīs are in the center, while the fourth group belongs to those on the outside.
Having observed this sequence of placement (*nyāsa*), one should thereafter determine the locations. (3.2.31)
In the east is Dākinīrājendrī, two-armed and white in color;
she sits upon a corpse-throne and is adorned with ornaments of snakes.
Having cast into his mouth that blazing, fierce weapon with disheveled hair, which possessed a radiance equal to the flames of fire,
he likewise let out a loud, roaring laugh.
In the north is Dīpinī, the queen of kings, yellow in color and fierce;
she is Karālī, of terrible form, yet beautifully adorned with garments and ornaments.
The deceased is seated upon a seat, possessing a radiance equal to a blazing fire;
with two hands joined in the añjali gesture, the head is raised like a lamp.
In the west is the goddess Cūṣiṇī, red in color and terrifying; she sits upon a corpse-seat, adorned with most beautiful garments and ornaments. (3.2.36)
One should drink blood from the hands with a red thread and a hollowed palm;
she is the goddess of the Lord, fierce, possessing the radiance of a blazing fire, and a drinker [of blood]. 3.2.37.
In the south, there is one named Kambojī, possessing a luster equal to the color black;
she sits upon a corpse-seat, adorned with disheveled hair.
She is beautifully adorned with red garments and decorated with ornaments of serpents;
holding a threatening gesture and a trident in her hands, she causes the delusion of all minds.
The omniscient one should always meditate upon Raudrī, who has the radiance of a flame of fire;
likewise, he should demonstrate the pledge (samaya) of the foremost [deity] through these forms and so forth. 3.2.40.
For the purpose of pacifying wind and fire, one should impel [the breath] with the seed-syllable of Vajrī;
when it is pervaded by Bindu and Nāda, it is known as "the raining down of a stream. (3.2.41)
Apastamba Śrauta Sūtra 3.80:
The Second Section of the Third Book.
Part 3, ap3.81:
Now I shall explain the proof of selflessness in brief, as it has been taught.
One should contemplate a solar mandala situated in the center of the space-element.
First, according to the proper rule, he [placed] the wheel of the deities according to their arising;
first, according to the proper rule, the wheel of the earth, water, and fire.
For the deities, there is the Great Wind as the manifestor according to its arising;
it is the wheel born from the Source of Phenomena (dharmodaya), consisting of two enclosures, pure and free from affliction.
With the filaments [of the lotus], one should visualize a single Vajrin of the supreme three bodies,
as well as a corpse, endowed with fifteen seats.
Above that, there should be the moon; above the moon, the seed-syllable.
Afterwards, the sun is superimposed [upon it], the great bliss of the union of the two. (3.3.5)
Sthitāli is in the form of the moon, and Bhāskara is in the form of Kālī;
the union of the moon and sun is proclaimed as Gaurī and the others. || 3.3.6 ||

The moon possesses mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*), and the sun possesses the sevenfold wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*); the seed-syllables and the insignia of one’s own deity are said to be the wisdom of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇajñāna*). (3.3.7)

3.88. Through the purification that brings about the manifestation of the image, the wise practitioner should perform a single practice with all [the deities], meditating upon the five forms according to the methods described.
The union of *āli* and *kāli* is the expansion of Vajrasattva; for the mass arising from the syllables, the utterances *hūṃ* and *phaṭ* are not desired. (3.3.9)
One should visualize the Lord of the Mandala, arisen from the reflection of the sentient being,
as before, with his faces, symbols, and so forth, possessing the luster of a moonstone gem. (3.3.10)
Thus, everything is entirely perfected by way of the nature of wisdom and means; for wisdom is Kālī and means is the Moon, due to the differentiation of the Sun and Moon. (3.3.11)
Since Gaurī and the others constitute the various distinct classes [of goddesses],
the mandala-deities should therefore be envisioned with every effort. (3.3.12)
And these five yoginīs reside within the internal chamber; the knower of yoga should always meditate upon them as having the nature of the five aggregates. 3.3.13.
In the east is Vajrā, in the south Gaurī, in the west Vāriyoginī,
in the north Vajraḍākinī, and in the center Nairātmayoginī.
In the outer enclosure (apara-puṭa):
Gaurī, Caurī, Vetālī, Ghasmarī, and likewise Pukkasī.
Śavarī, Caṇḍālī, Ḍombī, and the eight Pūraṇīs.
Furthermore, the upward-moving, the sky-farer, and the earth-farer are traditionally taught;
that path which exists as the very nature of both worldly existence and liberation.
They belong to all the deities;
they possess all colors, are exceedingly fierce, and are adorned with the five mudrās.
They have one face, four arms, and three eyes, and possess divine forms. || 3.3.17 ||
The wheel, the earring, the necklace, the bracelet, and the girdle in the hand—
these five are the pure mudrās through the purification of the five Buddhas.
All these are described as being like Nairātmyayoginī;
she holds a yogic vessel in her left hand, and likewise an upright khaṭvāṅga staff.
In the south, there is a blue vajra and likewise a flaying knife;
she is mounted upon a corpse, blazing with light, red-eyed, and has tawny hair standing erect.
Bluish-black in color, most divine, her hips draped in a tiger skin,
resembling the fire of universal dissolution, she stands there in a celestial form.
In the south she is yellowish-blue, while in the north she has a reddish-blue luster;
she has two arms and one face, and is adorned with all ornaments.
With one hand occupied with a skull-bowl and holding a ritual knife in the right,
laughing and manifesting both wrath and erotic passion, she assumes the form of that worship.

The wise one should meditate upon the central [deity], whose nature consists of the three principles (tritattva), surrounded on all sides by clouds resembling shimmering Buddhas and various rays of light. 3.3.24.
Ap 3.105: The third section of the third [book].
Part 4, ap3.106:
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme great maṇḍala.
Having the same form as the Vajradhātu, it is known as the Vajradhātu. || 3.4.1 ||
Having purified the site of the mandala and undertaken the great mudrā, the mantra-practitioner should accomplish all this while gazing upon it. 3.4.2.
The wise one should trace out the mandala with a new, well-prepared, correctly measured, and beautiful thread, according to his ability.
It is square, with four doors, well-illuminated by archways,
provided with four lines, and adorned with silk ribbons, garlands, and hanging wreaths.
In all the corner sections and at the junctions of the doors and projections,
one should trace the outer maṇḍala, inlaid with jewels and vajras.
Having entered its inner city, which resembles a wheel,
it is encircled by a diamond thread and adorned with eight pillars.
Upon the tips of the vajra-pillars, adorned with the five mandalas, one should then place the image of the Buddha in the center of the mandala. 3.4.7.
The procedure for the maṇḍala has been explained; now I shall tell you the means of accomplishment (sādhana). Ap 3.114.

There, having first entered the temple, the practitioner (mantrin), having visualized a moon disc by means of the syllable *A*, and having visualized a white five-pronged vajra upon it, worships and prostrates to all the Tathāgatas and others according to the ritual procedure, and speaks as follows: || 3.4.8 ||
May all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas attend to me! I, [name], from this moment until I sit upon the seat of enlightenment,
generate the supreme, unsurpassed mind of awakening.
Just as the Lords belonging to the three times have made their resolve for perfect enlightenment. || 3.4.9 ||
I firmly undertake the threefold training in ethical discipline, the gathering of wholesome qualities,
and the ethical discipline of acting for the benefit of sentient beings.
From this day forward, I shall undertake the vow born of the Buddha-yoga toward the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha— the unsurpassed, supreme Triple Gem.
I shall truly accept the vajra, the bell, and the mudrā;
and I shall accept the master within the exalted assembly of the Great Vajra Family.
I shall bestow the fourfold gift six times every day,
within the noble Mahāratnakula, at the appropriate and delightful time.
I receive the True Dharma— outer, secret, and belonging to the three vehicles—
within the pure Mahāpadma family, which gives birth to great awakening.
I accept the vow joined with all [beings] from every side,
performing acts of worship according to my ability within the exalted assembly of the Great Karma Family.
Having generated the supreme, unsurpassed mind of awakening,
and having undertaken the complete vow for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings.
I shall ferry across those who have not crossed; I shall liberate those who are not liberated;
I shall give rest to those who are weary; I shall establish all sentient beings in nirvana.

Then the Blessed One entered the meditative absorption named "The Source of the Foremost of All Vajra-Holders" and uttered this inspired utterance: ap3.124 atha bhagavān sarvavajradharāgrasaṃbhavaṃ nāma samādhiṃ samāpadyedam udānam udānayām āsa || 3.4.18 ||

Then, remaining in the abode of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one should thoroughly perceive the selflessness of all phenomena (*sarvadharmanairātmya*). Having mentally recited: "All this—whether external or internal—is conceptualized by the mind; nothing exists apart from the mind," [one reflects that] "all phenomena are unarisen and naturally luminous because they are primordially unarisen. Then, one should behold that very mind of one's own as having the form of a lunar disc by means of this mantra, which is naturally luminous and recited according to one’s inclination: *oṃ cittaprativedhaṃ karomi*. (3.4.19)
The great, pure sphere of density is stainless like the sky;
it is completely free from all mental distress and is supreme in removing conceptual construction.
Purified from all the stains of the afflictions, it is seen to be like the moon;
for all the qualities of a Buddha enter into this in the form of the letters beginning with *a*.
a ā i ī u ū ṛ ṝ ḷ ḹ e ai o au aṃ aḥ || 3.4.22 ||
"O Blessed One, what kind of qualities does the lunar disc possess? [3.4.23]
The Blessed One said:
"A triangle of noble form, the abode of all the qualities of the Buddhas."

These qualities of the Buddha, entering in the form of the syllable *a* and others, resemble a crystal moon. They enter for the purpose of expanding the mind that is naturally luminous (*prakṛtiprabhāsvaracitta*). With this mantra, the practitioner of mantra should generate the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*):
*Oṃ, I generate the thought of awakening.* (3.4.24)
Arising from the inclination toward action, it brings benefit to sentient beings;
it is perfected by wholesome qualities and crushes all afflictions. (3.4.25)
In the center of the lunar disc, however, is the second moon of awakening.

Here too, the qualities of the Buddha enter in the form of the syllable *tāra* by means of the method of reflection (*pratibimba-yoga*) in the form of the letters beginning with *ka*: *ka kha ga gha ṅa ca cha ja jha ña ṭa ṭha ḍa ḍha ṇa ta tha da dha na pa pha ba bha ma ya ra la va śa ṣa sa ha kṣaḥ*.

This entire procedure for the mandala has not been taught in other tantras. Therein, in the center, for the sake of strengthening the generation of the mind of Samantabhadra, one should visualize oneself as a vajra-form, white with five prongs and emitting rays, by means of this mantra:
*Oṃ tiṣṭha vajra*. (3.4.28)
The ground for that unsurpassed conduct of awakening is this easily understood, pure, and untainted knowledge. (3.4.29)
Furthermore, one should visualize a vajra within the center of the lunar disk.
The mantra practitioner should visualize himself as a vajra-body, equal in extent to the entire realm of space. (3.4.31)
By means of this mantra, through the yoga of emanation and reabsorption: Oṃ, I am of the nature of the Vajra. (3.4.32)
Among all the Buddhas, that body which is without appearance, without abode, unborn, uncreated, pure, and free from non-existence and the like— || 3.4.33 ||
The Dharma-body, which is indestructible, indivisible, and ungraspable, and which is free from the basis of rebirth—
having thus arisen as having the nature of a vajra, it is the unsurpassed Vajra-body.
Again [he asked]: "O Blessed One, what should I meditate upon as that vajra?"
The Blessed One said: "Listen, all Tathāgatas! Furthermore, one should meditate upon the image of the Buddha as Vajrasattva, endowed with the excellence of all aspects, by means of this mantra:
Oṃ, as are all Tathāgatas, so am I. (3.4.36)

The secret of the body, as well as conduct, the sphere of activity, and the awakening to reality— the auspicious [state] consisting of the nature of all Buddhas through the fivefold manifest enlightenment. (3.4.37)
Then the great bodhisattvas, headed by Vajragarbha, again addressed the Blessed One as follows:
“Blessed One, what is the name of this secret vajra-lotus family?”
The Blessed One said:
"The vajra resides among all the Tathāgatas; the lotus family is conjoined with the Great Goddess."
That vajra is situated upon a lotus; from it, all the Tathāgatas emerge. || 3.4.39 ||
Aitareya Āraṇyaka 3.144

Having thus transformed oneself into Vairocana and having placed the mantra-syllables above and below, one should duly produce Mount Sumeru, triangular in shape, of noble form, and adorned with a variegated mandala of light. Having visualized that beautiful world-system arisen, one should contemplate within it a universal lotus and sun-mandala produced from the syllable *paṃ*, joined by wind and fire mandalas, and embellished by the syllables *ya*, *ra*, and *la*. Then, upon that, by means of the mantra itself, one should meditate on a gabled temple (*kūṭāgāra*) with a pinnacle of vajras and jewels, blazing with the light of great mani-gems, its various colors praised and extolled by the invocation of all the Tathāgatas; it is hung with bells, and adorned by wind-swaying silk banners, streamers, garlands, necklaces, half-necklaces, and the moon. [One should do so] with this mantra: *Hūṃ*. (3.4.40)

Having placed this mantra upon the moon-maṇḍala of one’s own heart, one should meditate on it as being enveloped by a vajra. One should emanate a five-pronged vajra and repeatedly withdraw all the Buddhas. Then, Vajrasattva himself—enveloped by that very same vajra, endowed with the excellence of all forms, and possessing a radiance equal to the color of the moon—[appears]. (3.4.41)
Seated upon the lunar disc, adorned with all ornaments,
the hero holds the vajra and bell, uniquely beautiful through the bliss of wisdom. (3.4.42)
A sword, a goad, and likewise a skull-topped staff and a noose—
these are in his right hands; the one on the right is black in color, while the one on the left has a reddish luster.
One should meditate upon the circle of deities in union as having three faces, six arms, and three eyes, possessing a divine form, and seated upon the lotus of one's own vidyā. (3.4.44)
One should visualize [the deity] endowed with the excellence of all aspects from the maṇḍala. 3.4.45.
In the east is Vairocana; in the south is Ratnasambhava.
In the west is Amitābha;
in the north is Amoghasiddhi. 3.4.46.
In the northeast is Locanā;
in the southeast is Māmakī.
Pāṇḍaravāsinī is in the southwest; Tārā is in the northwest. 3.4.47.
In the outer enclosure, [in the east], Raudrī is white in color.
In the south is Vajrabimbā, yellow in color;
in the west is Rāgavajrā, with a red luster; in the north is Vajrasaumyā, with a green luster. 3.4.48.
In the northeast is Vajrayakṣī, with a white-yellow luster;
in the southeast is Vajraḍākinī, with a yellow-red luster.
In the southwest is Śabdavajrā, red and blue in hue;
in the northwest is Pṛthivīvajrā, green and white in hue. (3.4.49)
In the outer enclosure, in the northeast, is Vaṃśā.
In the southeast is Vīṇā;
in the southwest is Mukundā; in the northwest is Murajā. 3.4.50.
The deities beginning with Vaṃśā have two arms and one face. (3.4.51)
On the outer band, those yoginīs who bear the marks of flowers and so forth should be stationed, likewise with two arms. (3.4.52)

At the eastern gate, one should draw the goddess Vajrāṅkuśī, with a complexion dark as the sky, her right and left faces black and white respectively. In her first right hand she holds a goad, in the second an upraised sword, and in the third a wheel. In her left hands she holds a noose, a threatening gesture, and a bell; she has six arms. (3.4.53)

At the southern gate is the Mother Vajrapāśī, white and yellow in luster, with faces that are black and red on the right and left respectively. Her six arms are raised, holding a noose, a vajra, and a sword in the right hands, and a wheel, a bell, and a threatening gesture with a noose in the [left] hands. (3.4.54)

At the western gate is Vajrasphoṭā, red in color and of great luster, with faces that are black, white, and yellow on the right and left respectively; she has six arms, holding a chain, a vajra, a sword, a wheel, a bell, and a goad. (3.4.55)
At the northern gate is Vajraghaṇṭā, who is terrifying and has three faces— green, black, and white— with six arms holding a bell, a vajra, a sword, a wheel, a goad, and a noose.
All [the goddesses] should be stationed upon a solar mandala marked by a universal lotus, with their hair blazing upward. || 3.4.57 ||
Beginning from the southeastern direction, those yoginīs who bear the marks of flowers and so forth are considered to have two arms according to their fixed arrangement. (3.4.58)
In the eastern and other doors are the Yoginīs holding a hook, a noose, a chain, and a bell in their hands. Thus it is said: "endowed with the door-keepers. (3.4.59)

*Jaḥ*, *hūṃ*, *vaṃ*, and *hoḥ*—these are undoubtedly the designations for their hearts. Thus, even in the form of cast or engraved [images], they are endowed with symbolic seals (*mudrā*); this is the outer maṇḍala of Śrī Vajrasattva. (3.4.60)
As before, with half of that [measurement], inside it, there is a wind-maṇḍala in the shape of a crescent moon, adorned with eight pillars and surrounded on the outside by four lines. || 3.4.61 ||

In all the stations of the deities, one should arrange the seats for Gaurī and the others as previously described. Therein, in the center, one should visualize the syllable *hrīḥ*. One should place the syllable *hrīḥ* in its eastern compartment; *hiḥ* in the south; *gīḥ* in the west; *jiḥ* in the north; *taṃ* in the southeast; *jaṃ* in the southwest; *maṃ* in the northwest; and *haṃ* in the northeast. (3.4.62)
In the outer mandala: one should place the syllable Oṃ in the southeast corner, the syllable Aṃ in the southwest, the syllable Eṃ in the northwest, and the syllable Aiṃ in the northeast. (3.4.63)
One should place the syllable *jaḥ* at the eastern gate, *hūṃ* at the southern, *vaṃ* at the western, and *hoḥ* at the northern. 3.4.64.

Likewise, the nose is the envy-vajra, and the mouth is known as the passion-vajra;
the sense of touch is the stinginess-vajra, while Heruka, the Supreme Lord, is all the sense bases and elements.
The earth element is known as Pātanī, and the water element is remembered as Māraṇī; the fire element is Ākarṣaṇī, and likewise Vāyu is Narteśvarī. (5.2.56)
The space element has been described in the *Padmajvālinī* as being undisturbed;
thus, the body of embodied beings consists of the deities of the aggregates and so forth. (5.2.57)
Likewise, pleasure and pain, as well as karma and the afflictions, arise for the sake of rebirth;
by relying on the portion of rebirth, one attains both cyclic existence and nirvana.
Thus ends the second section of the fifth chapter: the purification of the aggregates and the sense-bases.
Part 3, ap5.84:
Now, the correct conduct that destroys the enemies of the ritual manual is fully explained.
The unsurpassed practice of reality arises from all phenomena.
For the benefit of the sons of the Buddha who are established in perfect enlightenment, the supreme Perfection of Wisdom is, in reality, the Anaṅgavajra. 5.3.2 ||
She is the boat that carries all sentient beings across the most terrible ocean of birth, which is agitated by the waves of old age and other afflictions, leading them to a state of safety.
Bringing swift accomplishment, divine, heart-pleasing, and the abode of all virtues,
she is born from the jewel of the mind and fulfills all desired aims.
Without this [wisdom], which is praised by the Holder of the Vajra and constitutes the very limbs of all the qualities of a perfectly awakened Buddha, [one cannot attain enlightenment].
Therefore, accomplishment is not born; hence, the wise who desire liberation should practice this incomparable conduct. 5.3.5
Those whose lotus-feet are worshipped by Murāri, Śakra, the enemy of Tripura (Śiva), the Giver of Wealth (Kubera), Brahmā, and others;
Having swiftly practiced this path that destroys evil,
the Tathāgatas have attained the supreme state.
This very practice of the Avadhūta has been taught by the illustrious Vajrasattva, who acts for the welfare of the world. (5.3.7)
In this way, the yogi should meditate upon the divine, inconceivable state that is well-guarded as a secret;
he performs the conduct of the pledge (samayācāra), free from all conceptual construction.
Established at the initial commencement [of practice], the yogi exists in the form of the outflow fruit (*niṣyandaphala*);
thereafter, he should bring to an end the childish play of withdrawing [the mind] through the dissolution of cultivation. || 5.3.9 ||
In order to discipline various types of people, he himself may appear in a beautiful form. (5.3.10)
All the aforementioned accomplishments are established,
including the unsurpassed one, through various modes of conduct.
"The practice for the incomparable accomplishment of Samantabhadra is that very same one," so the Blessed Vajrin declared. 5.3.11
Having prostrated in every way before the Lord, the glorious Ācārya-Vajrin,
the high-minded one who has accomplished his purpose should then take recourse in the secret conduct. 5.3.12
Then, having become autonomous and turned away from all attachments,
one whose self is united with reality should wander everywhere like a lion. (5.3.13)
One who perceives the reality of things as they truly are, whose intention is to uplift the world, whose self is engaged in right view, firm of mind, and free from dependence. (5.3.14)

Having understood in this way, in brief, that all this triple world characterized by the aggregates, elements, and so forth, is like a dream and an illusion, [one realizes the nature of reality]. (5.3.15)
The union with the conduct [of the bodhisattvas] consists of lives completely liberated from all obscurations;
likewise, it involves casting all eight worldly dharmas far away.
Always remaining free from conceptual construction, having made a firm resolve beyond dualities,
one should practice through the yoga of the six perfections for the sake of attaining the accomplishment of Buddhahood.
Devoted to the welfare of sentient beings with extraordinary zeal, yet not conceptualizing them as real entities,
one should fix the mind upon awakening and begin the practice of the conquest of the directions. (5.3.18)

One whose self is well-yoked with wisdom and skillful means, who has turned away from all attachments, and who has exerted effort in the practice of reality, shall achieve accomplishment in this very life. (5.3.19)
5.103 Completely free from all conceptual constructions, yet due to the particular dispositions of sentient beings,
one should indeed enjoy everything by means of the yoga of the illusion-like and other [analogies]. 5.3.20 ||
Since nothing arises as an obstacle for one who has emerged from the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu),
one should enjoy [the objects] at will with a mind free from apprehension. 5.3.21
All this triple world, without exception, has been emanated by Vajrasattva for the sake of enjoyment and for the benefit of practitioners. 5.3.22
Having attained infinite knowledge, one should indeed pay homage to the Tathāgatas;
being constantly engaged in meditative cultivation, what need is there to mention [the merit gained from] pouring water and other such acts?
This nature of all phenomena is, by its very essence, the nature of bodhicitta; that itself is the Blessed One, the Vajra-holder. Therefore, one’s own self is indeed the deity. (5.3.24)
Neither the mandala, nor the fast, nor the mudrās, nor the rites for the caityas—
whatever else has been shown by the glorious Vajranātha;
Some [act] by the power of resolute conviction; and do those who possess such [conviction] know reality? (5.3.25)
Just as one seeking nectar would discard the buttermilk after extracting its essence,
so too, having attained the nectar of Dharma, one should abandon all conceptual constructions without remainder.
When the wise one is free from conceptual construction, having abandoned all doubt and being without support,
then there is accomplishment without a doubt, according to the words of the Mind-Vajra.
Through conceptual construction, one goes to hell and wanders in the ocean of the saṃsāra of the six realms; yet,
when liberated from such construction, one is freed from kalpas and attains the stainless, peaceful state.

Therefore, those commitments (samaya) which were established by the Buddha in order to destroy the web of conceptual construction (vikalpajāla) must be practiced constantly; for it is by means of them that one truly becomes established in the commitments.
One who knows the mantra should not be excessively attached to any phenomena;
indeed, all things should be viewed through the yoga of the aspect of non-arising. (5.3.30)
Having drunk the blood of dogs, donkeys, camels, elephants, and so forth, one should constantly eat their flesh;
in order to perceive every particularity, one should consume great meat smeared with blood. (5.3.31)

The entire mass of loathsome flesh, joined with hundreds of thousands of living beings, is divine; it is the exceedingly putrid Vairocana, making a *simasima* sound as it is swarmed by hundreds of insects. (5.3.32)
Flesh mixed with the vomit of dogs and men, joined with vajra-water and flies, and blended with Vairocana, should be consumed by the yogins with enthusiasm. (5.3.33)
Having drunk the vajra-water, when there is no longer any flesh anywhere, one consumes other food that has taken on the form of the flesh of another, as a conceptualized flesh. 5.3.34.

"5.118. Those things which in the world are inedible by others are edible for the Lord of Reality; those who are unapproachable are approachable; those acts which are forbidden are to be performed by him. The practitioner of mantra should not entertain distinctions between the approachable and the unapproachable, nor between the edible and the inedible, nor between the undesirable and the desirable, nor between the drinkable and the undrinkable. (5.3.35)

5.119 One becomes equal in body, speech, and mind, so that there may be no mental distraction whatsoever. The yogi should always consume intoxicants in such a manner. Whether it be loathsome, excessively playful, beautiful, or ugly, whether afflicted by disease, or miserable—one should view all things like a Jina, as having a single uniform nature. (5.3.36)

One should not recite from a book, nor construct a mandala, nor gather flowers; one should not perform mantra-recitation, and deities, images, and so forth are not to be worshipped. One should speak untruths and consort with the wives of others. One should show friendliness toward the wicked, and living beings should be killed as Buddhas. (5.3.37)

The wise one should always worship the teacher who is honored by the Jinas, the pledge of gnosis, the foremost of beings, and the source of various accomplishments. For whatever merit belongs to the perfectly awakened ones and bodhisattvas residing in the ten directions is seen to reside at the tip of a single pore of the teacher; therefore, through the worship of the teacher, the bodhisattvas and the Buddhas are pleased. 5.3.38

5.122 Indeed, the Buddhas of one’s own tradition surely bestow the desired realization. One should not engage in disparaging the gurus, nor show disrespect toward one’s vajra-brothers. Whatever is given should be accepted; yet one should not perform prostrations before a shrine (caitya). Viewing even one’s brothers, sons, father, kingdom, enjoyments, treasures, wealth, and grain as being like a blade of grass, one should accomplish the sovereignty over the three realms. 5.3.39
Chapter 3 of the fifth [section]: Conduct; Embracing the Fifth.
Part 4, ap5.124:
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the characteristics of one who has reached the further shore of conduct. || 5.4.1 ||
By which one is known from afar as a Vajrayogin, there is no doubt; [he offers] the bali-offering to the ḍākinīs and others, as well as food and drink as they are obtained. (5.4.2)
Wearing a loincloth made of a corpse’s garment and adorned with the ashes of the dead, well-concealed in a broken clay bowl, he should wander about at night.
At a crossroads, on mountains, at a solitary tree, or in a cremation ground, as well as at public squares—
thereafter, the auspicious meditative visualization for the practitioner is described.
Likewise, in a mother’s house, at night, or in a secluded wilderness,
when some warmth has arisen, if one desires to perform the practice: || 5.4.5 ||
If one desires the realization of the self, one should again practice the state of a child;
the one of great intelligence should wander about for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.
With a mind free from obstruction, he is always adorned with beautiful garments;
[rays] issue forth from the openings at the tips of his pores into the ten directions.
Mañjuvajra himself, having become [the central deity], should fashion the members of the maṇḍala in delightful lotus gardens and at the confluences of rivers. (5.4.8)
Established there, the yogi should practice meditation; he quickly attains accomplishment.
Whether in a cave or on a mountain peak, he should dwell with a perfectly concentrated mind.
As it was obtained, so it was eaten; having eaten and not having eaten, one should offer the *bali*.
Likewise, with various fruits such as the *hāra* and others, and with [offerings] fashioned from *guñjā* seeds and the like. (5.4.10)
Seeking happiness, one should cause a garment made from animal parts to provide comfort;
at times, one should recite both the refined (Sanskrit) and the vernacular (Prakrit) in reverse order.

One should consume whatever is obtained as edible or inedible through the practice of the "insane" yoga (unmattayoga), whether in foreign kingdoms, in perfected mountain caves and groves, in the primordially perfected great cremation grounds, or on the shores of the great ocean.
Established therein, the wise one should meditate, free from all fear.
Having done this, the yogi should again commence the conquest of the directions.
Completely liberated from all obscurations, he fulfills all hopes for those situated in the ten directions who are veiled by the obscuration of birth.
Devoid of all conceptualization regarding the grasped and the grasper, and utterly free [from them], one who has abandoned all such conceptualizations is called a "world-conqueror. (5.4.15)
Having thus first stabilized himself in the yoga of reality, the unstruck yogi brings about the gathering of the goddesses of knowledge, making them into passionate women of exceeding beauty. 5.4.16.
He beheld the delightful Apsarases, the jewels among women, and likewise the wives of Vidyādharas,
Suras, Yakṣas, Nāgas, and Asuras.
Among these, the yogi should select one vidyā that is pleasing to his own mind and accomplish it by means of the application of the hook and the noose.
Because the deity bestows all objects of utility effortlessly, [the beings] are free from disease and old age, beyond the pairs of opposites, and blameless throughout the three worlds. (5.4.19)
Having given the gift of the body, one should thereafter undertake the practice;
therefore, no gift is given with a calculation of what is a portion and what is not.
One should consume whatever food, whether solid or soft, as well as drink, that is obtained;
one should not form a mental attachment here based on the discrimination between what is liked and what is disliked.
Freed from the vows of training and initiation, as well as from the acts of shame,
the yogi of great compassion should wander with the intrinsic nature of all phenomena.
Transcending burnt offerings, sacrifices, and ascetic penances, and devoid of mantras and meditations,
the excellent practitioner of yoga performs the conduct, liberated from the pledges and vows. (5.4.23)
Even if a Daitya equal to Śakra stands firmly before one,
one should not feel fear; one should roam about in the form of a lion.
Compassion is constantly drunk for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings;
the yogi, delighting in the drink of yoga, does not sink through any other drink.
Now, furthermore, the glorious conduct of the crown prince is described,
by which one proceeds toward the final goal for the sake of all sentient beings. (5.4.26)
The practitioner should place divine earrings upon the ears,
a circlet upon the head, and two bracelets upon the hands. (5.4.27)
A girdle on the hips, anklets likewise upon the feet,
armlets at the base of the upper arms, and a garland of bones around the neck.
Wearing a tiger skin as a garment and consuming the nectar of the five [meats],
a person engaged in the yoga of Heruka should wander about with a concentrated mind.
Having taken this daughter of Vajra— charming-faced, large-eyed, consecrated by herself, and compassionate— one awakens to the vow of conduct (caryāvrata). || 5.4.30 ||
5.153 Due to the absence of the Vajra family, [the initiation] may also be performed by means of the family of one’s own chosen deity;
or else, [one may initiate] a [deity] born from another family who has been consecrated by the seed-syllable of awakening (bodhibīja). 5.4.31.
5.154 If song is sung, then it is supreme when accompanied by the *vajra*;
if one dances when bliss has arisen, for the sake of liberation.
Then the yogin always performs the dance with the vajra-steps. (5.4.32)
Akṣobhya is in the form of the wheel, Amitābha is the nature of the earrings, Ratneśa is in the neck-garland, and Vairocana is said to be in the hand. (5.4.33)
Amogha resides in the girdle, and Prajñā has the form of the khaṭvāṅga staff;
one should always consume the medicine and drink the water.
Old age and death do not afflict him who is protected at all times;
a crown fashioned from *cauraka* hair is employed there, originating from the syllable *hūṃ*.
One should carry the five skull-bowls of the Buddhas through the practice of yoga;
likewise, having made them into pieces of five finger-widths, they are worn upon the crown of the head.
The *kacaḍorī* and the double-stranded cord (*dvidheṭā*) arise from the nature of wisdom and skillful means;
the yogin wears the sacred ash and hair as his observance. (5.4.37)
The recitation, the sound of the hand-drum, and the invitation of all sentient beings—
this becomes the state of recitation; once again, one becomes Vajrakapālī himself.
A yogin who has become the very self of Heruka should always avoid greed, delusion, fear, anger, and shameful actions; he should move about amidst the five colors. 5.4.39.
One should conceive of that which is endowed with five colors as being of a single color;
for no distinction arises from a single color through its multiplicity. (5.4.40)
Having cast off the self that consists of sleep, conduct is practiced; of this there is no doubt. || 5.4.41 ||
Thus ends the fifth chapter, the Sampuṭodbhava-caryā-kalpa.
Ap 6. Chapter A6,
Part 1
6.1.1 O Lord, I have heard of the curiosity regarding the sequence of the self-abidings (*svādhiṣṭhāna*). What is the purpose of the secret [teachings] and so forth?
Listen with a one-pointed mind, O Vajrasattva of great compassion;
I shall explain in brief the definitive conclusion of all tantras.
That which is declared by the letter *e* is the unmanifest locus;
having gone there, the constant movement of the mind is indeed the following of the elements.
Why is it called the word *dhātu*? [Because of] 6.1.4.
The Blessed One said:
"In the secret [teaching], this much has been stated regarding the sixteen-syllable [mantra]."

They say that the letter *ra* corresponds to the blood element (*raktadhātu*) and likewise the letter *ha* to the tactile sense; with the letter *si* they denote phlegm (*śleṣman*), and with the letter *pa*, bile (*pitta*). (6.1.5)
By the syllable *ra*, [one obtains] taste; likewise, by the syllable *me*, [one obtains] fat.
The syllable *ra* is said to be fire (*agni*), and *mye* is called flesh (*māṃsa*).
By the syllable *sa*, the merchant class (*viṭ*) is declared; likewise, by the syllable *rva*, fat (*vasā*);
the syllable *tma* is said to be skin (*tvac*); and the syllable *ni* is indeed bone (*asthi*).
With the syllable *sa* there is urine; with the syllable *dā*, however, the lungs;
with the syllable *sthi*, the lotus itself is said [to be produced]—the most beautiful substance, properly joined.
By the syllable *ta*, there arises semen born from the *bodhicitta*.
Thus it has been explained, O Goddess, according to the nature of the channels and the resonance (*nāda*). (6.1.9)
Indeed, it consists of the sixteen digits (*kalā*) by virtue of being the very nature of the *bodhicitta*.
The letter *ra* is declared to be fire; from blood, bile (*pitta*) arises. (6.1.10)
The conjunction is held to be phlegm, and sweat arises from the sinews;
its lord is said to be Vāyu, and the letter *ha* is remembered as all-pervading.
And the fivefold seed-syllable is fully attained in the joints of the bones;
the letter *ra* is in all the palates, as is the supreme fourfold seed-syllable.
In the regions of those initial squares, there is the beauty of the five seed-syllables;
conjoined with the letter *ha* and the sixth vowel, this is proclaimed as *vijñāna*.
By the letter *ha* alone, there is everywhere the assembly of all Buddhas;
having emerged from the source in the form of sound, they are the domain of the conduct of the *samaya*.
That which abides as the beginning, middle, and end is difficult to attain within the three worlds;
just as [it is produced] from the union of the churning-stick and the act of churning, so too [is it attained] through the practice of mantra-recitation, meditation, and the like. || 6.1.15 ||
Listen to what is declared in the Tantra:
there are two channels within the center of the womb, namely on the left and the right.
One should know that semen is in the left and blood likewise in the right;
their union is the perfect gathering of the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu).
Sattva is the body, rajas is speech, and tamas is the mind by their very nature;
sattva is semen, rajas is blood, and tamas is indeed the origin [of the embryo]. (6.1.18)
Through the union of the vajra and the lotus, existence and non-existence become of one flavor;
[the five substances are] feces, urine, phlegm, blood, and fifthly, semen. (6.1.19)
Then, the one who possesses the vajra is said here to consist of the mass of the five nectars;
likewise, it is stated that bone and marrow, as well as semen, are born of the father. (6.1.20)
Skin, flesh, and blood are said to be born of the mother; these are declared to be the constituents of the physical body that are gathered together. (6.1.21)
The single mass becomes twofold, and being twofold, it becomes manifold;
because it exists in the form of both one and many, he is therefore called Vajrī here.

The movement through the channels has indeed been described; however, at the gateway of those two, during the times of their conjunction, there should be the taking up of the deity as a support. || 6.1.23 ||
6.24 Thus, with the upper gate [one perceives] below, and with the lower gate, consciousness;
with the upper gate, the elements. 6.1.24.
The yogi should contemplate him as entering at the junction of all the channels; he,
the Vajrin, is eternally and constantly situated there at the upper door of the body.
And at the upper gate there is a triple mechanism, surrounded by nine gates.
"O Blessed One! What is called the 'threefold mechanism' (triyantra)? And how, by what manner, does the constant movement of the mind occur?"
The Blessed One said:
There are exactly three yantras; they are established as three-yantra systems through a threefold division.
By way of the essential nature of body, speech, and mind, they are inferior, superior, and intermediate. || 6.1.28 ||
It has a single pillar and nine gates; it is gross, with five presiding deities.
The gate leading to the nine streams is proclaimed to be ninefold. (6.1.29)
The inferior bodily gateway is gross and fashioned by destiny;
"the person" (puruṣa) refers to a specific kind of person, namely a yogi. || 6.1.30 ||
At all times, there is movement (gati) due to the specific nature of going;
thus it applies to those with one foot, two feet, four feet, and so forth.
The movement [of the mind] is always through the distinctions of the wind and so forth;
the wind is fourfold, and the stability of the mind is twofold.

6.33 And the rule for setting forth that which is latent: "Latent" means remaining; "setting forth" refers to the movement of coming and going among all beings. He who does not know this is insentient, is no true person, and is without wisdom—meaning he is not a yogi. 6.1.33.
In the southeast,
the northwest, the northeast, and likewise the southwest,
by means of the movement of the mind, [the yogi] directs [the breath] upward, to the sides, and downward.
The third door is mental, distinguished by the moon and the sun;
whether by way of entry or exit, this indeed becomes the supreme door.
The primary supreme gateway is proclaimed to be both below and above:
through the lower gateway comes discernment, and through the upper gateway come the elements.
The Buddhas, Vairocana and the others, abide moving within the upper gate; their stationing is below, while their emission occurs through the upper [gate]. (6.1.37)
The constant movement of the mind in the form of invocation and dismissal consists of all the Buddhas of the three times, the Ḍākinīs, and the Mothers of Yoga. (6.1.38)
In both engagement and withdrawal, through the manifestation of virtues and defects,
the natures of pleasure and pain are indeed established as existing inherently.
Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Vajra-holder, Vajrasattva, the Great Bliss.
Then the Goddess, having cast her *bola* into the *kakkolaka* of the Blessed One and having gratified the Great Being, uttered these words: (6.1.41)
How indeed does your *tilaka* reside during the spring season, and of what nature is it?
Relying on the indestructible and other [qualities], how does its location come to be for them?
Just as the supreme placement of the wheels (cakranyāsa) beginning with Pullīra has been described,
tell me how the channels (nāḍī) arise and explain their distinctions to me.
The Blessed One said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim that which is more secret than the secret, the supreme.

The twenty-four [pīṭhas] are proclaimed through the differentiation of the locations within the wheels of body, speech, and mind, corresponding to the nature of the channels, the pīṭhas, and so forth, as well as the ten bhūmis and pāramitās. || 6.1.45 ||
The head is the Malaya region, while the crest-lock is Jālandhara; likewise,
Oḍḍiyāna is said to be the right ear.
The *arbuda* is the spinal column; these four are known as the *pīṭhas*.
Likewise, the *godāvarī* should be known as having the form of the left ear.
Rāmeśvara is said to be located between the eyebrows;
Devīkoṭṭa is at the eyes, and Mālava is at the base of the arms.
Thus, these secondary seats (upapīṭhas) are established within the wheel of the mind (cittacakra);
they are declared to be the specific locations of the sky-faring goddesses (khecarīs).
Kāmarūpa is likewise [assigned to] the two armpits, and Oḍra is proclaimed to be the two breasts;
these are designated as the field (kṣetra), while the navel is considered Triśakuni.
Kośala is the tip of the nose and is declared to be an *upakṣetra*;
Kaliṅga is said to be the mouth, and Lampāka is called the throat.
That which is renowned as Chandoha is said to be in the heart;
Kāñcī is called Upacchandoha, and Meḍhra is Himālaya.
Thus, all the regions are established within the wheel of speech; they are declared to be the specific locations of the Bhūcarīs. 6.1.53.
The goddess who dwells in the preta resides in the *liṅga*, while the household deity (*gṛhadevatā*) resides in the anus;
these two are declared to be the meeting places (*melāpaka*). The thigh is said to be Saurāṣṭra.
The two shanks are renowned as being the nature of Suvarṇadvīpa;
likewise, Upamelāpaka is remembered as the finger-joints, and Nagara as the fingers.
The Sindhu is indeed the surface of the feet, and the cremation ground (śmaśāna) is declared to be [the soles];
the Maru desert is said to be the big toe, and Kulatā is called the knee.
This cremation ground, however, is described by the ḍākinīs as being "near the cremation ground" (upaśmaśāna);
these regions are born from one's own body, situated both externally and internally.
In the wheels of body, speech, and mind, through twenty-four divisions,
all the locations of the ḍākinīs are fully explained everywhere. (6.1.58)
In these locations, the ḍākinīs reside in the form of the channels (nāḍī).

Part 2, ap6.60:
<V 6.1 (prose)→> Now, I shall describe the wheel of channels (*nāḍīcakra*) belonging to a certain Tathāgata’s body, located according to its proper position.
In the center of the heart is a lotus with eight petals and a pericarp;
situated in its center is a channel whose nature is like oil and fire.
A hanging garland resembling a plantain flower hangs with its face turned downward;
in its center stands the Hero, about the size of a mustard seed.
The syllable *Hūṃ* is the unstruck seed-syllable that flows like snow;
it is renowned as "Spring," the delighter in the hearts of embodied beings.
Nairātmyā, known as Tilakā,
has the form of the submarine fire; fanned by the wind of karma, she blazes here in the circle of the navel.
Having attained the spring season, she remains satisfied and established in meditative absorption;
this is the heroic Śrī Heruka, known as Vasantatilaka.
Having assumed the form of a Yoginī, he remains within the world of the moving and the unmoving;
through the divisions of body, speech, and mind, he issues forth by way of the three gates.
Established within all bodies, this [breath] performs the coming and going;
it is proclaimed as the short vowel *a*, having the form of the letter *a* and being non-existent [as a separate entity]. 6.2.7.
In the heart as well, the syllable *hūṃ* is established with two long measures;
and in the throat, in the form of the syllable *oṃ*, it is said to have three protracted measures.
On the forehead, however, is that syllable *haṃ*, the sound (*nāda*), the point (*bindu*), and the unstruck (*anāhata*);
it consists of the great elements beginning with earth, according to the differentiation of the four wheels.
Presiding over the four junctions (saṃdhyās), he is born from the four lotuses;
he is the embodiment of the four joys and is devoted to the four yogas.
In the form of supreme bliss, through the state of action and agent,
he sports here at his pleasure in the form of Śrī Vajrasattva.
Furthermore, in the fourfold set of petals situated in the four directions,
there are four elemental channels (bhūtanāḍī) by virtue of their nature as oil and fire.
The four channels situated in the intermediate directions, which also extend into those [cardinal directions],
carry the five nectars; they are based upon the very nature of its worship.
The fourfold worship is renowned as being identical in nature to that [deity] through its internal disposition.
Thus, within the heart-center of the body, five channels are established.
They are declared to be twenty-four through the divisions of body, speech, and mind;
they are established in various locations based on the distinctions of the sacred seats (pīṭha) and so forth. (6.2.15)
The channels originating from the head are known as the *śiraja*;
they consist of the forms of *rajas*, *sattva*, and *tamas*, and among them, there are the principal channels.
In Pullīra, however, the channel named Abhedyā is known to carry the nails and teeth;
likewise, in Jālandhara, the subtle form carries the hair and body hair.
In the great sacred seat (pīṭha) of Oḍḍiyāna, she who is established as divine resides,
resting upon the right ear and carrying the impurity of the skin.
Likewise, the *vāmā* channel at Arbuda is the *ḍākinī* who carries flesh;
the channel situated in the *naharu* is established as the Godāvarī.
Known as Vāmanī, she stands with a firm form;
likewise, the channel at Rāmeśvara is well-known as Kūrmajā.
The channel located in Devīkoṭṭa is considered to be of a hard nature, established as a garland of bones; however, that which is in Bhāvika is regarded as soft.
She who dwells within the entire body constantly carries the *bukka*;
likewise, in Mālava, the Mistress of Jinas resides in the heart as Sekā.
The channel that carries the eye and is situated in Kāmarūpa is renowned as Doṣāvatī; it is cultivated by the perception of forms. (6.2.23)
In Oḍra, the Pittāvahā channel is known to be greatly pervaded;
in Triśakuni, the two Mātṛs together with the lungs have arisen. (6.2.24)
In Kośala, the divine Śabarī flows, filled with a garland of intestines;
in Kaliṅga, she is the Śītadā, while in Pārśva, she carries herself as Samāvahā.
The heat located in the stomach is indeed proclaimed as *ūṣmā* in Lampāka;
and *pramāṇā*, situated in the waist, always carries away excrement.

Or she who dwells in the middle of the boundary on the Himalayas with a joyful countenance; she who resides as the inhabitant of the realm of the departed (pretas), established in her own form through phlegm (śleṣman). 6.2.27.
She who constantly carries away pus, who is established as the deity of the house,
is renowned as the common *ḍākinī*, the Supreme Goddess.
The channel that flows in Saurāṣṭra is red and bestows the cause;
and that which carries perspiration is situated in Suvarṇadvīpa.
She who is agitated and whose limbs are intensely radiant is proclaimed as Viyogā.
In the city [of the body], she is beloved, thick with fat, and flowing with intoxication.
In Sindhu, she is well-established as Saśokāśruvāhinī;
in Marusthāna, she carries Kheṭa and should be designated as Pāvakī.
In Kulatā, there was Sumanas, as well as Bāla and Siṃhāṇavāhinī. || 6.2.32 ||
Ap 6.93: The second chapter of the sixth [section] on the assignment of regions.

Part 3, Chapter 6.94 “I have heard, O Lord, of the great curiosity regarding the ritual of the inner mandala worship and so forth; how does it come to be? I do not know the rite of fire-offering (*homakarma*). Please explain it, O One of Great Bliss.”
The Blessed One said:
"O deity, the form of the channels has arisen perfectly from Heruka and the others."
The body is a beautiful mandala with four gates, as previously described.
Supported by those eight pillars which constitute its own limbs, it stands firm;
because of its equanimity in all respects, it is proclaimed to be perfectly square.
The single triple wheel is said to exist in the form of body, speech, and mind;
it is situated on the peak of the mountain in its pericarp, beginning with Vairambha, in due order.
Thus, that mandala which has arisen through the lineage of the gurus remains established in this way:
at the soles of the feet is the Vairambha wind, shaped like a bow.
Varuṇa is situated in the region of the three hips, radiant with a triangular form; indeed, he who is circular in shape resides in the belly.
In the heart, the earth is indeed square on all sides;
likewise, the king of mountains, Sumeru, exists in the form of the spinal column.
Then, in the thirty-two-petaled lotus situated at the region of the head,
the thirty-two minds of enlightenment are well-established as vowels and consonants.
That which is said to be the lunar orb situated in the center of the lotus is declared to be the brain located in the middle of the head. (6.3.9)
In its center, however, is the syllable *hūṃ*, in the form of a drop (*bindu*), which is indeed unstruck (*anāhata*).
It is the root of all worlds, the foundation for all things, both stable and moving.
Indeed, it exists in the form of a seed, manifest through its unmanifest nature;
from that, the form of all embodied beings has arisen from the very beginning.
Flowing day and night in the form of nectar,
the *nāda* is split apart by that very [nectar] which brings satisfaction to the fire.
By that, the mandala indeed becomes complete; of this there is no doubt.
That very thing is called the mandala, the supreme essence of all things.
6.107 It is considered a *maṇḍala* because it seizes (*gṛhṇāti*) and takes (*lāti*);
indeed, the wheel of the thirty-two great channels (*nāḍī*) is considered the *maṇḍala*. 6.3.14.
The bodhicitta is the great jewel; it alone is the mandala.
Pervading the universe in both external and internal forms, it remains established as the totality.
The external [body], however, consists of the engagement of all the sense organs with form, sound, and so forth;
the internal [body] is established as the perfected substances such as semen and the rest.
6.110 By means of the *bodhicitta* itself, both external and internal, for the Vajra-holders who possess the nature of the kinsmen of the world in both gross and subtle forms.
But by means of the meaning of the pledge (samaya) proclaimed by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, Buddhahood is attained in this very life from the mandala; therefore [this is so]. 6.3.18.
From this mandala, there arises the accomplishment of the Śrāvakas, the Buddhas, and likewise the Pratyekabuddhas, as well as the gods beginning with Brahmā.
With the internal [offerings] such as semen and the like, and likewise with the external ones such as form and so forth,
the oblation is performed in the greatly blazing fire of wisdom.
6.114 Specifically regarding the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), the elements (*dhātu*), the aggregates (*skandha*), and so forth—
of those who possess divine forms, as well as of the *ḍākinīs*— [it is taught]. 6.3.21.
6.115 Yoga-worship has been fully described, for by it you are worshipped.
This skull, moreover, is called the vessel for the oblation. 6.3.22
The *sruva* ladle is called the tongue, consisting of the *lalanā* channel at the heart-cakra;
the vessel (*pātrī*) is designated as the mouth, and the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) is in the circle of the navel.

Shaken by the wind of karma, the fire of Brahman situated in the three regions [of the body] is called the "Sound" (nāda), which is said to be the mantra; its repetition constitutes the recitation (japa). || 6.3.24 ||
But the manifestation of meditative cultivation arises from the yoga of the non-dual maṇḍala;
this maṇḍala and so forth of the Victors is mounted upon the innate (*sahaja*).

The teacher, however, is the king of the mind in the form of the presiding deity of the mandala; everything mentioned here and so forth, as previously described, is to be understood as being right here. 6.3.26.

Even now, O Lord, I still have doubt as to how you sport in the forms of the Dharmakāya, Saṃbhogakāya, Nirmāṇakāya, and Mahāsukhakāya; I do not know the distinction between them. Please explain this, O Mahāsukha.
The Blessed One said:
"The wheel reaching from the head to the navel is situated in the form of the letter *e*."
The heart, situated in the throat, is considered to resemble the syllable *vaṃ*.
A lotus with sixty-four petals is situated in the middle of the navel;
a lotus with thirty-two petals is established in the middle of the head.
Furthermore, there is a sixteen-petaled lotus situated in the middle of the throat;
likewise, in the heart, a lotus with eight petals is traditionally taught.
In the sixty-four-petaled [lotus], emanation (nirmāṇa) is proclaimed;
in the great eight-petaled lotus, the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) proceeds.
In the sixteen-spoked [mandala], there is the sambhoga[kāya], and likewise the thirty-two-petaled [lotus];
the great bliss and great gnosis are established all around.
In the center of the emanation wheel (nirmāṇacakra), surrounded by the eight groups of letters,
this letter *a*— the foremost form among all phonemes— is the supreme syllable (*paramākṣara*).
In the wheel of Dharma (dharmacakra), however, the syllable HŪṂ is renowned; it is considered the unstruck sound (anāhata),
endowed with the five vowels and adorned by the consonants ya, ra, va, and la.
Situated in the center of the enjoyment wheel (sambhogacakra) is the syllable Oṃ, the illuminator of phonemes;
it is completely surrounded on all sides by four digits (kalās).
In the great wheel of great bliss (mahāsukha-mahācakra), the syllable *haṃ* exists in the form of a drop (*bindu*);
the moon and sun are renowned as being on the left and right sides.
Starting from the throat, the channel on the left is associated with the *saṃbhogakāya*;
though it rests in the center of the navel, it is downward-facing and brings about intoxication.
The channel that rises upward from above the navel likewise rests in the middle of the throat; it is proclaimed as the carrier of blood.
The one known as Mada is Candra (the Moon), and the one remembered as Rakta is Sūrya (the Sun);
they are mounted upon the two doors, resting respectively below and above.
Indeed, these two, the moon and the sun, are proclaimed as the two channels;
they are the basis for the coming and going of the heroes and the ḍākinīs.
For the purposes of setting and rising are like those of sleep and awakening; on the left and right sides, however, twelve vowels are situated. (6.3.41)
Those with upward faces are declared to be surrounded by the letters beginning with *ka*;
those with downward faces, however, are joined by placing them on the sides and in the center.
The letter *kṣa* is declared to be the *rākṣasa*, presiding over the lower parts;
when the moon is situated in the throat in the form of great passion (*mahārāga*). (6.3.43)
Then the supreme body of the Buddhas is known as the *sambhoga*-kāya;
it occurs when that [wind] is situated at the tip of the nose or at the tip of the vajra.
But when even the *saṃbhogakāya* has set, it resides in the center of the *bhaga*; this is known as the "mustard seed" (*sarṣapa*). || 6.3.45 ||
That which is designated as having the form of the sun is called the *nirmāṇakāya*; by means of it, the emanation of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas occurs. (6.3.46)
King Padmanarteśvara, possessing the yoga of the Lotus-Light,
exists in the form of a nirmanakaya when the sun has set.
That which is called the mind of awakening (bodhicitta), condensed and stainless, severed from the path of saṃsāra, the cessation of conceptual proliferation (prapañca), and auspicious; || 6.3.48 ||
Free from duality, supremely pure, the form of Śrī Vajrasattva,
known as Śrī Heruka, he resides within the tantra like a wood-worm within its host.
Established in the system of the *Tantra* regarding the sight of laughter and the attainment of the hand,
he remains like a woodworm, chewing upon both passion and dispassion.
Ap 6.144: The union of all channels is the *Ḍākinījālasaṃvara*; this is the third chapter of the sixth [section].
Part 4,
ap6.145: Then the great bodhisattvas, headed by Vajragarbha, together with Nairātmyayoginī and the others, spoke as follows:
The cultivation of the wheel is the path of the deities according to their arising; indeed,
it is the specific *ḍākinī*-wheel, which is particularly expressed in the sandhyā-bhāṣā.
The Blessed One previously said: "Tell me the vow. (6.4.2)
The Blessed One said:
"Within the body of the Yoginī, the syllable *A* stands as the Saṃvara."
Just as it is externally, so it is internally; that restraint has been revealed.
The bliss of the *ap* is Mahāmudrā; the Vajra-abode is the skillful means (*upāya*).
Through this secret union, the external duality is demonstrated. (6.4.4)
6.149 Within the center of the body, the three bodies (trikāya) are said to exist in the form of a wheel (cakra).
Through the thorough knowledge of the three bodies, the wheel is considered to be great bliss. 6.4.5 ||
The Dharma-body, Enjoyment-body, and Emanation-body, as well as Great Bliss itself—
these three bodies are established within the center of the womb, the heart, and the throat.
But where the birth of all sentient beings without exception is proclaimed,
there the emanation of the *nirmāṇakāya* is stable, because it is an emanation. (6.4.7)
Dharma, which is the very nature of the mind, is the Wheel of Dharma (dharmacakra) located in the heart;
Sambhoga is said to be that which enjoys the six [objects] in the form of flavors.
Because of its firmness within all phenomena, everything exists as its own essential nature;
the wheel of enjoyment (*saṃbhogacakra*) is at the throat, and great bliss (*mahāsukha*) is situated at the head.
In the syllable *evaṃ*, there is the outflow (*niṣyanda*) and the maturation (*vipāka*) from the Wheel of Dharma;
the result of human effort (*puruṣakāra*) is in the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhoga*), and purity (*vaimalya*) is in the Wheel of Bliss (*sukhacakra*).
The fruit is said to be fourfold, distinguished by its outflow and so forth;
the Blessed Wisdom is the enjoyer of karma, impelled by the winds of karma.
Sthāvarī is in the wheel of emanation (nirmāṇacakra), because emanation is stationary;
in the wheel of the Dharma (dharmacakra) of the Sarvāstivāda, the Dharma arises from speech.
Because consciousness exists in the *saṃbhoga* wheel at the throat, there is perception;
and because great assembly (*mahāsaṃghī*) exists in the wheel of bliss, great bliss resides in the crown of the head.
The body is called the *nikāya*; the belly is said to be the dwelling place. One who is free from passion is the womb; the placenta is the flaming robe. (6.4.14)
The preceptress and likewise the mother; salutation with palms joined at the head;
the training rules, worldly duties, and the recitation of mantras—these I [shall perform]. (6.4.15)
One born as a monk, reciting mantras, naked, with head and face shaved—by these collections of factors, beings are indeed Buddhas; of this there is no doubt. (6.4.16)
The ten stages and the ten months are the beings who are masters of the ten stages;
he is established within the wombs of women in Sukhāvatī under the name of Śukra.

Without that [the deity], there would be no happiness; and without happiness, he [the deity] would not exist. Happiness arises from union with the deity because, being dependent, it lacks independent capacity. (6.4.18)
Therefore, the Buddha would not be an existent entity, nor indeed would he be of the nature of non-existence;
for he possesses the forms of arms and faces, yet is formless by virtue of supreme bliss.
Therefore, the entire world is innate; it is called the innate nature (*sahajasvarūpa*).
That very nature is *nirvāṇa* when perceived by a mind in its purified aspect.
The application of the form of the deity is established as soon as [the body] is born; however,
the latent impressions of the material nature persist through the hands, faces, colors, and postures.

Thus, O Goddess, has been spoken this unsurpassed yoga of all. Then, the goddesses headed by the Yoginī Nairātmyā—namely, Locanā, Māmakī, Pāṇḍaravāsinī, Tārā, Bhṛkuṭī, Cundā, Parṇaśavarī, Ahomukhā, and Śaṃvarī—and other Yoginīs equal in number to the atoms of Mount Sumeru, were struck with supreme wonder; they fainted and became terrified. || 6.4.22 ||
Then all the Tathāgatas, headed by Akṣobhya, spoke thus:
“May the Blessed One cause the hosts of all yoginīs to arise.”
Then the Blessed One, having entered the meditative absorption named "Vajra that Conquers All Ignorance," raised up all the yoginīs and spoke thus: 6.4.24.

Sentient beings are indeed Buddhas, but they are obscured by adventitious defilements; through the removal of these, they become Buddhas. It is thus, O Blessed One, that sons of noble family [attain Buddhahood]. 6.4.25.
The world does not necessarily suffer from the consumption of poison; rather,
it is the one devoid of delusion who suffers grief for that which is the essence of the self.
By the very same portion of poison by which all living beings die,
one who knows the true nature of poison may expel that poison using poison itself.
Just as bean-based food is given to one seized by wind, and that very wind is overcome by wind through the application of contrary medicinal principles. (6.4.28)
Pure existence, by means of existence itself, brings about conceptualization through its own discrimination;
just as water that has entered the ear is drawn out by water itself.
In the same way, the conceptualization of existence is indeed purified by means of mental aspects (ākāra),
just as things burnt by fire are boiled again by fire. (6.4.30)
Likewise, those burned by the fire of passion are steamed by the flame of passion;
for by whatever fierce karma sentient beings are bound, [by that same means they are purified].
But by that very same means, when accompanied by the proper method, people are liberated from the bondage of existence.
The world is bound by passion, and by passion alone is it liberated.
Indeed, this inverted cultivation has not been understood by the Buddhist heretics;
in the *kundura* [yoga], there are five [elements] by virtue of the nature of the five elements. (6.4.33)
The single Great Bliss alone undergoes a fivefold division through various distinctions; by the union of the *bola* and *kakkola*, the latent impression of hardness arises from contact. (6.4.34)
Because the *kaṭhina* is of the nature of delusion (*moha*), Vairocana is considered to be delusion;
since the *bodhicitta* is fluid, the fluid is considered to be the water element.
Because water is by nature unshakeable, hatred is Akṣobhya-nāyaka;
from the friction and conjunction of the two, fire is always produced. (6.4.36)
Passion is Amitābhavajra; passion arises from fire.
That which is the mind within the *kakkolaka* has the nature of wind.
Envy is Amoghasiddhi; Amogha arises from wind.
Pleasure is red and is the mind; the Jewel, however, has the characteristic of emptiness.
Space is Piśuna-vajra, and Piśuna is born from space;
the one great mind alone is characterized by five forms.
Those born among the five families there are many thousands;
therefore, this Great Bliss is of a single nature and supremely eternal.
Through differentiation by means of the five mental states beginning with passion, it goes to a state of fivefold division.
In each family, there are assemblies of Tathāgatas equal in number to the sands of ten Ganges rivers.
In great families there are many lineages; in those lineages there are many hundreds. 6.4.42.
And those hundreds of thousands of lakhs become incalculable within the millions of families.
"In that regard, among those families, there are innumerable families born from the family of supreme bliss," so he said. 6.4.43.
Is this [body], which consists of a mass no larger than an atom, something that is intermingled? 6.4.44.
The Blessed One said:
"For indeed, upon the path of a single hair, there are many Buddhas."
And there is neither distress nor affliction. || 6.4.45 ||
Arise, arise, O gods endowed with the ten powers!
You desire to partake of the meal in my home.
“O sons of good family, they have arisen through the power of supernatural faculties,” he said. 6.4.46.
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the characteristics arising from the *sampuṭa*.
He is established in the secret earth element, likewise in the supreme water,
in the delightful one called fire, and in the wind which is the self of all.
This is declared to be the ever-abiding commitment (saṃvara) of the essence of all Buddhas;
or else, it is likewise found in the ten forms and in equanimity.
And likewise, this which is said to have a pure and purified nature is always established in the awakening of discernment and in the performance of duties. (6.4.50)
Likewise, O Vairocana, or similarly in Ratnasambhava,
or with Amitābha— whenever [the practice] is established in Amoghasiddhi, it is always so.
The mass consisting of the five nectars, in the form of a drop, composed of mind,
is the perfectly pure great gnosis, the very nature of all goddesses.
That which is renowned as Vajrasattva is declared to be supreme bliss;
this self-arisen form is proclaimed to be the Dharmakāya.
His very innate wisdom (sahajā prajñā), abiding there in that form,
is fanned by the winds of karma and blazes within the circle of the navel.
Known as Nairatmya, she is remembered as Vasantatilaka;
her body consists of hundreds of thousands of the tips of hair, and her radiance is like a flash of lightning. (6.4.55)
But at the time of union with the deity, [the rays] issue forth from the tips of the pores and the joints of the body toward the ten directions, threatening all the gods and asuras.
Having burned that [deity] in the heart and the wheel of dharma, they go to the sambhogakāya;
having emerged from the right nostril on all sides.
Even through the aperture within the sheath of wool, indeed in the ten directions, [the rays enter] through the left nostril of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. (6.4.58)
Having completely incinerated [the elements] within the *śikhācakra*, one should emerge;
then, by means of the very same aperture mentioned previously, one should enter back into the *śikhā*.
From that, she generates bliss for all the Buddhas who have been incinerated;
having returned to the navel-mandala, she remains as before.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The King of Rituals: The Vasantatilakā," from the *Mahātantra* known as the *Sampuṭodbhava*.
Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.1:
Chapter 7,
Part 1.
“O Blessed One, I wish to hear the characteristics of the seals of speech (*vāṅmudrā*). What is called ‘twilight language’ (*saṃdhyābhāṣa*)? O Blessed One, please explain this with certainty. (7.1.1)

The great commitment (*mahāsamaya*) of the Yoginīs is not breached by Śrāvakas and the like; it is [maintained] through laughter and glances, as well as through embracing, the couple (*dvandva*), and so forth. (7.1.2)
Even though the intentional language (*saṃdhyābhāṣa*) of these four has not been explicitly stated in the *Tantra*, O Vajragarbha, I shall explain it; listen with a one-pointed mind. (7.1.3)
The twilight language, the great language, the detailed conventions of the pledge;
likewise, passion, wine, strength, meat, sandalwood, and the closing.
Movement is the skull, the corpse, the refuge, and the bone-ornament;
nakedness is said to be the swing, while the fire-drill and the hand-drum are considered [the means of] attainment.
The vessel known as *dundura* is considered unfit (*abhavya*), while the *kāliñjara* is regarded as fit (*bhavya*).
