The *diṇḍima* is declared to be untouchable (*asparśa*), and the *kapāla* is the lotus-vessel (*padmabhājana*).
The food that provides satisfaction should be known as *bhakṣa*; the condiment is *mālatīndhana*.
*Viḍ* is said to be *catuḥsama*, and urine is remembered as *kastūrikā*.
Svayambhū is to be known as musk; śukra is considered camphor.
Mahāmāṃsa is declared to be saffron, while the union of the two organs is kunduru.
The *vajra* is known as the *bolaka*, and the *padma* is considered to be the *kakkolaka*.

*Muku*. Having thrown it into the mouth, the mark of this [mantra] is *Ḍākinī*. *Ghoghu*. Having placed it on the head with the hollowed palms (*añjali*), the mark of this [mantra] is *Dīpinī*. (7.1.10)
*Gughu* is the mark on the swollen thumb of one who is suffering from thirst.
*Mughu* is the mark of those whose hands have been struck against their ears; it belongs specifically to the Kambojas. 7.1.11.
Short [instruction]: One should place a tremor at the tip of the nose, for one is indeed asked about the news of one's welfare.
The observer—the yogi intent upon the signs—should show the Mṛgaśīrṣa [constellation]. 7.1.12.
The syllable *ḍā* is said to denote the male,
while *ḍī* denotes females.
*Pu* signifies immobilization (*stambhana*), *su* likewise signifies consumption (*bhakṣaṇa*),
and *mā* is said to mean mother (*mātā*).
The syllable *yo* signifies a wife;
likewise, *bhi* signifies a sister;
and *dhī* is remembered as a female friend.
*Lu* indeed means "daughter";
*strī* should be known as "beautiful";
and *sa* refers to the drinking of soma.
*Pe* is to be understood as such;
*phī* indeed means meat;
*bha* is declared to be eating.
*Bhū* is the meeting place (*melāpaka*),
*pī* is likewise the cremation ground (*śmaśāna*),
and *bhu* they know as the corpse (*mṛtaka*).
*Dī* is indeed Yoginī;
*ga* is likewise Lāmā;
and *tri* is indeed Rūpiṇī.
*Ku* refers to Ḍākinī, *kha* to Khaṇḍarohā,
and *ja* to the pair of shanks.
*Ke* refers to the pair of arms;
*bha* refers to the act of salutation;
*sva* refers to the rite of welcome. || 7.1.13 ||
These are the single-syllable secret signs (*chommaka*); they should be known as the Hero’s Sisters (*vīrabhaginī*). This is the knowledge of the syllable, the pledge, and the mudrā. 7.1.14.
Vajragarbha said:
"I do not know the secret signs of speech; tell them to me, O Great Bliss."
The Blessed One said:
"I shall speak in brief; listen as I utter it."
A woman who has reached puberty should offer a greeting; a woman who has reached puberty should return the greeting. || 7.1.16 ||
In *gamuḥ*, it is said that "I go" (*gacchāmi*);
in *lumbā*, likewise, "I come" (*āgacchāmi*).
"Give the *nigara*" means "give [it]"; "take the *caṭuka*" means "take [it]"; "the heart is the hero" means "it is said [to be] the hero."
The killing of the Kaurava is said to occur;
the bell is said to be the pericarp;
the forehead is said to be the head.
The boar is said to be the hair;
the ear is Śravaṇa;
the churning-stick is the nectar.
"Man" (nara) refers to the assembly;
"tālikā" refers to the ḍākinī;
and "hell" (naraka) refers to the maṇḍala.
Such-and-such a cremation ground;
Kākhilā is the door;
Śvasana is the Brāhmaṇa.
The *paridhi* is the Kṣatriya;
the *virati* is the Vaiśya;
and the *krūra* is the Śūdra.
Inwardly, the Caṇḍāla’s house;
outwardly, a beast;
the sister, a ḍākinī.
"Mudaka" means fat.
"Take [it]" is, in some cases, a mudrā.
It is said that one who is hungry touches the tooth with the tongue.
Craving is the carrier of fragrance.
As for "coming," from where? As for "staying," in what place?
*Kiraṇa* means a flower;
*lambodara* refers to what is called "teeth-smiling."
Cessation is rain;
manifestation is satisfaction;
smoke is clouds.
The mountain ridges are fond of smoke;
the rivers are streams;
the fingers are the limbs.
The mouth is the face;
the tongue is the *rājikā*;
the teeth are the *adanā*.
The line is the banner; the meter is the garland;
the moving one is the wind.
The lord of beasts is the sacrificial animal;
the mandala is level;
the breaths are the crossroads.
The people are Phalguṣa; the great animal is the Great Imperishable. 7.1.17.
*chā* refers to the goat;
*nā* refers to the man.
*Go* means a bull;
*ma* means a buffalo;
*bhā* sometimes means eating.
"Hā" is a synonym for lamentation;
"apyakāḥ" refers to royal officers;
"stha" denotes staying or remaining.
At the touch of the mouth, [one thinks] "I have eaten";
at the touch of the teeth, "I am satiated.
Sometimes *ho* is used as a synonym.
*Hrīkā* means shame.
"Perform sexual intercourse upon touching the void. "Upon touching the thighs, do so now. (7.1.18)
Speech is the knowledge of the secret signs.
The *samā*, *krūrā*, and *lalāṭī* glances are always said to be for the purpose of casting down;
the *vaśyā* glance is directed toward the left, as are the *puttalī* and the two [others] on the left.
For attraction, one should employ two upward-gazing eyes on the right side;
for paralyzing, the gaze is centered between the nose and the brow.
With a sidelong glance for the purpose of killing, two *puttalīs* [should be visualized] at the tip of the nose;
by means of *recaka* one causes a fall, and by *kumbhaka* one brings about subjugation.
By means of inhalation (pūraka), there is attraction; by means of retention (stambhana), there is pacification (śāntika).
Casting down is performed upon oily trees, while subjugation (vaśyā) is proclaimed to be accomplished with flowers.
Attraction is achieved among diamond-trees (vajravṛkṣa), and immobilization among moving grass;
through the practice of yoga for six months, this is accomplished— of this there is no doubt.
One should not entertain doubt in this regard; the supernatural powers of the Buddhas are inconceivable.
The salutation and the return salutation are performed toward two teachers. 7.1.25.

Through the yoga of Śrī-Vajrasattva and others, one should rise by means of the gesture of raising the right eyebrow and the visualization of traveling through the sky; success (*siddhi*) will be attained. By raising the left eyebrow, there is defeat of the enemy army, and likewise, by that very same yoga, there is the crushing of the forces of Māra. 7.1.26.

Through the sign of the throbbing of the left eye and the meditation on forms such as Gaurī, the accomplishment of the perfection of those forms occurs; through the sign of the throbbing of the right eye, the perfection of the form of Śrī Vajrasattva and others occurs. || 7.1.27 ||

Without verbal communication, even the worldly conventions well-known to the world would not be established; likewise, the success of the communal chanting of yogins—whether mundane or supramundane—as well as the success of eloquent speech, would not be achieved. (7.1.28)
Thus ends the knowledge of the gaze-mudrā (dṛṣṭimudrā).

Just as the form of the glorious Vajrasattva in union exists according to its natural constitution, so too, having placed mustard seeds within this human skull according to the ritual procedure... (7.1.29)
One who consumes food prepared with *pāka-taila* and likewise performs head-massages with fruits,
as well as the binding of the directions, boundaries, space, and earth, possesses unsurpassed protection against all things. (7.1.30)
The glorious Śrīvajrasattva, joined in union, has his upper and lower lips firmly pressed together;
the glorious one holds pride in his left hand and clearly displays the gestures of the wheel of the southern direction with his right.
One should cause [the disciple] to be established below and above, and seal him himself with *bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*;
thus he becomes composed of all Buddhas and bestows accomplishment. 7.1.32.

Having placed this [substance] in a skull-bowl belonging to a twice-born, one should afterwards place it on a human head. Then, having extracted it, [one obtains] women, men, eunuchs, and so forth; it is the supreme means for various supernatural powers (*siddhi*), involving crows, owls, vultures, and sparrows. This is the procedure for the practice of white *guñjā*. By will, one becomes endowed with the form of an elephant or a horse. By will, one becomes a bearer of the form of a bull or a buffalo. By will, one becomes a bearer of the form of a dog, a cat, or a jackal. By will, one becomes a bearer of the form of a woman or a man. (7.1.33)

Entering the hollows of the mouths of corpses and ignited by the fires of the funeral pyres, on the day of the black Bhūta, it causes the entire world to enter into possession through incense. Golden fruits, citrons, *citraka*, *vacā*, and whole hen’s eggs—through this incense, it causes the entire world, including all that is moving and unmoving, to enter into possession.

With these—namely, the root of the white horse (sitaturaga), the sun-tree (ravitaru), and the locust (śalabha)—combined with a hundredth part of the venom from a scorpion’s sting, [when applied to] the hand, it becomes gonāsa.

A *vānarī* plant and chalk, both smeared with the milk of a cow that has calved for the first time (*dinakara*), [are used] for seven days; by touching what is written [with them], one becomes a lord of serpents (*bhogīndra*) with hands free from poison. The method for reversing these two is now stated.

Malaya-bhavana, Ageśvara, Rogendra, Madanaphala, and Tagara, when combined, destroy even the most extraordinary poisons. This antidote should indeed be mixed with rice-water. One should eat a pill placed in a pit of *tagara* along with the excrement of a calf born on that very day; thus, one may drink poison at will, like Vajrapāṇi. (7.1.37)
A decoction of frogs, two-faced snakes, and *vāsaka*, along with the fruit of the *śleṣmāntaka* tree—by anointing one's hands with these, one destroys poison through touch. || 7.1.38 ||
One whose body is smeared with cow’s ghee, vajrī, peacock’s blood, the flesh and bones of a two-headed snake, renders even the three worlds free from poison. || 7.1.39 ||

One who is concentrated on the ritual injunctions for the naked and so forth causes a child to lose seven parts of its life-force by reciting the *mūla* mantra on a day presided over by the spirits; likewise, those [fevers] that are bound to the hands, such as the quartan fever, are destroyed.
Born with the armor of the lord of serpents and allied with the faction of the enemy of serpents, he causes hatred in the three worlds by the mere application of incense.
Alternatively, on the second day, one should offer incense to the limbs of Hara according to the prescribed rite for the two fortnights of fear; it must not be done otherwise.
Accompanied by the tongue of a mad dog whose head is placed upon the hole made by a horse's hoof, this [mantra] uproots an enemy buried at the door of one's house within seven days.

One who possesses the strength of a boar, whose hair is like a corpse, and whose neck is long with protruding bones— the best of practitioners can cause even the three worlds to vanish in seven days through this rite.
Having cleansed the form of a horse, a donkey, or a camel with these—red *hayamāra*, *kusuma*, *bhallātaka*, and *amlavetasa*—one should look into a mirror.

By burning the hooves of a horse, cow, boar, monkey, donkey, and camel with a sealed fire (*puṭāgni*) mixed with the fat of a frog, one will see their forms as before. By anointing the eyes with the oil and milk of *aṅkoṭaka* seeds under the Puṣya asterism, one sees within a mirror the forms belonging to other births.
A person whose eyes have been anointed with a paste of *tagara*, *phala*, and *aṅkoṭaka* oil beholds a divine being; yet, through that very oil-anointing, he returns to his natural state.
By applying a foot-ointment made from rabbit, water-leech, frog, oil, and the roots of *pāṭalā*, a man wanders about amidst a mass of glowing coals.
By applying a plaster made from the fat of a female ascetic, a frog, a leech, and a moon-creeper (*soma-lata*) to the hands and feet, one makes fire as cold as snow.

Having cast the blood of a *duṇḍubha* snake into the middle of his mouth and entered into the midst of water, the wise one may, by his own will, remain within his dwelling as if he were outside. 7.1.50.
Having filled a pair of sandals with the seeds of the *śyonāka* tree and stepped upon them, a person who is thoroughly purified wanders upon the water as if upon a path.
By massaging all his channels with a paste of butter, gold-dust, red ochre, stinking fish, and oil, even a wise man wanders about like a crocodile.

Seeds from a golden tree (kanakaviṭapa) mixed with the powder of woodworms and combined with female cuckoos cause a man to become a ghost (preta). The restoration [of life] is achieved through jaggery and sugarcane juice.
The hair of a twice-born man, a cat, a monkey, a dog-cooker, a crow, an owl, and a mongoose, when crushed with the final excrement, causes madness for all people.
(7.1.54) The tail of a jackal joined with the right wing of a crow, when placed upon a bed, soon releases a terrible seizure of epilepsy upon the enemy. (7.1.55)
Gold, fruits, and *mātuluṅga* [citrons] cause a single instance of intoxication in pigeons, peacocks, and cocks; they become sober again through the act of grooming their feathers. (7.1.56)

Taking golden fruit and mixing it with wood-worm powder according to the great ritual procedure (*mahāsamaya*), one should add it to food and drink. At that very moment, [the victim] becomes insane; within seven days, he dies. 7.1.57.

Having anointed [the victim] with mustard oil, one takes a branch from a *picumarda* tree and uses it as a hand to burn the wood from a cemetery; having taken the ashes and placing them upon someone's head, one causes that person to be driven away. || 7.1.58 ||

7.48 Having combined the feathers of a crow and an owl with the hair of a Brāhmaṇa and a Nirgrantha, and having kindled a fire with *dhūrta* wood and burned it until smokeless, one should take that ash and cast it into the secret bedchamber of whichever two men or women are lying together; at that very moment, enmity arises between them. 7.1.59.
The knowledge of consciousness.

Alternatively, one desiring to bring [a woman] under control should take white beeswax attached to the heart, crush it with honey, and strike her with that powder; joined with his own seed, it brings even a devoted wife under control when administered during the Puṣya asterism.
Pīlu resin, mixed with a paste of sprouts from a man-tree (narataru) extracted by women, when placed in the hand of a maiden, brings her good fortune and she marries.
Bhūtakeśī, Rudantī, Daṇḍotpalā, and Sahadevā—by means of the pride of their own essence infused with the water from [her] eyes, she certainly brings women under her control in an instant. (7.1.62)

A woman of the world, having obtained the powder of *putrañjīvaka* while weeping with a staff-lotus, brings others under her control by sprinkling it with tears from her eyes or by means of physical touch. (7.1.63)
In an instant, she—whose gait was like that of a flowing river, marked by grace, and whose eyes were downcast—was brought under the power of the celestial queen through the water of her gaze. 7.1.64.

With these—sida, dinakara, and tarumūla; mañjiṣṭhā, which is the dwelling-place of the house-sparrow; and kuṣṭha, smeared with blood from one's own body-wounds—one brings the three worlds under control.

This Khadiraguḍikā, acting as Rāma’s messenger and weeping with the pride born of her own essence being superior to milk, instantly brings Śambhu under the power of a woman when mixed with betel leaf.

The nose-rope of the tethered buffalo was scorched by the funeral pyre’s wood; the ashes of the dead woman’s bangles were extinguished by liquid gold; and the powder [of the ashes], when sprinkled with the fluid of one’s own passion, instantly brought the daughter of the Lord of the Gods under one's control—at the mere touch. (7.1.67)
The knowledge of making [something] one's own.

A forehead mark (*tilaka*) consisting of the circle of the Lord of Birds (*khagapati*), the protector of the gods (*surapati*), combined with *śilā*, *rocanā*, and *tāla*, brings one under control in an instant.
A tilaka mark on the forehead made with white dūrvā grass, mṛgadūrvā, and yellow pigment (rocanā) brings a king of men under one's control by the mere sight of it.

In an instant, the circle of the lords of birds and the lords of gods, their topknots bowed down in reverence, were reduced to a state of powder by the tears of the king’s wife as she wept, falling under the power of the monarch.

The flower of a man recently married and then deceased, the flower of the head of Śiva worshipped with *bandhūka* flowers, and the left side of a dead man burnt [on the funeral pyre]—these are equal to the ashes of the funeral pyre when used together with one's own menstrual blood; a woman struck [with this] follows behind [the practitioner]. (7.1.71)
Viṣṇukrāntā, Surapatigopā, Lakṣaṇā, and Rudantī, together with Udarakīṭa, ground into powder and moistened with tears, bring someone under control in an instant. (7.1.72)
Ugrā, sitacchinnaruhā, vatsaka, nābhi, indrayava—when combined with these in equal parts, she who is auspicious brings one under control by means of applying them as a forehead mark (tilaka).

One who has mastered the world brings it under control by means of *talaka* prepared from equal parts of *śrīsakala*, *aruṇacandana*, and *śaśadhara*, combined with the juice of the son of a sage (*ṛṣisuta*) and red *kharā*. 7.1.74.

Having ground together the seeds of the *jayantī*, white *girikarṇikā* seeds, yellow orpiment (*rocanā*), and a boar’s tusk under the asterism of Puṣya, one who applies a forehead mark (*tilaka*) with it on the brow will not become angry upon seeing a king, O Indra among kings, but rather will be pleased. (7.1.75)
The knowledge for performing the Tilakābhyudaya rite.

Alternatively, one desiring to make a pill [should take] the blood from the eye of a black cat, the eye of a black crow, and the left ear of a black boar, and grind them together. Encased within a relic of the Sugata, the pill is placed between the sun, moon, and fire. Accomplished under the Puṣya asterism, it succeeds once the mantra of one’s chosen deity has been recited. When placed in the mouth, one traverses the earth like a Yakṣa, assuming forms at will.

Alternatively, [one may use] the eye of a *kṛṣṇapecikā* (black fly), the eyes of a black crow and an owl, and the eye of a black cuckoo; together with faith in the relics of the Sugata, these are wrapped in *vajrī* milk and made into a pill. When placed in the mouth, it causes invisibility while situated amidst the sun, moon, and fire. || 7.1.77 ||

Alternatively, take the funeral ashes of a corpse burnt on a pyre, along with the powder of a fully ripened *kapittha* fruit and *sarjarasa*; these are rubbed together with heat. This is the sign of the presence of the Sugata’s relics. Encased within those very [relics], the pill is processed under the asterism of Puṣya while placed within the sun, moon, or fire. When it is held in the mouth, one wanders the earth like a *yakṣa*, able to assume any form at will.

Alternatively, a pill composed of *srotoñjana*, *śaśāṅka*, *kaṇṭaka*, honey, *madhuka*, the first flower of [the season], and the filaments (*kesara*) of fresh *halinī*, when placed within a cavity made of the three metals, conceals [the wearer]. (7.1.79) Alternatively, a sprout from the blossom of a blue *aśoka* tree, smeared seven times with the blood of a left-handed woman (*vāmā*), and placed within a cavity made of the three metals, when held in the mouth, conceals the entire world. (7.1.80)

Alternatively, the northern root of *tagara*, uprooted while the moon is eclipsed by a planet, forms a pill (*gulikā*) situated between the sun, the moon, and fire; when placed within the mouth, it makes one invisible.
Gorocanā, the flower of the iṅgudī tree, the hair from the eyes of a *udbaddhikā* bird, and the bile of a peacock—this pill, when combined, is known as the "Kalpalatā" (Wish-fulfilling Woman).
Alternatively, semen from a maiden who has been deflowered in a cemetery and mixed with realgar, when applied as a tilaka mark on the surface of the forehead, conceals even the three worlds.

Alternatively, a man who has applied a tilaka on the surface of his forehead with sprouts from the nest of a crow in a blue aśoka tree in the northern direction conceals himself from all that is moving and unmoving. Srotāñjana, having entered the belly of a pigeon and been cooked in a funeral pyre fire, becomes *siddhāñjana* (the "perfected ointment"). The blood of a black cat is *niryāṇa*. (7.1.84)

Alternatively, one who has extracted honey from earth using fresh, thick grass sprouts, combined with *tāla* resin, when prepared under the *puṣya* asterism, conceals [the mark] even from the perfected ones (*siddhas*) by its application as a forehead tilaka.

Alternatively, even another substance becomes a pill. This pill made of *śilārocanā* (red ochre), prepared together with the aforementioned [ingredients] as before, is a pill for specific purposes and a supreme means of accomplishment. || 7.1.86 ||
The knowledge of invisibility.
Now, I shall explain the application of collyrium.

A wick made from a cloth from a cemetery, combined with oil produced from *śālija* [sesame], should be used to set up a lamp with oil upon three funeral pyres in a cemetery at night on a *bhūta* day. Having placed a lotus leaf over that, one should collect soot (*kajjala*) from the flame. Then, having burned the head of a woman who fears the day, and having infused it with red sandalwood, one should grind it many times on a stone slab during that very night to produce a fine powder. Having mixed this with the previously collected soot and bound it within a vulture’s foot-skin, one should fill a tube made from a vulture’s leg bone with a human-bone probe. Regarding how one should accomplish the application of that collyrium, he says: "The practitioner of mantras should accomplish it according to the ritual procedure within the vulva. (7.1.87)
Knowledge of the application of the accomplished ointment.
Now I shall describe the ritual procedure for the practice, by which practitioners attain success;
constant devotion to meditation and recitation is known as the ritual procedure for the elixir (*rasakarma*).
Due to the absence of the fulfillment of the prescribed rules, it brings happiness only to those of weak character.
Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.2.68: *na yvābhyāṃ padāntābhyām eka-pade* (The augment *it* is not applied to a long vowel following *y* or *v* when these are at the end of a word within a single *pada*).

Mercury born from mountains or oceans is repeatedly treated with sour substances. Through intense grinding within a pit of heated stones in a vessel, it is certainly joined with the juices of *snuhī*, *girikarṇikā*, *jaṭikā*, and *śākhā* along with *āranāla* in a copper cauldron; having applied these, one should grind it until it becomes like fresh butter. Thereafter, it dissolves with rock salt (*sindhu*) and borax (*ṭaṅgaṇa*) processed with the milk of *vajrī*. Having melted half a *karṣa* portion of copper and lead in a sealed crucible (*andhamūṣā*), one should add half a *mātrā* of sulfur (*gandhapāṣāṇa*). Then, one should mix in half a part of gold. || 7.1.90 ||
Thus ends the knowledge of the tastes.
Now, I shall describe the procedure for elixirs (*rasāyana*), which is a compendium of the essence of everything.

Relying upon the seasonal bond (*ṛtubandha*), one should accomplish the yoga-seal (*yogamudrā*). These six great medicinal herbs, which possess the power of the seven beings, are: the four equal parts (*catuḥsama*), musk (*kastūrī*), red sandalwood (*raktacandana*), camphor (*karpūra*), *śālija*, *sihlaka*, *kunduru*, *kakkola*, and *nalikākṣa*. (7.1.92)
Spring, summer, and likewise the rainy season;
the autumn time, the cool season, and further, the arrival of winter.
In spring, the wise man should perform the rite in the forenoon; in summer, at midday;
in the rainy season, in the afternoon; and likewise in autumn, at dusk.
O fair-faced one, this yoga has been described to you by those who know the laws of time: during the winter, during the half-moon, at dawn, and upon the arrival of the frost.
At midnight, one impelled by the winter season should take *puṣpāsava*;
likewise, in spring, one should take *catuḥsama* in the forenoon, which likewise bestows success.
At the end of the rainy season, in the afternoon, the *kastūrīka* [bead] is delightful;
the *nalākṣa* [bead] at midday in summer accomplishes all goals.
In autumn, affection for the lotus brings success at nightfall;
and upon the arrival of winter, camphor— especially at dawn— is most effective.
This is the most excellent and supreme yoga for one who practices it with concentrated mind;
liberated from old age and death, he shall become [so]— of this there is no doubt.
Sūta and gandhaka,
combined with śekhara and mixed with ghee, should be employed in all ritual acts.
Having taken fourteen substances, one should diligently consume them in nine ways;
according to the division of moon and sun, one may perform whatever rite is desired.
Success is achieved within three weeks of seven days. Teeth, nails, and hair fall out and grow back again. Once success is attained, one turns all elements into gold. 7.1.102.
Now, I shall describe the procedure for oil (tailavidhi).

Clarified butter from *nalini* (lotus), clarified butter from *bala*, oil, and the four-fold equal mixture (*catuḥsama*)—these should be combined in equal proportions, along with a paste of black turmeric (*asita-haridrā*) and water decocted from *balā*. Having extracted the essence of *gudūcī*, it should be combined with cow’s milk. Now, I shall describe the proportions to you: take thirty-two *palas* of powder and double that amount of water; one should boil this until four *śarāvas* remain. One should prepare three excellent decoctions from *balā*-water in sequence. Four times the amount of oil is milk, and half of that is *gudūcī*. The paste (*kalka*) should be half of that. Having combined all these with the previously mentioned substances, one should cook them over a gentle fire. If it is to be drunk, then the medium consistency is that which remains outside the *gudūcī* [decoction]. For anointing the head, a coarse consistency is prescribed, for that is intended for the three stages of cooking. For nasal administration (*nasya*), two *pañcaka-palas* (ten *palas*) are prescribed; for drinking, one hundred *palas* are prescribed; likewise, one hundred and eight for anointing. The yogi, being well-composed, should perform this. By using it as a nasal drop (*nasya*), one lives for a thousand years; by drinking it, five hundred years; and by anointing the head, three hundred years—this is my word, there is no doubt. One becomes possessed of a divine form, a beautiful voice, and is always beloved; one becomes an expert in all scriptures, with a radiant body and great splendor, a destroyer of all obstacles. (7.1.103)

Having taken four parts of *catuḥsama* and dried them thoroughly, one should saturate them repeatedly with milk. Having burnt them internally by means of a fire fueled by cow-dung (*gokarṣa*), the yogi should extract the oil and combine it with twice as much oil of black sesamum (*dvikṛṣṇataila*) and double the amount of milk; then he should boil the mixture according to the prescribed method. Four parts of gold, three parts of *triphalā*, and the grasses of the king’s servant (*nṛpaceṭī*)—these are considered the exudations (*niryāsa*) that increase in sequence.

One should cook oil with these substances: *rajanī*, black *bākucī*, *utpala-sārī*, iron-dung (*lohapurīṣa*), *gandhādri*, *guggulu*, resin (*sarjarasa*), camphor, and musk. This oil promotes longevity and increases health; when used as an anointing for the head, it removes wrinkles and graying hair. It undoubtedly effects the removal of all diseases. (7.1.105)
Now, I shall describe the procedure for the rubbing oil (*udvartana-taila*).

That same oil [is used], but the practitioner (*mantrī*) should prepare the liquid according to the previously mentioned method using *raktāpahā*, *kanakadrumā*, *dṛkprarohā*, and *sinduvāra*. Subsequently, these—*śyāmā*, *priyā*, *keśarī*, *bakula*, *vidyādharī*, *nāga*, *cakramardanī*, *śābarī*, *kanaka*, *śikhī*, *pravara*, *bhūtāri*, *parahṛdvallabhī*, *muktakarāra*, *mañjarī*, *hemataru*, *vacā*, *avakucā*, *ghana*, *dāruśarvarī*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *rogendra*, and *nāgabalā*—are the removers of all diseases.

O Goddess, when sandalwood is used as fuel, musk, camphor, guggulu resin, and nakha-incense combined with jaggery accomplish all desires; it destroys itching, scabies, ringworm, and all skin-born ailments—of this there is no doubt, for these are my own words. (7.1.107)

Rajanī, bhavarajas, sinduvāra, ukareṇu, the resin of kanakapattra, and kastūrī, combined with the four-fold equal parts (catuḥsama) and corakeśuna, destroy various diseases, as well as worms, leprosy, and poisons arising from the body; how much more so when combined with bākucī? || 7.1.108 ||
The procedure for the ritual of anointing with fragrant unguents.

Now, having made a powder of *trikaṣāya* together with *catuḥsama*, one who observes the vow should drink it with *śītalakastūrī* for one year. In this way, he causes various ailments such as old age and disease to fall away. When [the powder] has been digested, the practitioner destroys gray hair and other signs of aging; not otherwise. (7.1.109)

Alternatively, having taken four equal parts [of the ingredients] and made them into a fine powder, one should mix it with *triphalā*, ghee, and honey, and consume one *karṣa*. Thereupon, one becomes possessed of a divine form and lives for three hundred years. {C56v} 7.1.110.

Now, it may indeed be taken with a moistening agent, but it should be accompanied by ghee and honey. Then, having collected the three decoctions, one should have them made into a fine powder. Taking a portion the size of a cat's paw (*viḍālīpada*), the yogi should drink it at a moderate dose of musk, gradually increasing the amount. Having made it very cold, he should drink it according to his own strength, up to the measure of a *pala*. It destroys wind-disorders when taken at the proper time and removes wrinkles and gray hair; however, if taken in the heat of the sun, it would cause gray hair.
Alternatively, having taken the three myrobalans (triphalā), one should steam them with milk and water and extract the essence. 7.1.112.

AP 7.90: One should grind red rice and *indrāsaṇa* together with their husked grains. One should then form them into pills (*vaṭaka*). Having cooked them in ghee, one should consume them with honey. Thereafter, on the third [day], it removes all diseases and especially gray hair. By the practice of this for six months, the practitioner becomes melodious-voiced and wise. In the ninth [month], he attains a divine body, moves at the speed of thought, and possesses a retentive memory. After a year, he gains the strength of an elephant and lives for three hundred years. (7.1.113)

Alternatively, one part each of *nāgamūla*, *palāśa*, and *kuṣṭha*, ten parts of *māgadha* (long pepper), and one part [of another ingredient]—these being taken in equal proportions as a powder—should be stirred with cow’s milk. A wise practitioner should consume this, mixed with one *karṣa* of the powder, day after day. (7.1.114)
For yogins dwelling on empty mountains and such places for hundreds of years,
there is constant and perfect satisfaction, while hunger and thirst are abandoned.
For one who dwells in empty mountains and such places, employing this medicinal preparation,
the practice of other methods becomes futile, for he is indeed equal to a Buddha.
But by means of non-attachment, the yogi should meditate upon that state within the solitary world of conventional reality, in caves and mountains. (7.1.117)
He who does not know the bond of the seasons, yet strives for the state of a yogi,
strikes at empty space with his fist and drinks a mirage.
The word *kṣudhāvin* means "one who scratches the husk. (Pāṇini 5.2.118)
The effort of those [who practice otherwise] is in vain, and they shall not obtain its fruit.
Thus has yoga been described by me according to the prescribed rule for the well-composed yogi.
Thus ends the Āyurveda named *Sarvajñānodaya*.
Chapter 98: The First Section on the Sevenfold [Classification] of the Sevenfold [Factors].
Part 2, ap7.99:
O Blessed One, I wish to hear what the nature of recitation, fire-offerings, and so forth is.
How are pacification, enrichment, subjugation, and malevolent rites, as well as offerings, worship, and so forth, performed?
Listen, O Vajra, to the characteristics of the ritual of fire-offerings and so forth according to reality:
first, the practitioner of mantras should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times, and thereafter he should commence the rite.
Having likewise performed the āliḍha, the pratyāliḍha, the samapāda, and the viśākhila postures, the yogin should thereafter cause the vidyā to enter.
The Brahmin, the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, and likewise the Śūdra;
having thus performed the ritual procedure, one should then commence the fire-oblation (homa).

7.103 For a rite of pacification (*śāntika*), one should mark out a circular sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) measuring exactly one cubit. Having marked it, one should dig half a cubit into the ground; the trench should be one span deep. It should be smeared with white sandalwood on both sides. Outside of that, the ground should be circular, and there should be a rim (*pālī*) four finger-breadths high. || 7.2.5 ||

The *pauṣṭika* sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) is two cubits in width; it has a square excavation one cubit deep with a rim eight finger-breadths high. It is strewn with yellow flowers and anointed with yellow fragrant unguents. || 7.2.6 ||

The sacrificial pit for malevolent rites (abhicāra) is triangular and twenty finger-breadths in width; it has a hollow ten finger-breadths deep below. At a height of three finger-breadths, there is a rim, which one should smear with charcoal from a cremation ground. 7.2.7.

In verse 7.106, he describes the common characteristics of subjugation (*vaśya*) and attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*) by means of the single characteristic of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). The shape of the pit for nourishing rites (*pauṣṭika*) is that of a half-moon. The depth of the pit should be half the size of the pit itself. Having fashioned a rim (*pālī*) according to the measurements, one should smear it with red fragrant unguents. (7.2.8)
White powder is used for pacification (śānti), and yellow likewise for nourishment (pauṣṭika);
for killing (māraṇa) it is black in color, and for subjugation (vaśya) it should be red.
As it is in subjugation, so it is in attraction; as it is in killing, so it is in hatred. (7.2.10)
I shall describe the division of directions for you:
the rite of pacification (śāntika) should be performed in the eastern direction, and the rite of malevolent magic (abhicāraka) in the south.
In the west is the fire-pit for subjugation and attraction; likewise, in the north is that for nourishment.
And the royal [sacrifice] has been described previously according to one's karma; thus it is said: "One should dig the sacrificial pits. (7.2.12)
Now, I shall describe the ritual procedure for various types of rice.

Rice grains, sesame, barley, and *dūrvā* grass; milk-rice with ghee and honey, as well as the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), constitute the sacrificial offering (*havya*). Fresh twigs from the five milk-exuding trees, complete with their leaves, are the portions here; they should be offered with both ends smeared with sweet substances, milk, and ghee. Having kindled a fire produced from *udumbara* and *palāśa* wood, one who desires peace (*śānti*) should stand facing the east and offer one hundred and eight oblations at the three times of day. Thereby, peace shall also come to the mandala. 7.2.13
Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.112: *kṛtya-lyuṭo bahulam* (The kṛtya suffixes and lyuṭ are used diversely).

Now, for one desiring to perform a rite for nourishment (*puṣṭika*): [the materials are] sesame, black beans, red rice, barley, and so forth. These same substances are prescribed for the fuel-sticks (*samidh*), but they should be the size of a fist, a cubit in length, soaked in milk and ghee, sprinkled with fragrant water and saffron, and combined with the three sweets, fine rice (*paramānna*), curd, honey, and clarified butter. Also, *śatapuṣpā*, bilva fruit, lotus, *nāgakeśara*, and *vrīhi* rice. Then, having kindled the fire with *udumbara* wood, and having established the connection with the deity according to the ritual procedure, standing facing north, one should offer oblations (*juhuyāt*) one thousand times at the three periods of the day with a well-concentrated mind. When seven days are completed, one becomes a great lord of wealth. (7.2.14)
Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.113

Alternatively, for one desiring to bring someone under control: take red or black sesame, *priyaṅgu*, *nāgakeśara*, *campaka*, *aśoka*, *bakula*, *bāṇa*, and *śatapuṣpa*, along with fragrant substances mixed with ghee and honey; likewise, wood from *devadāru* and *vaṭa*, and pieces eight finger-breadths long from trees such as *pippala* and *udumbara*, as well as the milky sap of the *śallakī* and *guggulu* trees, and other such fragrant materials. Then, mixing these with menstrual blood and "vajra-water," and assuming a red form, one should face west and perform the fire-oblation while reciting the name of the person one desires. Within seven days, that person will be brought under control and will not leave until the end of one's life. (7.2.15)
Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.114

Now, for one desiring to perform an act of sorcery (*abhicāra*): having mixed black sesame, black beans (*māṣa*), and so forth, with the fruit of the *bhallātaka*, black pungent oil, and blood; and having gathered the thorns, bitter, and pungent parts of the black *kubja* tree, as well as [parts] from all other trees, each measuring ten finger-breadths; together with human bone, *vairocana* (cow dung), donkey dung and hair, dog dung and hair, and nails—all this being thoroughly stirred with oil, one who is composed should offer oblations one hundred and eight times, facing south, into a funeral pyre fire (*cityagni*) while reciting the name of the victim; by this, the victim dies within three days. If not, then staying in a secluded place, having prepared a triangular fire-pit (*agnikuṇḍa*), one should offer oblations into a *caṇḍāla* fire using those same aforementioned substances. By that very yoga, the victim is led to the realm of Death (*kṛtānta*); of this there is no doubt. || 7.2.16 ||

Alternatively, one desiring to cause expulsion should mix mustard seeds, mung beans, black gram, and road dust, stir them with blood and pungent oil, and perform the rite with that very mixture. If one offers oblations with the name of a person while adding the ash of a *kāñcana* tree and the excrement of a crow, that person is expelled at that very moment. (7.2.17)

Alternatively, having become naked with disheveled hair, if one offers into the sacrificial fire (cityagni) the flesh of a crow together with camel dung mixed with liquor while uttering the name of someone, that person is expelled at that very moment. || 7.2.18 ||

Alternatively, if one desires to paralyze: having mixed the blood and honey with small grains of rice and pieces of fish-meat and other substances, combined with a crow’s wing-feather, and together with the wood, etc., and tooth-sticks used by a house-crow as *ucchiṣṭa*, one should offer oblations into a square sacrificial pit (*caturasra-kuṇḍa*) while uttering the name of the person; that person becomes paralyzed in all his activities. (7.2.19)
Alternatively, standing facing north with turmeric, yellow orpiment, realgar, and gorocana, if one should offer oblations while uttering the name of someone, that person becomes paralyzed.

With the flesh of a dog and a cock, mixed with camel dung and the blood of a cat, one should kindle a fire with *picumarda* wood and offer oblations while uttering the name of someone; that village shall be destroyed. (7.2.21)

Having stirred [the substance] with liquor according to the Great Pledge (mahāsamaya), one should offer oblations up to one hundred and eight times at the three junctions of the day for six months; [thereby] one becomes the sovereign of the maṇḍala.
One should offer a hundred oblations with a jackal; after three months, poverty is destroyed instantly. (7.2.23)
Having mixed [the substance] with beef and blood, one should offer a thousand oblations; he becomes submissive for as long as he lives, without a doubt.

One should mix that very same flesh with liquor and offer it as a sacrifice with the left hand; even a Buddha becomes submissive, let alone ordinary humans. Furthermore, by offering saliva, a tooth-stick, or one's own body-unguent mixed with liquor as a sacrifice, one brings [the target] under control without a doubt. (7.2.25)
Household flowers that have been chewed and spat out, combined with human hair, become a supreme means for immediate summoning through the performance of homa.

Having stirred [the substance] with crow feathers in pungent oil, one should offer it as an oblation in a fire of *dhuttūra* flowers while reciting the name of the person; this brings about immediate expulsion and death.

One should offer into the fire in the house *atimuktikā*, *kuṣmāṇḍa*, mung beans, black gram, hemp, emetic nut, and black mustard along with *tamāla* leaves. This brings about the binding of the mouth; of this there is no doubt. (7.2.28)
If one should offer dog meat together with vajra-water while reciting the name of a person, that person will be brought under control within seven days. || 7.2.29 ||
One should offer horse-flesh together with Vairocana at night; within seven days, one brings a king under one's control.
One should offer elephant flesh with semen; it brings a city under one's control.
Ap 7.123: Fish meat together with liquor should be offered as an oblation. Up to one hundred and eight [times], all women become subject to one's will. 7.2.32.
If one should offer a thousand oblations of crow meat alone under someone's name for three days, even Vajrasattva would flee, let alone insignificant humans. (7.2.33)
If one offers oblations of crow and hawk flesh into a fire of *dhuttūraka* wood while reciting the name of someone, that person is driven away. 7.2.34.
If one should offer human flesh and the flesh of a bird under someone's name, that person becomes insane; by offering oblations into a fire of chaff, he becomes restored to health. (7.2.35)
Therefore, the rites must indeed be performed by means of the preliminary service (*puraścaraṇa*);
otherwise, there is no doubt that one will become an object of ridicule for all the world.

7.126 No one should be granted access to the secret [of this practice]. When there is such disclosure, a person attains neither accomplishment (*siddhi*) nor happiness. Therefore, the practitioner of mantra (*mantrin*) must not carry out this application of ritual action (*karmaprasara*) in the presence of anyone. If he wishes to perform it, he should do so entirely alone; then all the rites of the practitioners of mantra will succeed.
Thus ends the second section of the seventh [chapter], the Ritual for the Fire Offering (Homa).
Part 3, ap7.128:
O Lord, I have heard [of this]; how is the procedure for extracting the mantras [to be performed]? What is the source of this curiosity?
I do not know their distinction; please tell me, O Mahāsukha.
The Blessed One said:
Listen, O goddess of great wisdom; I shall tell you their mantra.
In the beautiful triangular mandala, Māmakī is indeed the secret lotus.
Having fashioned an eight-petalled lotus with its pericarp in a hidden location,
one should extract from there the Hero who accomplishes all desires and goals.
Through the divisions beginning with the letter 'a', the mantra is the supreme Lord of the classes.

The second letter of the first [vowel-series] is conjoined with the "void-of-void" (the zero); the third letter of the seventh [consonant-series], adorned with the half-moon of the fifteenth; having then taken the seed-syllable of awakening (B), it is honored by the fifteenth. This is declared to be the Heart-mantra. 7.3.5.
Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.1.133: *na yvābhyāṃ padāntābhyām* (The augment *n* is not applied after the vowels *i* and *u* when they occur at the end of a word).
She is said to be the mother who generates peace for the Buddhas, the accomplisher of all activities,
the reviver of the dead, and the impeller of the vajra-samaya.
And so it is said: Oṃ vajravairocanīye svāhā. 7.3.8.
The fourth [syllable] of the second [group], adorned with water (vāri), is likewise called the upahṛdaya.

The first seed-syllable of the *ūṣman* [letters] is *Khecarī*, adorned above. The first of the second [group] and the second of the seventh, joined with *Caurī*. Likewise, the first of the eighth is *Vajrā*, the supreme benefactor. Taking these twenty syllables, the seat is formed with the sixteenth; this is considered the beautiful seat of *Gaurī*. Taking the first of the second and the twenty-seventh, one should likewise apply *Caurī* to that. The fourth of the second is the seat of *Vajraḍākinī*. The first of the third is doubled. The fourth of the second is joined with *Vajraḍākinī*. Taking the eleventh syllable, differentiated by the third vowel, one should join the fifth of the fifth, which is *Gaurī*. The fourth of the second is *Vajrā*; then taking the supreme heart, the sixteenth, as well as the twenty-sixth doubled. The fourth of the second is adorned with the fifth vowel.
Of the fourth [verse], one should join the first which was completed with Gaurī;
of the fifth, however, one should join the fifth of that very same [verse] with Gaurī.
In the applications of the vajra for protection, she is always the accomplisher of rites;
she is remembered as the one who bestows strength upon those afflicted by the fear of the great vajra.
Thus he said.
Oṃ jvala jvala hūṃ phaṭ bhyo svāhā. || 7.3.11 ||
Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.1.139

The first of the second [vowel] and the first of the fourth [consonant], with *Caurī* joined below—it is considered beautiful. The fourth of the seventh, with *Gaurī* placed above it; then taking the first of the second and the eleventh [vowel], adorned on the head by *Caurī*. The fifth of the fifth, joined with the third vowel; the first of the second and the first of the fourth, with *Caurī*—it is supremely beneficial. The first of the second and the beginning of the fourth, adorned on the head by *Khecarī*; and from the second, the first and the eleventh, together with *Caurī*, thus completed. (7.3.12)
Dharmapuṣṭi always provides strength, as does Mahākoṣavatī;
by the mere recitation [of their mantras], they act according to the word of Vāgvajra.
Oṃ vajradharma hrīḥ svāhā. || 7.3.14 ||
Having taken from the sixteenth mantra the most beautiful Vajrī,
and the second of the semi-vowels joined with Caurī of that very same [mantra]. (7.3.15)
Taking the first of the fifth [vowel] is considered the seat of Ḍākinī;
then, taking the sixteenth, with the first of the fifth, Vajra is applied as its seat.
Having taken the twenty-seven syllables as conceived by Caurī,
that which is the first of the fifth [group] is joined below the position of Ḍākinī. (7.3.17)
The second [syllable] of the seventh [group], which is the divine *caurī* manifested from the heart,
is the great army of Buddha-vajra throughout the entire realm of sentient beings.
One performs everything like a slave; one will certainly bring [the subject] under control at that very moment. || 7.3.19 ||
Thus spoke the Blessed One, Mahāvajradhara.
All [mantras] have the syllable *oṃ* as their lamp; one should extract the mantra ending with *svāhā*.
This grants success and fulfills all desires, just as the word of the Tathāgata declares.

Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.1.147: *na yvābhyāṃ padāntābhyāṃ pūrvau tu tābhyām aic* (The suffixes *a* and *i*, as well as *ā* and *ai*, are not substituted for the final *i* and *u* of a word, but rather *ai* and *au* are substituted in their place).

Oṃ kara kara kuru kuru bandha bandha trāsaya trāsaya kṣobhaya kṣobhaya hraḥ hraḥ pheṃ pheṃ phaṭ phaṭ daha daha paca paca bhakṣa bhakṣa, O you who hang with a garland of entrails, blood, and fat, seize, seize the serpent or snake dwelling in the seven netherworlds, threaten, threaten, draw near, draw near hrīṃ hrīṃ jñaiṃ jñaiṃ kṣmāṃ kṣmāṃ hāṃ hāṃ hīṃ hīṃ hūṃ hūṃ kili kili sili sili cili cili dhili dhili hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā! This is the mantra of the King of Vidyās, which accomplishes all rites. 7.3.21.
Having first placed Vairocana (A), then the fourth of the sibilants (Ś), one should apply Pukkasī (Ū), which is adorned by Śūnya (the nasal bindu), followed by Svāhā at the end. (7.3.22)
By this recitation of one hundred thousand times, one shall always paralyze the world.
Having first placed the lord of the syllables (A), followed by Khecarī (Ī),
and joined them with Svāhā at the end, one brings even the Buddhas under one's control.

Taking the first [letter] of the Vedas and the second of the second, one should join it with the void at the beginning and *svāhā* at the end; by this, a wise person can even cause Buddhas to be eradicated. 7.3.25.

Having first placed Vairocana (Oṃ), [one should place] the third letter of the third [group], joined with the neuter [vowel], adorned by water (U), and [followed by] the void (H) at the end of Svāhā; this causes enmity. || 7.3.26 ||

Having first given the Lord of the Letter (A), followed by the fourth of the seventh [letter] (Ū), which is the Void (bindu) conjoined with Vajraḍākinī, ending in Svāhā—this is the mantra for malevolent rites (abhicāraka). || 7.3.27 ||
Furthermore, having bestowed the Lord of Colors (Varṇeśvara), which resembles a red HŪṂ and ends with SVĀHĀ, one may attract the entire world, including Tilottamā and the likes of Rambhā.
First, having uttered the syllable *moha*, one should employ the sound *ghuḥ*;
then, having again performed the utterance *svāhā*, one may slay gods and humans.
Between two of the eight [syllables], adorned with eight sets of eight, having placed the beginning of the Mohakula and joined it with the partless [seed-syllable] ending in *svāhā*.
Then, having taken the seed-syllable of karma joined with "Vairocana Svāhā" at the end...
In all the door-keepers,
there is the fourfold seed-syllable of the neuter, as well as the remaining vowel in the same manner.
Having placed the beginning of the Vedas [the syllable Om] at the start, one should recite the mantra ending with "svāhā."
Puṣpā, Dhūpā, Gandhā, and likewise Dīpā the goddess;
Vaṃśā, Vīṇā, Mukundā, and likewise Murajā.
In this manner, one should indeed arrange the ritual procedure within the circle of the Gaṇas.
Now I shall describe the arising of the Tārikā, which is the miraculous manifestation of all ritual actions.
There should be a four-faced lotus situated in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
The practitioner of mantra should, according to the ritual procedure, draw that seed-syllable (varaṭaka) marked with three lines, circular in shape on all sides. It is as follows: [7.3.36]
Oṃ, O gracious Tārā, whose face is nectar, whose eyes are nectar, accomplisher of all aims, bringer of all beings under control: whether woman or man, or kings, bring them under control, svāhā!
In its center there should be an eight-spoked wheel endowed with syllables.

In its hub (varaṭaka) is the first letter of the fifth [varga], adorned with a crescent moon and a bindu. Then one should encircle it in the form of a garland, ending with *svāhā*. In the petals (*puṣkara*), the syllable *hrīḥ* is interspersed. By means of these two wheels, the practitioner of mantra, following the ritual rules for seven days, shall bring even a king under his control.
Furthermore, O knower of mantras, one who places the ten-syllable mantra within a ten-spoked wheel in the center of a lotus,
with the name of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*) interspersed in the pericarp (*puṣkara*), brings that person under control for as long as they live; of this there is no doubt.
Having drawn a six-cornered wheel, the knower of mantras should place the six-syllabled mantra [around it];
in the center, he should employ the syllable *hrīḥ*, followed by "bring under control" (*vaśaṃ kuru*), *hrīḥ*, and the word *svāhā*.
Having written this on birch bark together with yellow orpiment, lac, and red sandalwood paste, whoever should wear it— 7.3.41.
If one can bring even gods and other such beings under one's control, how much more so lowly human beings? (7.3.42)
In the center of the Varuṇa-maṇḍala, one should draw a three-pronged vajra;
its central hub (varaṭaka) should have four faces, with the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) interwoven within it.
Having properly inscribed [the mantra] twice upon two shallow bowls with chalk, one should cause them to be fixed as pillars. 7.3.44.

There should be an eight-spoked wheel with lotus spokes all around. One should arrange the placement of syllables according to the ritual rule, interspersed with the syllable *gaḥ*. The center of the lotus heart should be adorned with eight instances of the syllable *gaḥ*. Having written "gaḥ svāhā gaḥ" interspersed with the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*), one should inscribe this on a stone slab with turmeric juice and place it face down. It becomes well-stabilized; it is not otherwise. (7.3.45)

That very same wheel, however, interspersed with the syllables *hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*, should be drawn upon a human skull using poison, blood, and mustard seeds with a human bone. One who stands in a cremation ground shall thus cause death. (7.3.46)

However, having interwoven that very [mantra] with the syllable *oṃ* and having written it on birch bark with saffron, one should worship it with yellow flowers or with the five types of offerings (*pañcopacāra*). Within seven days, nourishment (*puṣṭi*) occurs. || 7.3.47 ||
By interweaving that very syllable with the word *svāhā*, it becomes a protection. 7.3.48.

That same [practitioner], knowing the mantra consisting of ten syllables interspersed with the syllable *āḥ*, having written the name with white sandalwood paste, having worshipped it in a shallow dish with white fragrant flowers, and having performed worship according to his means, should perform the recitation of one hundred and eight [times] three times a day according to the rule. Within seven days, peace occurs. 7.3.49.

One should write the syllable *āḥ* of [the name of] such-and-such person with the letter *e* in the middle. Above and on both sides of that, one should place *hūṃ*, and below it, *vaṃ*. It should be surrounded by three lines on the outside in the intermediate directions. Having written this on birch bark with yellow pigment (*gorocanā*), one should place it in the midst of ghee and honey. Within seven days, one will certainly bring [the person] under control. (7.3.50)

In a four-petaled [diagram], one should place the syllable *hrīṃ* in the center, with *hrīḥ devadattaḥ* [in the middle]. Then, one should write four *hūṃ* syllables on the outside. Having drawn this with red sandalwood paste upon an unbaked clay bowl, it pacifies anger; of this there is no doubt. (7.3.51)

One should write [the mantra] on birch bark with saffron and *gorocanā*, or else with lac juice. One should wear one wheel, while placing the other wheel in the midst of clarified butter and honey. Whomever one desires, that person becomes beloved.
A separate mantra: Oṃ sarvamohani tāre tutāre ture, delude, delude all the wicked ones, O Blessed One! Bind, bind all the wicked ones! Hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā. (7.3.53)
Having tied a knot at the end of one's garment, if one travels on the road, one is not robbed by thieves.
Having consecrated a lotus marked with a wheel seven times with mantras, whoever one gives it to becomes submissive. [This applies] to a wheel marked with a lotus. 7.3.55.

An eight-petaled lotus should be drawn, endowed with the syllables *hrīḥ* and *śrīḥ*; in the pericarp, one writes *hrīḥ*, [the name] Devadatta, and *śrīḥ*. Having written this on birch bark with yellow pigment (*gorocanā*), one should wear it; good fortune will be attained at all times.

Having drawn an eight-petalled lotus, one should extract the mantra of the Moha family. It should be surrounded on the outside by a circular line and encircled by eight three-pronged vajras. Following this procedure, one should draw it with saffron. Having tied it on the arm, one should wear it; it provides constant protection for that person. || 7.3.57 ||

That same [mantra] is a wheel, but it is devoid of the *vajra*. It may be placed either upon the pericarp or on the outside. It is as follows: *oṃ hūṃ hūṃ budhya budhya khāda khāda chinda chinda dhuna dhuna matha matha bandha bandha amukam amukena saha vidveṣaya hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā* || 7.3.58 ||

Ap 7.185: This [mantra] belongs to Hayagrīva for the purpose of inciting enmity. Having inscribed it with substances used for malevolent rites in the middle of the hooves of a buffalo and a horse, it causes enmity at that very moment; if it can do so even against Hara together with Durgā, how much more so against insignificant mortals? (7.3.59)

Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.1.186: *na yvābhyāṃ padāntābhyām pūrvau tu tābhyāmaic* (The vowels *ai* and *au* do not undergo *vṛddhi* when followed by *ya* or *va* that stand at the end of a word; rather, *ai* and *au* themselves are substituted in place of those *ya* and *va*).

Having drawn two fire-mandalas according to the method of the pair of upper and lower corners, one writes *hūṃ gaḥ hūṃ hūṃ gaḥ hūṃ* above that, and again *hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ* in the lower portion; then *hūṃ gaḥ hūṃ hūṃ gaḥ hūṃ* with an outer head-mark. In the center, one writes *hūṃ gaḥ hūṃ* using poison, blood, and mustard seeds, along with charred cemetery ashes, neem-leaf juice, and vajra-water. Having written this on a cloth from a cemetery or a rag from a corpse, and having encircled it with the Mahābala mantra, one places it over a blazing fire; thus, one paralyzes the enemy. (7.3.60)

Oṃ! Having established a lotus in the center, adorned with eight *āḥ* syllables, situated within the Maheśvara maṇḍala of the Oṃkāra and bound by the eight locations; and having placed the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*) upon its pericarp, resplendent with four *hūṃ* syllables; and having recited the mantra of the injunction for the Vajradhara who stands upon the head of the [target] contained within a pair of shallow bowls (*śarāva-sampuṭa*), and having visualized it surrounded on all sides with a vajra-thread; by this, one paralyzes all men, gods, and those born of the three bodies. (7.3.61)
The Maheśvara mandala is marked with three prongs and eight vajras. In its center is a square mandala, as follows:
Oṃ pāta pātanī svāhā! To the east. Oṃ jambha jambhanī svāhā! To the south. Oṃ moha mohanī svāhā! To the west.
Oṃ stambha stambhanī svāhā. In the north. 7.3.62.

Furthermore, one should draw a square mandala and, in its center, a Maheśvara mandala; in the middle of that, one should write "Paralyze so-and-so! Having inscribed this very yantra on birch bark with a solution of turmeric, one should place it inside the mouth of a frog, pierce its mouth with a *madana* thorn, and set it upon the cheek of an upward-facing frog with its head turned downward. At that very moment, it paralyzes the enemy army.

The wheel should be circular in shape. The vajra has five prongs situated in the intermediate directions. At the head of the central prong of that [vajra] is the top of four *hūṃ* syllables. Upon its hub (*varaṭaka*), one should write the garland of mantras as follows:

Oṃ! You step upon; you stride forth; you are rising; you are descending; you are the sun; you are the moon; you are the wave; you are the forest; you are the thicket; you are the robe; you are the great robe; you are invisibility; svāhā! || 7.3.64 ||
Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.193: *na saṃjñāyām* (Not so when it is a technical name).

The syllable *oṃ* is everywhere. In its center is a three-pronged vajra situated toward the cardinal directions. On the central prong, one should write *oṃ vattāli*; likewise on the left and right, *oṃ varāli* and *oṃ varāhamukhi*. One should write [the mantras] on all the prongs in sequence, starting from the head: *oṃ mārīcyai* in the intermediate directions beginning with the northeast. Thus, in the center: *oṃ varāli vattāli varāhamukhi, jambhaya stambhaya the body, speech, mind, and mouth of all the wicked and malicious ones!* In the middle of that, the syllable *māṃ*; in the middle of that, the name *Devadatta*, followed by *rakṣa rakṣa* (protect, protect!). Outside the syllable *māṃ*, [one writes] *oṃ mārīcyai devatāyai*. Having drawn this wheel with saffron on birch bark (*bhūrja*), one should wear it. Protection is obtained everywhere. (7.3.65)
Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.1.194: *na yvābhyāṃ padāntābhyām* (The augment *n* is not applied after the vowels *i* and *u* when they stand at the end of a word).

One should draw a man facing the cardinal directions with disheveled hair and earrings on both ears, with a three-pronged trident and a thunderbolt (*vajra*) marked with the syllable *haṃ* situated above his head. Above his forehead, [place] *lāṃ lāṃ*. Starting from the chin on the right, one should write: "May those who strike at my mind fall [under the power of] Pratyāṅgirā! One should draw the shape of a *caitya* extending from his navel up to the top of his face. Above that, one should draw a five-pronged *vajra*. Inside the hollow of the *caitya*, one should write the *dharmas* in the form of a garland, starting from the right turret (*harmya*) down to the left side. At his neck, one should place the syllable *hūṃ* facing downward. In its center, one should draw a five-pronged *vajra* facing upward. There should be twelve *hūṃ*s on the sides. Below the *caitya*, on the thighs and shanks, one should write the vowels excluding the neuter ones. On the man’s chest, one should write "May the Pratyāṅgirās fall [upon them]" as before, but arranged in rows. Again, on the shanks and the penis, there should be rows. [The syllables] *puṃ puṃ raṃ* are on the eight limbs; *tāṃ tāṃ* on the surface of the water; *puṃ raṃ* on the feet. Under the constellation Puṣya, one causes this figure of a man to be drawn using poison, salt, black mustard, neem leaves, the juice of the *unmattaka* plant, and charcoal from a cremation ground. For Devadatta, one should interlace [the name] with white sandalwood paste in the center of the *vajra*’s hub. The venerable *caitya* is [drawn] with white sandalwood paste, and the *vajra*’s hub with saffron. One should maintain it with the mantra (*vidyā*). It provides great protection for him at all times. (7.3.66)

One should draw the eight-sided Mount Sumeru, marked with a three-pronged vajra. In the center of each corner, one should draw the syllable *naṃ*, marked with a *hūṃ* and surrounded by two *hūṃ*s. Between the two corners, starting from the northeast direction, one should draw lac, meat, and iron. On the outside, it is enclosed by a circular line. In its center, one should draw Gaṇapati. Narteśvara [is to be depicted] with a gesture holding a vessel of sweetmeats (*modaka*) to his right; to his left, a three-pronged vajra and a radish with its leaves. Mounted upon a mouse and standing on a lotus, he should be thus installed. (7.3.67)
HŪṂ GAḤ HŪṂ HŪṂ GAḤ GAḤ HŪṂ VṚṢṬIṂ KURU HŪṂ GAḤ GAḤ HŪṂ || 7.3.68 ||

One should briefly draw [the diagram] on the surface of a jar, on the heart, on the belly, on the navel, and above; using the juice of the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*) mixed with blood, one should draw this upon an unbaked clay bowl and heat it over a fire of *khadira* wood. This will certainly produce rain, and not otherwise. Having drawn that same [diagram] on the inner surface with yellow orpiment (*haritāla*), one should heat it over a fire; this will arrest the clouds. (7.3.69)

Having drawn an eight-spoked wheel adorned with eight *ga* syllables, one should inscribe within its center the name of the target (*sādhya*) interlaced [with the mantra], according to the ritual procedure, on a cloth from a cremation ground or on a cloth struck by a weapon, using a mixture of yellow orpiment and turmeric juice. Having fashioned a Gaṇapati out of rice flour, one should place this wheel in its heart, set it within a pair of well-baked earthen bowls, encircle it with a yellow thread, and worship it with yellow flowers according to the oral instruction. Thus, O Goddess, has the method for paralyzing even the best of kings been described.
In the middle of the syllable *māṃ*, one should write this very mantra:
*oṃ vattāli varāli varāhamukhi sarvaduṣṭapraduṣṭānāṃ mukhaṃ stambhaya*. (7.3.71)
Having drawn [the mantra] on two bricks with turmeric juice and having enclosed them within a casket, one should bury them in the ground; this will paralyze all wicked beings, and not otherwise.

Now, having drawn a diagram on the ground in the shape of a vulva together with a linga, one should write the name [of the woman] there. Remaining alone by himself, he should urinate for seven days; by means of the ritual involving the encirclement of the *hrīḥ*-syllable noose, he attracts whichever woman he desires. (7.3.73)

7.202 One should draw an eight-spoked wheel situated in the center of a moon-maṇḍala, along with a vajra-banner, an axe, a trident, and a noose; likewise, a double-vajra, a khaṭvāṅga, and a goad—one should draw these in brief. In its center is a full moon-maṇḌala. In the middle of the moon, [one should state]: "So-and-so, so-and-so, shall obtain a son. At the hub of the wheel, one should write this mantra, as follows:
Oṃ maṇidhari vajriṇi mahāpratisare hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā.
Then, in the center of the lunar disc, one should write this mantra:
Oṃ amṛtavilokini garbhaṃ saṃrakṣaṇi ākarṣaṇi hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā.
Under the Puṣya asterism, having inscribed [the mantra] on birch bark with saffron and gorocana, one should wear it; thus one obtains a son. (7.3.76)

The wheel should have the shape of a jar, and its neck should be long like that of a camel. Following this procedure—namely, *yaḥ*, *de*, *yaḥ*, *va*, *yaḥ*, *da*, *yaḥ*, *tta*, *yaḥ*, *mu*, *yaḥ*, *ccā*, *yaḥ*, *ṭa*, *yaḥ*, *ya*, *yaḥ*—one should write the name of the person [to be expelled] with the blood of a crow on a cloth banner from the temple of Īśvara. Having tied it to the neck of a living crow, one should release it in the northwestern direction (*vāyavyā*); it will swiftly cause expulsion. 7.3.77.

Having drawn an eight-spoked wheel situated in the center of the solar disc, with the *hūṃ*—the seed-syllable of reality—enclosed within its core, and having meditated upon the Vajra-Sun, one should subsequently interlace the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Having written this on birch bark with saffron and *gorocanā*, the yogi should wear it according to the prescribed rite; for him, there will always be protection. (7.3.78)

There should be a lotus with twenty-four petals and three lines all around. By writing this—*oṃ hrīṃ klīṃ*—and holding it in the hand according to the rules under the Puṣya asterism, one brings others under control through mere touch, like a servant. (7.3.79)

The wheel should have the shape of a drum and be marked with a vajra and lotus; it is surrounded on the outside by three lines. This is the summary of Kāyavajra and the others. Through the manifestation of the Karma-vajra, there is the subduing of all enemies. One performs all rites by means of the mantra as seen in the ritual procedure. Regarding this mantra, he says: Ap 7.209: [Mantra follows] Ap 7.209: [Mantra follows]
Oṃ sumbha niḥsumbha hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ gṛhṇa gṛhṇa hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ gṛhṇāpaya gṛhṇāpaya hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Ānaya ho bhagavān vidyārāja hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā ||7.3.80||
The eighth seed-syllable from the *ya*-group, likewise combined with twelve vowels and separated by intervening syllables, is called the six-limbed *heruka*. (7.3.81)
The conjunction of the six heroes is established in each individual syllable:
the first is the heart, and the second is traditionally known as the head.
The third should be given as the crest-lock (śikhā), the fourth becomes the armor (kavaca);
the fifth shall be the eye (netra), and the sixth is called the weapon (astra).
Absorbed in union with Vajravārāhī, he is resplendent with four arms,
adorned with a yellow radiance, divine, and has his hair bound with a crescent moon.
Having made oneself Heruka, wearing a garland of bones and holding a *khaṭvāṅga* staff in hand, one should contemplate the state of being Heruka.
Having meditated on the Jñānasattva in the heart, one should assign the rampart to the directions;
having meditated upon it as filled with the flames of wrath and adorned with formidable ornaments.
Having driven away the hosts of obstacles and having bound up all directions while threatening them, he thus girded himself with armor, becoming impenetrable even by the gods. || 7.3.87 ||
Then one should draw a mandala, square and with four doors;
having placed in its center a six-petaled lotus provided with filaments.
The mantra-practitioner should scatter [the offerings] twofold and draw the *ḍākinī*-circle;
he should place the hero in the pericarp and likewise the *ḍākinī*.
The gate, marked with a three-pronged vajra and yellow in color on all sides,
should be placed in the center of the wheel; one should then place the female messenger and the sequence of the rite at the gate.

Having performed a great worship under an auspicious constellation, the observer of the vow should wear this wheel; O Goddess, it wards off untimely death, the stroke of weapons, and other such calamities. My word is without doubt: this is the wheel named "Bringer of Victory over Enemies."

Alternatively, one should bury it in a copper plate under the Puṣya constellation, having written that very *cakramantra* interspersed with the name of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*) and devoid of a door. Having placed it in water, one should worship it three times a day; then all [obstacles] become paralyzed. When there is a lake that does not dry up, the concentrated mantra-practitioner performs the rite of pacification (*śānti*) according to the rule. (7.3.92)
Oṃ, O gracious Tārā, whose face is nectar, whose eyes are nectar, who accomplishes all aims, svāhā!
For the purpose of subjugation, one should write this mantra. || 7.3.93 ||
Now, regarding the warding off of all malevolent beings, they recite this mantra: atha sarvaduṣṭanivāraṇe idaṃ mantram āhuḥ || ap7.225 ||
Oṃ, O Deluder of All, Tāre Tuttāre, delude, delude all the wicked! O Blessed One, bind, bind all the wicked! Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā! || 7.3.94 ||
Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.2.26: *na yvābhyāṃ padāntābhyām* (The augment *n* is not applied after the letters *y* and *v* when they stand at the end of a word).

In its center there should be a moon; in the middle of the moon, one should draw a circular shape with the first [syllable] of the fourth [mantra], in the form of a filament. In its center, the knower of mantras should scatter a hexagon, interwoven with the syllable *hrīḥ* according to the ritual rule. This is called "The Victory over All Armies and the Arising of Tārā. By reciting this one hundred thousand times, one causes the earth to tremble. One dries up oceans, ponds, and the like. One turns poison into nectar and nectar into poison. Having consecrated a sugar-cake (*sarkaroṭaka*), one should throw it upward, downward, in the cardinal directions, and in the intermediate directions. All gods, asuras, yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas are bound. It removes the yoga of all ḍākinīs. It removes the poison of all nāgas. Having recited over a sugar-cake, one should throw it into rivers; it makes them flow upstream. With that very sugar-cake, one paralyzes waves. Reciting a thousand times while ascending upward, one wards off a great rain. Having performed a thousand recitations facing the enemy army, one should enter into battle. Even when being struck by hundreds of weapons, no pain arises, nor is one cut by weapons; one becomes a body of diamond (*vajra*). One performs many wonders, shimmering, impelled by the King of Mantras. (7.3.95)
Thus ends the third section of the seventh [chapter], titled "The Arising of the Wheel for the Expansion of All Ritual Actions."
May [the Blessed One] teach, according to the proper method, the auspicious characteristics of consecration.
I do not know the practice of recitation or meditation; how is the ritual procedure for the fire-oblation performed?
Blessed One, whose essence is the adamantine core, the sole synthesis of all phenomena,
please out of your grace explain that which is difficult to attain even through great passion.
The Blessed One said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the practice of meditation according to the rule.
By the mere application of meditation, one should accomplish all activities.
Regarding that, first he speaks in order to explain the purification of the ground:
"Assuming the majestic display of Vajrasattva, standing with pride in the double-legged posture."
Having become the Conqueror of the Three Worlds, one should destroy all obstacles. || 7.4.4 ||
The placement of the steps for the goddesses exactly as prescribed,
as well as the ritual of the fire-oblation as directed, and the characteristics of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Then, having performed the yoga of the mudrās, one should subsequently draw the maṇḍala.
Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.2.34.

Having become Krodhavijaya and having meditated upon himself as three-faced and six-armed, he should emanate clouds of wrathful deities. With those very [deities], one should meditate upon all the Tathāgatas together with their retinues in the ten directions by means of the empowerment-mantras of yourselves; thus, protection must be established for the preceptor and his disciples. Having exhorted [them] in this way, he should then withdraw and internalize them, placing them within the *hūṃ* syllable at the center of the moon and vajra at his own heart. Then, having merged into a single unity with the Blessed One and all the Tathāgatas—this Vajradhara-form yogin of his own consort—and having preceded this with the empowerment of the three syllables, he should perform the lotus-turning (*kamalāvarta*) and brandish the vajra with his right hand. With his left, he should ring the melodious vajra-bell. With a *hūṃ* blazing like a vajra placed on the sole of his foot, possessing the pride of the wrathful *hūṃ*-born form, and preceded by the utterance of *hūṃ*, the wise one should overwhelm all evil beings—the gods, asuras, and guhyakas—while pronouncing these words through the visualization of the wrathful body. (7.4.7)
Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.2.35

"Let those who are here—be they gods, asuras, yakṣas, rākṣasas, pretas, piśācas, apasmāras, bhūtas, ḍākinīs, ostārakas, mahallakas, mahallikās, attendants, retinues, garuḍas, kiṃpuruṣas, or mantra-attainers—depart from this spot on earth. Here, by the preceptor [Name], for the sake of fulfilling the enlightenment of the disciple [Name], and for the purpose of causing all sentient beings to attain unsurpassed gnosis, the King of Mandalas [Name] is to be drawn. Therefore, having heard the command of Vajradhara, depart immediately! Should anyone not depart, Vajrapāṇi, his face wrathful with the blazing syllable *HŪṂ*, shall shatter that person’s head into a hundred pieces with his great gnosis-vajra, which is ablaze and fiercely flaming. || 7.4.8 ||

When [the mantra] has been recited three times, by means of the great vajra-formation, one should emanate the forms of one’s own vajra-wrath deities and, moving with haste around the entire mandala ground while stepping with the vajra-step, one should cover all the malevolent ones. In this way, the appropriation of the site (bhūmiparigraha) shall be accomplished.

Then, having invoked the deity Earth with the mantra, one should perform the rites of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and consecration (*adhivāsana*), and so forth. Having paid homage to the Guru—that is, having saluted the preceptor of the mantra—one should subsequently summon the deity Earth, who is golden-hued and holds a water-pot in her hand; having caused her to enter, bind her, and worship her with the five offerings such as fragrant perfumes and the like, one should perform the consecration (*adhivāsana*) and bring about her presence (*saṃnidhāna*). || 7.4.10 ||
Then he states the invocation mantra:

Oṃ, come, come, Great Goddess, Mother of the World of Earth, adorned with divine ornaments full of all jewels, resounding with the tinkling of necklaces and anklets, worshipped by Vajrasattva; taking this *argha* offering, accomplish the fire-offering rites! Hrī hī hī hī haṃ svāhā! (7.4.11)

Having performed the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) and other rites with this mantra, the sweeping of the ground should be carried out. With the words "feces and urine" and so forth, one should sprinkle and smear [the site]. Then, one should fumigate it with the incense of *mahāmāṃsa*. Having worshipped there, the *mudrā* should be established in the center; immediately after the fumigation, one should cause the *vidyā* to enter. Thus [ends section] 7.4.12.
"O Blessed One, should one cause a knowledge-deity (vidyā-devī) fashioned from wood and the like, adorned with poured-out consecrated substances, to enter [the disciple]? Thus he asked. 7.4.13.

The Blessed One said: "One should cause a maiden of the *caṇḍāla* or other such castes to enter; in their absence, any common woman. One should place the limb-mantras: the syllable *hrīḥ* on all the limbs. One should place the syllable *hrīṃ* on the heart, the *ūrṇā*, the throat, and the head; the syllable *bhruṃ* in the centers of the *bhaga*s. (7.4.14)
"What, O Blessed One? How could the syllable *bhrūṃ* exist in their midst?"
The Blessed One said: [Ap 7.243]

"Noble sons, by the word 'middle' the navel is meant; there one should place the syllable *Bhrūṃ*. Having thus arranged the syllable, he says that one should meditate on the form of Locanā and the others: 'There one should meditate on the form of Locanā—either a Brahmin woman or a Śūdra woman—in the case of pacifying rites (*śāntika*); as having the form of Locanā, white in color and adorned with all ornaments, one should meditate. For subjugation (*vaśya*), one should manifest a Caṇḍālī or Tārā, red in color. For nourishing (*pauṣṭika*), [one should meditate on] a dancer of royal lineage, Pāṇḍaravāsinī, yellow in color. Thus, having worshipped according to the specific ritual action with the five offerings, one should cast a handful of flowers. One should cast a flower or semen into her vulva; in this way, the ground for the fire-offering (*homabhūmi*) becomes consecrated. (7.4.16)

In the ritual procedure for the mandala, a girl who is either common or otherwise should be understood [as required]. The fire-offering (homa) procedure connected to the mandala is that which demonstrates it, including the secret Dharma-mandala. One should delineate the two kinds of mandalas by this method: the external powder-mandala (rajomaṇḍala) and the secret Dharma-mandala, up to one's own commitment (svasamaya).
