Thus, on a plot of ground that serves as the site for the yogin’s seat, one should construct the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa). So he said. 7.4.17.
I shall now proclaim the rite of oblation (homakarma), which accomplishes various ritual acts.
For those gods who have fire as their mouth are established in the true essence of the oblation.
By means of the fire oblation (homa), the gods are gratified; being gratified, they bestow accomplishment.
Those mantras which are deficient or excessive—all of them are made complete by the fire oblation. || 7.4.19 ||
Therefore, those who hold the vajra of the three bodies praise the fire offering;
the fire arising from churning performs auspicious deeds. (7.4.20)
The one born in the Mātaṅga cremation ground, who accomplishes inauspicious rites,
[is associated with] the circle, the square, the half-moon, and the triangle.
The vajra-mark shines upon the rampart at the corner of the mandala;
the uṣṇīṣa, the lotus, and the vajra are set within the jewel-lotus.
One who knows the rules for the true nature of the fire-oblation (homa) should perform it in the center of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa),
sitting as is appropriate with his hands between his knees.
The sacrificial ladle (sruva) soaked in clarified butter, as well as the oblation (huti) which is full to the brim;
on the right side, the implements required for the fire-offering, and on the left, a vessel of water.
In front [is placed] the vessel for the *argha* offering. Once the sprinkling and sipping of water have been performed with [water] consecrated by the *sarvakarmika* mantra,
the sacrificial pit is encircled on all sides with the tips of *kuśa* grass held firmly in place.
Having recognized the blazing fire, one should invoke the deity of fire according to the rule with this mantra,
while moving the right thumb and the hand in the gesture of fearlessness.
Come, come, O Great Elemental Deity, best among sages and brahmins!
Having taken this oblation as your food, remain present here.
Oṃ, O Agni, blaze, blaze; enter for the sake of great glory, for the bearer of offerings to the gods and ancestors, svāhā!
One should sprinkle [the deity] with the Vāma-vajra mantra, accompanied by the five offerings of worship. Then,
one should [visualize] the three-eyed Lambodara who has arrived from the south-eastern direction.
Four-faced, four-armed, red in color, with matted locks,
seated within a circle of fire, and adorned by the rays of his ritual actions.
In the first right hand he holds the gesture of granting boons, and in the second a rosary;
in the left hand a water-pot, and in the second a staff.
Having meditated upon such a form— one of red hue, adorned with ornaments, and surrounded by sages— one should cause it to enter into the center of the sacrificial pit.
An oblation should be offered for him, along with three boons and a complete homa;
then, having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should transform [the fire] into the form of a flame.
By this sequential method, the wise one should satisfy the deity;
having satisfied them, he should ask for forgiveness and inform them of his desire for spiritual accomplishment.
Adorned with parasols, banners, vajras, vases, lotuses, and hooks,
they sport with single-crested, double-crested, and triple-crested forms, which are respectively superior, inferior, and middling.
And especially one that spirals to the right.
The wise one should observe a flame that is white in color and auspicious at its end;
it resembles Indra’s bow, is brilliant, very smooth, and has a luster like that of an *indragopa* insect.
Resembling saffron and lapis lazuli, fragrant and delightful;
shining like gold and silver, smokeless, radiant, and as stainless as the sun.
In rites for pacification, she has the luster of white; in rites for nourishment, she resembles yellow;
in rites for enchantment, she is red; and in rites for malevolent sorcery, she is most excellent blue-black.

One should observe it thus: if smoke with abundant crests arises gradually, accompanied by sparks and with flickering flames that are repeatedly breaking off, it is [the sign of] fire. Its color is rough and dark like the leaf of the *palāśa* tree, resembling a spear or the sun, and likewise similar to *gośīrṣa* sandalwood. It has the smell of a corpse, the smell of raw meat, or a harsh odor. If there is an obstacle, one should then dispel those obstacles and examine it by means of the signs of the flame.
One who is devoted to the recitation and meditative cultivation [of this mantra] will swiftly attain all accomplishments.

Beginning with the syllable *oṃ* and ending with *svāhā*, accompanied by the chanting of songs and joined with uninterrupted vowels, this brings about pacification (*śānti*), nourishment (*puṣṭi*), and subjugation (*vaśyatā*).
In the state of *śānti*, one is peaceful, tranquil-minded, and expansive; it is an increase through nourishment.
In the state of *vaśya*, however, the mind is submissive, characterized by the playful confusion of one afflicted by passion.
With a body blazing with flames from the syllables *hūṃ* and *phaṭ*,
his mind intent on devouring the three worlds, he stands established in the rite of sorcery (*abhicāra*).
Having arranged the section of the injunctions and separated the syllables of the mantra,
one should worship those deities who are assigned to each [deity] by means of various rites.

In all procedures for the fire-oblation (homa), the practitioner who knows the ritual rules and masters the mantras should first offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) and thereafter increase the performance of the rite.
One should offer oblations according to the true nature of the fire; this is the sequence for the procedure of homa.
In rites for pacification (śāntika), nourishment (pauṣṭika), and subjugation (vaśya), the offering should be made with auspicious substances.
By means of an oblation of feces, urine, blood, marrow, bone, and great flesh, all become filled with happiness. ||7.4.46||

Then the Blessed One, Mahāvairocana-vajra-tathāgata, entered the samādhi called the Vajra that Accomplishes the Wheel of Wisdom, and spoke this expansion of the ritual application for accomplishing all wheels, both external and internal.
The mandala described by the Buddhas for whichever deity is situated in the center of the wheel is called the "Vajra of Exaltation" (Abhyudayavajra). || 7.4.48 ||
One should perform the rites of pacification, enrichment, subjugation, and malevolent magic through applications,
by means of the visualization of the wheel-knowledge with the Cakrin as the presiding deity. (7.4.49)
One should meditate upon a full moon disc in the center of the bhaga,
[and within it] the goddess Tārā of great supernatural power, who is perfected from the gnosis of the syllable *Tāṃ*.

The practitioner should meditate upon her who abides in the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*): seven-faced, three-eyed, sixteen-armed, with a smiling countenance, having the luster of emerald, endowed with fresh youth, clothed in variegated garments, adorned with necklaces, anklets, neck-chains, crest-jewels, armlets, earrings, waist-bands, and various other ornaments; her head adorned with a blue lotus, her lips like the *yava* flower, standing in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, while another [figure] stands with palms joined in reverence, terrified by the fear of the Lord of the Gods; glowing with a red radiance, surrounded by shimmering Buddhas, the beloved mother of all sentient beings. By doing so, one shall swiftly attain Buddhahood. (7.4.51)

In the first [right hand] a sword, in the second a blue lotus, in the third an arrow, in the fourth a vajra, in the fifth a goad, in the sixth a staff, in the seventh a scimitar, and in the eighth the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*). In the left hands, he should hold: in the first a skull-cup, in the second the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*), in the third a bow, in the fourth a *khaṭvāṅga*, in the fifth a noose, in the sixth three severed heads, in the seventh a jewel, and in the eighth a vase. (7.4.52)

The first face on the right is blue; the second is brilliantly yellow. The first on the left is white; the second resembles green beryl. The upper face is distorted, smoke-colored, and most terrible, hideous, fierce, and fearsome. One should thus meditate upon the Goddess, the bestower of all accomplishments.
Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.2.79: *na saṃjñāyām* (Not so when it is a technical name).

Then, one should meditate upon the supreme form known as Heruka—one who has an upward-turned face, the appearance of a donkey, the ability to take any form at will (*kāmarūpin*), four feet, and is entwined by tridents and serpents. Within the center of the *bhaga*, one should visualize a smoke-colored wind mandala arising from the syllable *yaṃ*. Above that, in the center of a moon disk, one should contemplate oneself in the form of Mañjuśrī, transformed from the syllable *dhīḥ*. Having visualized a sun mandala within his heart from the syllable *āḥ*, and having performed worship according to the ritual rules by emitting rays of light from that sun mandala, one should meditate upon the syllable *hūṃ* endowed with five-colored rays above it. From its transformation arises Vajrabhairava, who has nine faces, the form of a buffalo, sixteen feet, thirty-four arms, is naked, black in color, possessed of great majesty, adorned with a crest of skulls, extremely terrifying, with an erect *liṅga*, standing in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, with a large belly and massive body, hair standing upright, a blazing and radiant appearance, adorned with ornaments of garlands of skulls, roaring like the time of the great dissolution, and devouring human blood, fat, serum, flesh, marrow, and bone; one should contemplate him swallowing the three worlds along with Brahmā, Indra, Upendra, Rudra, and the rest. (7.4.54)

Laughing with a loud laugh, with a lolling tongue, and terrifying even fear itself—this is the first face, that of a buffalo. On the right horn are three faces, blue, red, and yellow, with mouths wide open in rage; on the left are white, smoke-colored, and black. Between those two is a deep red face from which blood flows. Above that is the beautiful form of Kumāra, very yellow, slightly wrathful, adorned with youthful ornaments, five silken rags, and a crest-jewel. Having thus made this firm, the practitioner, well-composed, should meditate. (7.4.55)

Ap 7.281: Then, in the first right arm is a knife; in the second, a slingshot; in the third, a mace; in the fourth, a small dagger; in the fifth, a *kaṇaya*; in the sixth, an axe; in the seventh, a spear; in the eighth, an arrow; in the ninth, a hook; in the tenth, a club; in the eleventh, a skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*); in the twelfth, a discus; in the thirteenth, a thunderbolt; in the fourteenth, a thunderbolt-mallet; in the fifteenth, a sword; and in the sixteenth, a hand-drum (*ḍamaruka*). ||7.4.56||

In the first left arm is a skull-cup; in the second, a head; in the third, a shield; in the fourth, a foot; in the fifth, a noose; in the sixth, a bow; in the seventh, intestines; in the eighth, a bell; in the ninth, a hand; in the tenth, a cloth from a cremation ground; in the eleventh, a man pierced by a trident; in the twelfth, a fire-pit; in the thirteenth, a drinking cup; in the fourteenth, a threatening gesture (*tarjanī*); in the fifteenth, a triple-bannered gesture (*tripatākā*); in the sixteenth, a wind-cloth. With two [arms] he holds an elephant hide. (7.4.57)

On the right foot [of the deity] are a man, a buffalo, a bull, a donkey, a camel, a dog, a ram, and a jackal; on the left foot are a vulture, an owl, a crow, a *sigha*, a hawk, a minister, a great bird of omen, and cranes. One should thus meditate upon or have painted this Vajrabhairava. (7.4.58)

Below that is the great cremation ground (*mahāśmaśāna*), inhabited by *rākṣasas*, *kṣetrapālas*, and *vetālas*. It contains men impaled on stakes, men hanging from banyan trees, men being burned, and men pierced by spears. It is filled with many crows, birds, and dogs, and is tumultuous with cries of "Hā! Hā! The yogin should thus visualize this Great Bhairava, known as the "Accomplisher of All Fierce Deeds. Thus spoke the Blessed One. (7.4.59)
Then, [one should visualize] Mārīcī, produced from the syllable *māṃ*, possessing the radiance of the sun,
seated upon a chariot drawn by seven horses, and blazing with a circle of flames.
She has three faces, three eyes, and six arms, with a yellowish complexion;
the face on the right is blue, while the one on the left resembles a kunda flower or the moon.
Divine, with the radiance of many rays, intent on protecting the ten directions,
she smiles with all her faces through amorous gestures, exultant in her youth.
Her limbs were draped with various garments, and she was adorned with all kinds of ornaments;
her matted locks, crowned by the five Buddhas, shone brilliantly with flowers.
In the right hand, [he holds] a vajra; in the second, a needle and thread;
in the third, a Śaravartinī; and in the left, a noose with the threatening finger (tarjanī).
In the second [hand] was an ashoka sprout, and in the third likewise a bow;
[he was surrounded] on all sides by various rays from clouds consisting of shimmering Buddhas.
"By cultivating this, sentient beings indeed come under one's control," so said the Blessed One, the Vajra-holder, the Tathāgata Vajrasattva. (7.4.66)
One should indeed visualize the solar disc situated in the center of the space-element,
[and upon it] the goddess born from the transformation of the syllable *paṃ*, yellow in color and most brilliantly radiant.
She has three eyes and three faces, with a countenance of wrathful laughter;
she is adorned with all ornaments, possesses six arms, and is in the bloom of youth.
In her right hand she holds a thunderbolt; in the second, an axe; and in the third, she bears an arrow. (7.4.69)
In her left hands she holds a noose with the index finger, in the second a bunch of leaves, and in the third a bow; her matted locks are beautifully entwined with flowers.
Seated upon a white lotus, adorned with a red radiance,
she emits flashes of wrathful flames and is terrified by those very flames of wrath.
For those planets that, being scorched, cause harm to the subjects.
Blazing with anger, unimpeded, with her veins fixed and motionless,
she is again white, raining down the nectar of the five-colored Buddhas.
As before, she has faces on the left and the other [right] sides. In this way the yogi should meditate for the sake of pacifying all illusion; she is named Parṇaśāvarī, the remover of all diseases.
Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Mahāvajra. 7.4.74
Listen, O highly fortunate goddess, to the visualization of Vajrakrodha:
having assumed the form of Wrath, one should manifest the King of Wrath. (7.4.75)
Having four arms and four faces, or likewise up to a hundred thousand arms,
with a white body and great wrath, he gazes upon Vajravārāhī, who possesses the same color and holds the same weapons.
The hero is garlanded with skulls, his limbs smeared with ashes,
adorned with the five mudrās, and marked by a crown of matted hair and a trident.
With a face slightly terrifying with fangs, seated upon a great corpse,
he possesses a radiance equal to the color of red within a great eight-petaled lotus.
Endowed with the fourfold knowledge and adorned with the image of the Buddha,
she has the form of a horse, possesses four arms and four faces, and is decorated with ornaments of serpents.
Joined with the manifest and the unmanifest, situated within the skull, white in color,
adorned by the four faces, and embellished with the letters ya, ra, la, and va.

Starting from the foot up to the head, according to the prescribed method, one should visualize [the elements] in sequence—smoky, red, yellow, white, and those belonging to the wind and so forth. By merely visualizing this through meditation, one causes a woman to melt like a milk-tree; it is not otherwise. (7.4.81)
Joined with the syllable *raṃ*, red in color, four-armed,
surrounded by a garland of flames, terrible, four-faced, and adorned with the face of a jackal.
Precisely by means of the syllable *hūṃ* as a preliminary, when the subtle vajra has been fully manifested at the tip of the nose, one should fill the body of the one to be accomplished.
When all the joints of the limbs are bound together by the universal vajra,
by that vajra-strike, his body becomes a mass of flames and blood. (7.4.84)
One should visualize the Vajraḍākinīs sucking [the essence] from all sides.
Oṃ vajraḍākinī, attract the blood of [Name]! Hūṃ phaṭ!
By this sequential application, the supreme attraction of blood is achieved;
thus it has been taught, O Goddess, and there is no doubt that [the victim] withers away.
Then, the form of Mahiṣa was manifested, complete with all its essential characteristics:
terrifying, black in color, most formidable, four-faced, and fearsome.

He has eight arms and is adorned with four feet; in his [right] hands he holds a vajra, a mace, a sword, a discus, and likewise a hand-drum (ḍamaru); in his left hands he holds a khaṭvāṅga staff, a skull-cup, a bow, and a noose.
One should again emanate Vajra-angry deities bearing various weapons,
having mentally extracted the protection of the subject according to the ritual procedure.
One should contemplate the goal to be accomplished by means of those nooses, having bound [the victim] toward the southern direction,
while striking the slayers with the Vajra-krodha or another vajra.
Indeed,
with a sword he was tearing apart those whose bodies were dripping with entrails and excrement.
Oṃ vajrarākṣasa, devour this! Phaṭ!
Then, having assumed the face of a dog, one should perform the meditation on the Vajra-rākṣasa.
Oṃ hrīḥ ṣṭrīḥ vikṛtānana hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā! This is the mantra of the buffalo-faced one in the form of Yama. (7.4.95)
One should meditate on [the deceased] being surrounded on all sides by crows, jackals, and vultures, and being torn apart by them with piercing cries. (7.4.96)
One should visualize Vajradaṃṣṭra mounted upon the circle of wind;
one should imagine the person to be converted (sādhya) mounted upon his back. (7.4.97)
Being tormented by Vajrakrodha, he was led toward the southern direction; indeed,
his footprints were like the leaves of a whirlwind and like dust.
By uttering its name, one should indeed conceal the thunderbolt from the feet of Vajramuṇḍa;
thus, through the yoga of visualization, one should perform the rite according to the injunctions.
One could cause even Śakra to be eradicated, let alone the creatures upon the earth.
Having wrapped it with the feathers of an owl and the hair of a Brahmin ascetic,
one should bury it in the ground after incanting the name-mantra over it, in order to effect suppression.
One should visualize the end of the battle with just two Vajrakrodhas;
by visualizing thus, the yogi causes hatred according to his desire. (7.4.102)
Having joined the syllable *cī* with the form of a horse's head,
this is the supreme method for attracting liquor.
The Great King Hayagrīva, the Supreme Lord, who is green in color, four-faced, four-legged, and four-armed, attains accomplishment.

First, one should visualize [the deity] according to the ritual procedure: dark blue, slightly yellow, with three eyes, and faces that are black, white, and green, with the horse-head at the top, appearing fierce. In the right hands, he displays the *tripatākā* gesture; in the second, a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*); in the third, a sword; and in the fourth, an arrow. In the left hands, a double-lotus (*viśvapadma*); in the second, a spear (*śakti*); in the third, a mirror; and in the fourth, a bow. He stands in the *pratyālīḍha* posture upon the sun, engaged in the *tāṇḍava* dance, and causes Hari, Hara, and others to fall. Thus the mantra-practitioner should meditate. (7.4.105)

One should visualize the syllable *maṃ* at the navel of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*). One should visualize a belly full of liquor produced from the syllable *maṃ*. Afterwards, appearing to vomit, he is seen disgorging the liquor. || 7.4.106 ||

Having gone toward the direction of the wind, one should draw a square mandala and apply seven drops of perfume. The wise practitioner should conceal it with a shallow bowl. Upon that, one should fashion Mount Sumeru with eight peaks arranged all around, traversed by a flashing vajra, and impregnated with the seed-syllables of the seven wombs of the wind (*yaṃ*) and the syllable *laṃ*. This is the Māhendra [mandala], which has its internal breath concealed and is marked by the syllable *laṃ*. When this is constructed through such application, it effects a binding that is like the dissolution of the wind.

On the eight petals of an eight-petalled lotus that has been visualized, one should place the eight nāgas. In their center, one should visualize the form of Vajrakrodha with blazing masses of flames; pressing down with the soles of his feet, he causes the serpents—who are clouds of water—to vomit forth. One causes rain to fall by reciting the *hūṃ* syllable while squeezing the seed-syllable of the nāgas, which is encircled and flanked by two *hūṃ*s, in the middle. (7.4.108)

One should lick the clouds filled with sevenfold water, which have been drawn in by inhalations and expelled by exhalations, as light as cotton wool—[clouds] that are the agents of the great dissolution, possessing the brilliant luster of a red sun, standing in the sky with gaping mouths, their tongues blazing with the syllable *hūṃ*. Then, one should dispatch the hosts of one’s own mudrās, blazing [with power]. In an instant, they rend and pierce [the clouds], making them tremble with the *hūṃ* syllable.

With a complexion like the autumn sky, situated within a mandala of fire, the Immovable Servant (Acalaceṭa) emerges from the center of the forehead. In the station of Vairocana, he rains down six arms holding a sword, a noose, an arrow, a bow, a bell, and a vajra; victorious over Māra, surrounded by innumerable wrathful deities, terrifying all obstacles and filled with the sound of the syllable *HŪṂ*, he could shatter even the three worlds in their entirety. ||7.4.110||

One should fashion a human form out of earth mixed with human blood and human bone-dust, and nail it down with a human-bone peg. After reciting the Mārīcī mantra twenty times over it, one should visualize that [form] having entered the mouth of Gaṇapati; then, from behind, it is struck with a vajra-mace. "Oṃ sumbha niḥsumbha, crush the obstacles with the vajra-mace! Hūṃ phaṭ! By means of such meditations and ritual actions, one wards off human obstacles in an instant. (7.4.111)

Arjuna, whose eyes were described [by Indra], his body adorned by hundreds of thousands of serpents, gave commands to the eight classes of *nāgas*. Those *nāgas*, visualized with hundreds of thousands of faces stationed in the sky, having heard the command, halted the rain with masses of clouds. (7.4.112)

Garuda, too, should meditate thus while reciting the mantra: extinguishing the fire of the *āśī* with the wind from his wings, and creating a river with the strike of his beak. *Oṃ vajranārāyaṇa, extinguish the fire with fresh water clouds! Hūṃ.* 7.4.113.

Situated in the midst of the space-element, he has three faces and three eyes, adorned with all ornaments, clothed in a tiger skin, red in color, possessing great splendor, and radiant like the rising sun.
A sword and a skull-topped staff, as well as a bow and an arrow,
a vessel for human flesh and likewise a hand-drum.
In her left hands she holds a noose and a goad, adorned with a blue lotus;
in her right hand she displays the gesture of granting fearlessness.
Standing in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, most formidable, stationed upon the sun and engaged in the *tāṇḍava* dance,
he creates within the cremation ground a canopy of great garments filled with red flames.
The goddess Tārā, who delivers one from cyclic existence, arises from the syllable *hrīṃ*.
By merely visualizing her in this way, the yogin attains the state of Buddhahood.
How much more so, then, other accomplishments? || 7.4.118 ||
Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.3.41

Alternatively, one who desires to bring [another] under control should go to the foot of an *aśoka* tree on the eighth day of the month of *aśoka*, put on red garments, and, adorned with all ornaments, recite the mantra. Abiding in the three-faced yoga and visualizing oneself as red in color, one should subsequently emanate from one’s own body a red two-armed goddess holding a hook and a noose in her hands. Having pierced the heart of the object of practice (*sādhya*) with that [emanation], one should contemplate her being drawn into one’s own body. One should cause the bewildered *sādhya* to enter. One should place the ten-syllable mantra, red in color, upon his heart. Furthermore, one should cause the *sādhya*—in the form of gnosis—to enter those syllables, and contemplate him as having become unified with them. By this yoga of meditation, one brings even a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) under control within seven days; for as long as life lasts, there is no doubt. (7.4.119)
Now, for the purpose of warding off obstacles caused by thunderbolts, he says:

Having visualized oneself as the form of Śrī Paramādya—three-faced, four-legged, four-armed, with a blazing radiance of red color, surrounded by the four goddesses Vajrā and the others; having visualized [the central deity] holding a vajra, a goad, and an arrow in the right hands, and Garvā standing at the hip holding a bow in the left; then, one should visualize clouds of Buddhas adorned with all ornaments, bestowing fearlessness with their right hands and pouring down from their jeweled necks the vases of consecration, while Vajranivāraṇa remains in the sky.
Oṃ, O Vajra-splendor of Great Bliss, hūṃ! 7.4.121
When the surata-bond has been performed, thus the unsurpassed state, which unfolds through the yoga of speech, is revealed.
Regarding killing, he said this:
"In the rite of pacification, there is the elision of the final *ya* and of the two instances of *nikāra*."
Thereafter, the remaining letters [are placed] after the middle *yakāra*, as desired. (7.4.123)
Thus it has been told, O Goddess, that which accomplishes all rites.

One who desires to bring a woman under one's control should again, on the eighth lunar day, remain in the yoga of Kurukullā and perform this meditation. Having consumed a madana fruit, one should then apply a tilaka with the juice of kāñcanāra and recite the mantra while making offerings. Ap 7.347.
Oṃ, may [Name] be brought under my control, hrīṃ!
When it is accomplished, he comes with ten thousand. 7.4.125.

Now, regarding the restoration of one bitten by the Time-Snake (Kāladaṣṭa): one should visualize an eight-petaled lotus in the heart. Above that, upon the eight petals, one should contemplate the third vowel (I) as white in color. One should also visualize oneself in the form of the Naga Śeṣa, white in color, dripping with the nectar of the vowel *i*. One should contemplate that nectar being emitted from the eyes of that Naga and falling upon the body of the person to be treated. By means of this yoga of meditation, one renders poison that pervades the three realms free of its toxic power. 7.4.126.
Now, one who wishes to turn back the moon and the sun should fashion an image of the moon and sun out of rice flour and cast it into adamantine water (*vajrodaka*). One should recite the mantra:
*oṃ candrārka mā cala mā cala tiṣṭha tiṣṭha hevajrāya svāhā*. (7.4.127)
After reciting the six-pointed mantra, one should then undertake this rite; the moon and sun remain [in their courses], and there is no distinction between night and day.

One who desires to destroy an enemy army should accomplish the rite of *khaṭikā*. Having ground *khaṭikā* with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and *kuṭhāracchinnā*, one should fashion a pill (*vaṭikā*). (7.4.129)
Oṃ vajrakartari hevajrāya svāhā. || 7.4.130 ||

For the sake of accomplishment, one should recite [the mantra] ten million times; then it becomes effective. Having accomplished that, one should wrap around the neck of a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*). Having wrapped it, one should break it; all enemies have their heads severed.

One who desires to split open the gods should accomplish the *tilaka* [mark]. O Wielder of the Vajra, one should grind with Akṣobhya during a solar eclipse a *vajrabandhaka* flower that has been consecrated, mixed with *kuṭhāracchinnā*. Having ground it, one should prepare an axe. Treading upon it with the foot, one should recite the mantra:
*Oṃ vajrakuṭhāra sphāṭaya sphāṭaya phaṭ phaṭ svāhā*. (7.4.132)
For the sake of accomplishment, one should recite [the mantra] ten million times. Afterwards, one should pay homage to the *tilaka*. Whoever pays homage to it bursts asunder. 7.4.133.
Now, I shall describe the ritual application for the end of the rainy season.

Oṃ Āḥ Phūḥ. Having fashioned Ananta in his essential nature according to the ritual rule, one should bathe him with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*). One should worship him with black flowers and smear him with the juice of *nāgadamana*. One should anoint his head with elephant ichor and place him within two shallow bowls (*śarāva*). One should fill [the bowls] with the milk of a black cow and wrap [the image] with thread spun by a black maiden. Having constructed a lotus pond in the northwestern direction, one should install that Ananta there. On its bank, one should construct a mandala according to the ritual rule; in its center, one should place Ananta. One should visualize Hevajra treading upon Ananta, eight-faced, four-legged, adorned with sixteen arms, and possessing twenty-four eyes. Thereafter, the master, inflamed and with a fierce mind, should recite the mantra in a solitary place. (7.4.134)

Oṃ ghuru ghuru ghaḍa ghaḍa śama śama ghoṭaya ghoṭaya! To the one who causes infinite agitation, the Lord of Nagas: He! He! Ru! Ru! Ka! Draw forth the nagas who have gone to the seven underworlds; cause rain to fall; threaten; roar! Phuḥ phuḥ phuḥ phuḥ phuḥ phuḥ phuḥ phuḥ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā! || 7.4.135 ||
If it does not rain, then one should recite this mantra in reverse. [Then] it rains. If it still does not rain, then their heads shall burst like the flower-cluster of the *arjaka* tree. (7.4.136)
Then, by one desiring to split the clouds, one should write this mantra upon a cloth from a cremation ground:
*oṃ tarjaya tarjaya śmaśānapriyāya phaṭ svāhā*.
Thus ends the seventh king of manuals, titled "The Arising of Meditation for All Rituals," from the *Śrī Sampuṭodbhava Mahātantra*.
Ap8.
Chapter A8,
Part 1
“O Blessed One, I wish to hear about the definition and the defined by others;
I do not know the four principles— please explain them, O Mahāsukha.”
The Blessed One said:
Listen, O Vajra, to the characteristic of crossing over saṃsāra according to reality.
The bell is also the second [initiation] of the previously mentioned Vajra-reality.
The third is the rosary of beads, and the fourth is characterized by knowledge;
these are the waves of the four principles that lead one to the desired further shore.
In the center is the Lord Vairocana, and in the east is Akṣobhya;
one should place Ratna in the southern needle and Amitābha in the west.
In the north, one should place the deity Amoghasiddhi upon a lotus with eight spokes representing the eight factors of enlightenment, according to the respective stages, using a five-pronged vajra.
Padmaprabha, Maitreya, Gaganagañja like Samantabhadra,
Mañjuśrī the lord of yakṣas, Viṣkambhin, and Kṣitigarbha as well.
One should establish these eight according to the respective levels of the deities;
in the center of the three groups of ten, the deity of knowledge is absorbed.
In the lotus, one should assign the eight goddesses to their respective places; likewise, the four beginning with Vajrāṅkuśī are placed in the directions starting from the northeast.
In the center of the needle are the five Ḍākinīs; by name, Jñāna is in the middle.
Vajraḍākinī is in the east, and in the north is she named Ghorī.
Vetālī is at the ends of the directions, and Caṇḍālī is the Mistress of the South.
A wise person should know these deities as the vajra-elements. 8.1.10
Since the principles of the vajra reside within the vajra-nature of one's own consciousness,
the yogi, beginning with the vajra, should cause the vajra-mind to arise.
One should strengthen the purification of the *vajra*; it is considered supreme in the *vajra*-dharma.
All those *vajra*-principles arise from the application of *vajra*-activity.
By means of the yoga of the vajra radiation, he is the one who ferries sentient beings across the ocean of saṃsāra;
through the yoga of the vajra attraction, he is the knower of the yoga of the vajra-stambhana (stiffening).
Just as darkness is destroyed by a lamp together with consciousness, so too should one destroy the afflictions with the vajra of knowledge and attain the direction of light. 8.1.14
It is shown that for all [beings], the Vajra is accomplished as the Vajra-nature;
he is devoted to the essence of Vajra-dharma and to Vajra-liberation. (8.1.15)
Having stepped upon the lotus with the vajra, one should accomplish [the rite] through all the principles;
the wise one should accomplish Vajrapadmāvatī for him. 8.1.16.
Listen, O Vajradhara King, to the characteristics of the vajra-bells; all the deities listen to the reality of the sounding of wisdom. (8.1.17)
The grasp is clearly three parts, beautifully adorned with a girdle;
it is auspicious, resembling a blue lotus or a water lily, gentle, and set within a jewel-lotus.
In the center of the eight directions and intermediate points is the Buddha as the ninth;
one should consecrate the nine deities, beginning with the first of the nine, within the needle-like [mandala] of the nine deities.

The needle emerging from the mouth of the sea-monster (makara), positioned within the moon-rays, is renowned as the "Nine-Needle" (*navasūcī*); it is the Vajra of Gnosis, supreme in the world. 8.1.20.
Established at the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa) as far as the limits of the space-element,
he is the All-Knowing One who abides in all places throughout the infinite world-systems of the ten directions.
The eight directions are indeed known by these names, and they are proclaimed as the eight goddesses;
one should assign the eight-syllable seed-mantra to the eight directions.
The goddess Tāriṇī is in the east, and Pāṇḍarā is in the north;
Māmakī by name is in the west, and Buddhalocanā is in the south.
The fourth [deity] is golden, sweet, and lovely, adorned with a garland of diamonds;
her form is like the center of space, and she is an abode of the qualities of beauty and grace.

Born from a fully blossomed lotus, it is like a vessel of the nectar of wisdom; situated within that [lotus] is the mind, the abode of the nectar of knowledge, located in the realm of formless existence.
The goddess Prajñāpāramitā is the beauty of form and the abode of virtues;
one should visualize her, as before, upon the upward-pointing lotus and vajra. (8.1.26)
Regarding the "staff of knowledge" (jñānadaṇḍa), it is the cause of both universal dissolution and creation for those of middling capacity.
One should move the eight locations; this is the purpose of the *āli* and *kāli*.
By means of the application of the vowels and consonants, they sever all of saṃsāra;
the vajra and bell are indeed the means and the very essence of that means.
One should extend both hands there; thus, the *kamalāvarta* [mudrā] is fivefold.
Having meditated upon the Sun on the right and the Moon on the left, [one performs it]. (8.1.29)
As for the method regarding the bodies, one should contemplate one's chosen deity;
having brandished the vajra in the north, the wise one should then perform the re-establishment.
By means of the form of the *hūṃ* chant-song, one should please all the Buddhas;
he is the Vajra-Ullāla, the savior in the liberation of sentient beings.
In the liberation of phenomena, one should see the high as low and the low as high.
hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ ho ho ho || 8.1.31 ||
Through wisdom and means, there is no sound; it consists of the hand of wisdom and means.

Oṃ vajradharmaraṇita praraṇita saṃpraraṇita, you who move through all buddhafields, whose nature is the resonance of the perfection of wisdom, who gladdens the heart of Vajrasattva, hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ ho ho ho svāhā. || 8.1.33 ||
Oṃ! O Vajra-samaya of the accomplishment of all Tathāgatas, abide! I hold you fast: hiḥ hiḥ hiḥ hiḥ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā! || 8.1.34 ||

Awakened by the dharma of wisdom and skillful means, she may sound [the drum] for the sake of sentient beings who are submerged in the mud of ignorance, beginning from the very origin of the world. || 8.1.35 ||
One should grasp the vajra with its true essence and ring the bell according to the Dharma;
by means of the application of wisdom and skillful means, accomplish the welfare of sentient beings, O yogins! 8.1.36
Like the ringing of a bell on an elephant, the self-perfection of one who lacks the intent for reality and is devoid of the principles of yoga appears far off. (8.1.37)
Thus ends the first section of the eighth [chapter], concerning the principle of the bell (ghaṇṭātattva).
Part 2,
Chapter 8, Verse 39:
Listen, O Vajra, to the characteristics of the rosary and other implements as they truly are.
By which correct procedure they are accomplished; of this there is no doubt. || 8.2.1 ||
Crystals, pearls, and other white substances are for special pacifying rites; such are the characteristics of the rosary. (8.2.2)
For the rite of nourishment (*pauṣṭika*), a wise person should calculate the rosary using beads made of gold, silver, copper, or especially lotus seeds.
Saffron and other such substances, as well as various perfumes and specific fragrances,
should be dyed and made into pills; this is proclaimed for the purpose of subjugating others.
One should employ rudrākṣa, kālabīja, and likewise human bone for fierce rites; this is proclaimed as *abhicāra* (sorcery).
Peace, nourishment, subjugation, and malevolent rites; the *putraṃjīva* [mantra] which performs all actions;
the fifty [syllables] for mantra accomplishment, and half of that for subjugation. 8.2.6.
One hundred and one [recitations] are for pacification (śāntika), likewise one hundred and eight for nourishment (pauṣṭika); however,
for malevolent rites (abhicāra), one should employ the specific ritual of sixty.
According to the division of the ritual actions, one should fashion the rosary beads and so forth;
in each of the eight directions and with the Buddha in the center as the ninth.
Regarding the sūtra on the nine deities and so forth: one should install the nine deities.
All the Arhats, fashioned as pills, are placed upon the stūpa. (8.2.9)

One should contemplate the syllable preceded by *Sva* (SVA) as the witness of the Dharma for the stupas and the Dharmadhātu above; then, one should visualize the sun upon the palm of the hand. (8.2.10)
The yogi should meditate upon the syllable of nectar in the center of his hand,
visualizing it as white in color and emitting manifold rays of blazing light.
With the finger [he forms] the vajra-needle, while on the left is the lotus petal;
for him, there is the lotus-vajra-avatī, the hollowed palms joined, and the thread in the middle.
One should meditate with the totality of all principles and consecrate the rosary;
thereafter, the mantra-practitioner should recite the mantra, specifically using the fingers and so forth.
The state of being the Vajra-holder of the left [hands] arises from the non-dual nature of the Vajra;
in rites for pacification (*śāntika*), it is applied as the Wrathful One, while in rites for prosperity (*pauṣṭika*), it is applied through the central principle.
The ring finger is said to be for subjugation up to the limit of malevolent rites; the thumb is for the vajra-hook through its nature of attracting the deity. (8.2.15)
Through the power of recitation while in a state of meditative concentration, [the goals] are accomplished; there is no doubt about this.
However, for yogins who lack the true reality, their meditation on mantras lacks true reality.
For those who possess the vajra and bell of reality, because the reality of the unproduced mudrā is such,
the yogin, having taken recourse to that reality, should perform all rites according to reality.
The reality of the Akṣaruka-karaṇḍa is purified by the expansion of mantra; it is counted as a conch, written in letters, and meditated upon as the essence of yoga. (8.2.18)
Oṃ, at every step may I become the Great Wisdom, the state of all Buddhas; hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ ho ho ho aḥ svāhā.
Whatever is desired through the mantras for purifying the rosary, that very thing one shall accomplish.
The rites of reality are mastered; however, that which is indistinct remains far away.
Listen well, O possessor of great knowledge, especially to the reality of knowledge:
when one is composed, the wheel is worshipped through the distinction of the equanimous mind.
One should meditate upon [the deity] seated on a lotus throne, white in color, fashioned from the seed-syllable of primordial wisdom and situated in the center of the lunar disk.
Two-armed, seated upon a sattva, adorned with all ornaments;
the two hands in the mahāmudrā gesture, pressed together at the heart.
[He saw] the Lord Ārya-Vairocana, beautiful with a white complexion,
surrounded on all sides by clouds consisting of radiant Buddhas and various rays of light.
The recitation of mantras is proclaimed as being performed both simultaneously and by means of sequential arrangement;
it revolves with the left and right hands, [yielding] the bliss of the ḍākinīs.
The seed-syllables of the vowels and consonants are strung together by the thread of the syllable *hūṃ*.
A yogin should meditate upon this seed; he shall swiftly attain the state of Buddhahood. (8.2.26)
Thus ends the second section of the eighth [chapter], concerning the cultivation of the recitation of the mantra beginning with *ap*.
Part 3,
ap8.66 <Sz 4.3.34a→> Listen, O Vajra, to the true nature of the characteristics of the yoga of the upward transition.
But by means of the right path, I shall show you the beautiful course of the yogins.
O Jñānendra, I wish to hear: what are the nine gates like?
According to the distinction of these gates, what are the virtues, defects, and so forth of knowledge like?
Listen correctly to the application of the means of knowledge regarding the time of death:
there is a beautiful state on the right path, and due to the faults of existence, there is [a state] on the wrong path.
The characteristic of the nine gates— the bindu, the navel, the upper [apertures], the eyes, the nose, the ears, and the gateways of inhalation and exhalation— is as follows. 8.3.4.

In the navel is the *kāmika* [center], which leads to heaven; by means of the *bindu*, for those possessing a formal body, the coming and going to the progressively higher stations above is proclaimed. || 8.3.5 ||
May the yakṣas be [the guardians] of their noses, and the accomplished deities of their two ears;
may the knowledge that has entered the eyes of men be [the protector] of those who follow the king. (8.3.6)
In the urine of the door of existence are the hungry ghosts and likewise the animals;
in the anus are the eight divisions of the hells. Thus, O son of noble family, is the characteristic of the transition of existence.
Since the emergence of the various distinctions of cyclic existence arises from specific gateways,
therefore, through those specific gateways, the minds of yogins become well-composed.
The signs of death have been shown for those who have reached the time of death;
one should not disclose this supreme yoga of the departure of the soul to the elderly and others.
First, with the *kumbhaka* breath-retentions, there is the commencement; all the gates are blocked.
There is the visualization of the five *sphoṭika* stupas at the openings of the gates. (8.3.10)
Of that downward-opening gateway, the seed is like white water;
of inhalation and exhalation, the fire is its seed, and it is like a blazing flame.
Being well-composed, one should meditate upon that preceding exhalation,
with a mind focused on the circle of wind, [visualizing] the color of the wind and the body as the wind-circle.
One should draw forth the roots of the seed-syllable of air, which are the roots of the end of air, by means of the union of the bindu and nāda with the seeds of consciousness.
One should apply the hook and other [mudrās] of the terrible ones to the seed-syllable of Vajrī;
by means of the ten places for attracting the terrible ones, from twenty-four places.
At each station of the feet, there are nine joints extending upward;
one should purify the syllable of the body by means of the seed-syllables of the *ūrṇā* and *palita*.

Having uttered it with a terrible sound by means of the seed-syllable at the end of the eighth, one should join the half-syllable to each preceding letter of the first group of the most terrible [syllables]. 8.3.16.
One should impel [the breath] with sound or without sound by means of the downward flow of the seed-syllable of air;
one should focus the mind on the sphere of air for the seed-syllable that possesses the appropriate wind.
With twenty-four locations, one should go higher and higher from there;
by means of the grey hair [of the yogis], one should consume the supreme color above.
For those who have reached the ultimate state of the nine joints, the mental practitioner effects an immediate departure upwards;
this applies even to those who have committed the murder of a deity, the killing of Brahmins, or the five acts of immediate retribution.
One is liberated by means of this path from the enjoyment of thieves and sensual desires;
but for one smeared by evil, the fault of existence remains far away [from being overcome].
Just as the beauty of a lotus born from mud is utterly stainless, so too is the desired [purity] of bodies arising from mud-like [defilements] through the bodies of gnosis (jñānakāya). 8.3.21
When the time for departure has arrived, it is an untimely slaughter by the gods.
Therefore, a wise person should apply the yoga of observing the signs of the bodies.
Listen, Vajra, to the reality of yoga as it truly is, which is to be accomplished specifically through the state of a mind characterized by equanimity in all its prior aspects. (8.3.23)
In the heart, situated in the center of the mandala by means of the seed-syllables of the five Buddhas,
its form is perceived as having the appearance of the rays of the blazing sun.
One should cause all forms and so forth to be dissolved by means of a mind established in the syllable *hūṃ*, endowed with the previously mentioned characteristics of emptiness. (8.3.25)
Having produced the form from the seed-syllable in the center of the lunar disk,
one should contemplate oneself as Jñānaḍākinī seated upon a lotus throne. (8.3.26)
He has three faces, six arms, and three eyes; he is adorned with a crown,
possesses a smile, anger, and the erotic sentiment, and is decorated with all ornaments.
[He saw] him, white as a jasmine flower or the moon, adorned with most beautiful garments and ornaments,
radiating with clouds of Buddhas, and seated upon a lion throne of living beings.
In the first [hand] there is the arrangement of arrows, likewise an elephant goad in the second;
in the third, a raised vajra; and in the left [hands], the threatening finger and a noose.
In the second [phase], one should meditate on the Kalpalatā; in the third, the Saṃnāhadhanus and the Raśmimālā above; thus, with the breath stilled, one should contemplate these in many ways.

One should then arrange the placement of the letters, specifically that which consists of the eight seed-syllables; having extracted them like seeds according to the application of the vowels and consonants (āli-kāli).
All [the syllables] are white in color, joined with seeds associated with moonlight;
there is the placement of the heart-egg-born within the lotus of the plantain flower. 8.3.32.
In its center, however, one should meditate with both knowledge and discernment, through the state of being that is unmoving and free from affliction.
Then, the wise practitioner should hold the external [breaths] of yoga,
focusing on the quarters, the worlds, and the conscious beings with a mind fixed on the circle of wind.
In the center of that, indeed in the midst of the fires, is the Sun; it is the red [syllable] of that very seed-mantra joined with the vowels and consonants. || 8.3.35 ||
By means of the swinging recitation (dolāhāra-jāpa), especially for yogins,
the seeds of knowledge within the swings are struck at the center.
In the *Hāra*, the knowledge of the heart is destroyed like a flower;
by means of the swinging of the swing (*dolādolena*) through recitation, one who recites [attains] the taking away of the *hāra* through recitation.
For yogins, one should cause the self and the external to be made like a swing; having characterized the characteristics of the swing, one should observe the characteristics of the necklace. 8.3.38.
Through the practice of the yoga of the swing, by contemplating the reality of equanimity,
one who is concentrated through the state of pure being attains perfection; of this there is no doubt.
Then, the wise one should cause the external bodies of the practitioner, which have been fashioned, to be known by one who perceives the minds of others.
One should contemplate the excellent paths through the specific recitations of the state (*bhāva*) with a concentrated mind; one will succeed here, there is no doubt.
Then, moreover, the wise one should perform the ritual action with a mind in the form of a lamp, having the nature of gnosis.
Indeed, the reality of the Śrāvakas and others has been well-spoken;
having stabilized the crystal-like mind, one possesses a consciousness in the form of a lamp.
Having taken recourse to all conceptual proliferation, one should bring that proliferation to a state free from proliferation;
having taken recourse to the yoga of intrinsic nature, one should relinquish all of this.
"O Blessed One, by what is knowledge distinguished?"
The Blessed One said: Knowledge is declared to be fivefold. 8.3.46.
For the Guhya [deities], there is the mirror-like knowledge (*ādarśajñāna*); for the gods, it arises from the knowledge of the wrath of the asuras;
for the miserable [beings], it is the knowledge of the pretas; but for those in hell, it is fear and wailing.
The animal kingdom, the deluded, and those with deluded knowledge; the insentient, such as the stationary beings and so forth—knowledge is said to be of five kinds. || 8.3.48 ||
The knowledge of the ignorant consists of being shrouded in dullness like the mute; however, for the wise,
it is the specific essence of knowledge, which is attained through the particularities of the Yoga scriptures.
Indeed, throughout thousands of millions of births, I have been impelled by knowledge;
having generated faith with effort, the wise one [should study] the Yoga-śāstra.
The words of external scriptures and the like are comparable to a theatrical stage;
one should strive for the state of enjoyment and liberation in accordance with the Yoga scriptures.
O fair-faced one, this yoga, which is the essence of all essences, has been declared to you.
Thus ends the third section of the eighth [chapter], titled "The Removal of the Knowledge of the Heretics."
Part 4, ap8.118:
Listen, O Lord Vajraprabha, to the characteristics of the mantras of the kings.
Oṃ vajrāmṛta mahāsukha haṃ svāhā. This is the heart mantra. 8.4.1.
Oṃ āḥ hūṃ hūṃ svāhā | This is the recitation mantra of Vajrasattva. || 8.4.2 ||
Oṃ āḥ aṃ haṃ svāhā | To Raudrī.
Oṃ āḥ āṃ haṃ svāhā | To Vajrabimbā.
Oṃ āḥ iṃ haṃ svāhā | To Rāgavajrā. Oṃ āḥ īṃ haṃ svāhā | To Vajrasaumyā.
Oṃ āḥ uṃ haṃ svāhā | To Vajrayakṣā.
Oṃ āḥ ūṃ haṃ svāhā | To Vajraḍākinī.
Oṃ āḥ aṃ haṃ svāhā | To Śabdavajrā. Oṃ āḥ aḥ haṃ svāhā | To Pṛthvīvajrā. || 8.4.3 ||
Oṃ āḥ oṃ haṃ svāhā | To Vaṃśā. Oṃ āḥ auṃ haṃ svāhā | To Vīṇā.
Oṃ āḥ eṃ haṃ svāhā | To Mukundā.
Oṃ āḥ aiṃ haṃ svāhā | To Murajā. Oṃ āḥ vajrāṅkuśi jaḥ haṃ svāhā | To Vajrāṅkuśī.
Oṃ āḥ vajrapāśe hūṃ haṃ svāhā | [This is] for Vajrapāśā. Oṃ āḥ vajrasphoṭe vaṃ haṃ svāhā | [This is] for Vajraśṛṅkhalā. Oṃ āḥ vajraghaṇṭe hoḥ haṃ svāhā | [This is] for Vajraghaṇṭā. || 8.4.4 ||
The practitioner should recite the mantra of Locanā and the others as before. 8.4.5.
Oṃ ṛṃ svāhā! To the flower. Oṃ ṝṃ svāhā! To the incense.
Oṃ ḷaṃ svāhā! To the goddess Gandhā.
Oṃ ḹṃ svāhā! To the goddess Dīpā. || 8.4.6 ||
Thus [is the mantra] of Vajrasattva. 8.4.7.
Oṃ hrīḥ svāhā. [This is] of Heruka. 8.4.8.
Oṃ vajraguhya siddhaparamayogeśvari kapālamālādhāriṇi rudhirapriye śmaśānavāsini hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | [This is] for Gaurī. 8.4.9.

Oṃ vajracaṇḍeśvari, wielder of the skull-topped staff, great wielder of the thunderbolt, crowned with a garland of skulls! Summon, summon the hearts of all the wicked! Summon! Rulu rulu bhyo hūṃ phaṭ! [This is] of Cauryā.

Oṃ, O invincible Vajra, supreme secret one adorned with a garland of skulls, enchantress of all the wicked, beloved one, come, come, Blessed One, Sovereign Lady of the Vajra Secret, wearer of many diverse guises, warder-off of all the wicked, hūṃ phaṭ! [This is for] Pramohā. 8.4.11.

Oṃ vajravetāli kha kha khahi khahi! O you who wear a distorted appearance, adorned with distorted ornaments, strike, strike! Burn, burn! Cook, cook! Do not delay, do not delay! Remember your pledge! Cause [them] to enter into the center of the maṇḍala; raise them all up! Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ! This is for Vetālī. 8.4.12.

Oṃ, come, come, O Blessed One, Vajra Mistress of Secrets, wearer of many diverse guises, nourisher of all Tathāgatas! Remember the pledge! Slay, slay! Raṅga, raṅga! Cause to dance, cause to dance! Fulfill, fulfill! Enter, enter all spirits! Dance, dance! Cause to dance, cause to dance! Haḥ ha ha ha ha hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ! [This is] Pukkasī. 8.4.13.

Oṃ! O you who are at the tip of the vajra-spear, pierce, pierce the hearts of all the wicked! Draw them in, draw them in! Strike, strike! Burn, burn! Grind, grind! Kill, kill! Do not delay, do not delay! Remember the pledge! Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ! [This is] for Caṇḍālī. 8.4.14.
Oṃ vajra Māheśvarī, haṃ haṃ haṃ haṃ haḥ, rulu rulu bhyo hūṃ phaṭ! Devour all the wicked; crush their hearts, hūṃ phaṭ svāhā! [This is] for Ghasmarī. 8.4.15.
Oṃ sumbhanī dīptasamayavajre hūṃ phaṭ! [This is] for the one who resembles Heruka. 8.4.16.
Oṃ vajravaṃśe hūṃ svāhā | To Vaṃśā. Oṃ vajravīṇe hūṃ svāhā | To Vīṇā.
Oṃ vajramukunde hūṃ svāhā | [This is] for Mukundā. Oṃ vajramṛdaṅge hūṃ svāhā | [This is] for Murajā. || 8.4.17 ||
Oṃ vajravaḍavāmukhe yogeśvari hiḥ hi hi hi hi hūṃ jaḥ | [This is] for the one with the horse’s face. Oṃ vajradaṃṣṭrāvarāhamukhe trāṃ va va hūṃ | [This is] for the one with the vajra-face.

Oṃ candrasūryahutāśani siṃhanirnāde siṃhavaktre siṃhini ṭāṃ ṭāṃ vaṃ. [This is] for Siṃhāsyā. Oṃ vajradhātusaṃjīvani mahāyakṣiṇi śvānarūpiṇi mahāpralayanirnāde kāmarūpiṇi trāṃ traṭa traṭa hoḥ. [This is] for Śvānāsyā. 8.4.18.
"SVĀHĀ" [is uttered] from all sides. Thus [ends the section] for Heruka together with his retinue. 8.4.19.
Oṃ aṃ svāhā! To Nairātmyā.
Oṃ āṃ svāhā! To Vajrā.
Oṃ iṃ svāhā! To Gaurī.
Oṃ īṃ svāhā! To Vāriyoginī. Oṃ uṃ svāhā! To Vajraḍākinī. || 8.4.20 ||
Oṃ ūṃ svāhā! To Pukkasī.
Oṃ ṛṃ svāhā! To Śavarī.
Oṃ ṛṃ svāhā! To Caṇḍālinī.
Oṃ ḷṃ svāhā! To Ḍombinī. || 8.4.21 ||
Oṃ l̥ṃ svāhā! To Gaurī. Oṃ eṃ svāhā! To Cauryā.
Oṃ aiṃ svāhā! To Vetālī. Oṃ oṃ svāhā! To Ghasmarī. 8.4.22.
Oṃ auṃ svāhā! To those who move upon the earth. Oṃ aṃ svāhā! To those who move through the sky. 8.4.23.
Thus [is the mantra] of Nairātmyā together with her retinue. 8.4.24.
Oṃ deva picuvajra hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. This is the heart mantra of Hevajra.
Oṃ trailokyākṣepa hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. [This is] for the two-armed [form].
Oṃ jvala jvala bhyo hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | [This is] for the four-armed one. Oṃ kiṭi kiṭi vajra hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | [This is] for the six-armed one. || 8.4.25 ||
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, the Lord of Heroes, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ, to him who resembles the fire at the end of a great aeon, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!

Oṃ, to the one fierce with a crown of matted locks, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ, to the one whose face is terrifying with fearsome, formidable fangs, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ, to the one resplendent with a thousand arms, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!

Oṃ, to the one who wields the axe, the noose, the raised trident, and the khaṭvāṅga staff, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ, to the one who wears a tiger-skin garment, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ, to the one whose body is like great smoky darkness, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!
Of the one with a hundred thousand arms. || 8.4.26 ||

Oṃ śrī he he ru ru ka vajra ḍākinījālasaṃvara hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. [This is] for the one who delights in charnel grounds and has two arms. Oṃ śrīherukavajra sarvaduṣṭasamayamudrāprabhañjaka hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. [This is] for the one with the fierce posture and two arms.
Oṃ hrīḥ ha ha hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ. Of the King of Vidyās. 8.4.27.
Thus ends the mantra for the arising of Heruka. 8.4.28.
Oṃ vajravairocanīye buddhaḍākinīye svāhā. This sixteen-syllable mantra is the root mantra of the Ḍākinī. 8.4.29.
Oṃ, svāhā to Mārīcī! This is the heart-mantra of Mārīcī. Oṃ, svāhā to Mārīcī, Vattāli, Vadāli, Varāli, O you with the face of a boar! This is the subsidiary heart-mantra (upahṛdaya-mantra). 8.4.30.
Oṃ piśāci parṇaśavari, O pacifier of all plagues, hūṃ hūṃ mahodari phaṭ! [This is] the mantra of Parṇaśāvarī. 8.4.31.
Oṃ vajrāṅkuśa ākarṣaya hūṃ!
Oṃ vajrapāśa bandha hūṃ!

Free from the pairs of opposites, full of enthusiasm, established in reality, and girded with firm resolve.

Whatever mudrā has been taught by the Omniscient Ones according to the various divisions of families— each of those should be grasped and accomplished through its respective ritual procedures by that very same [practitioner].
Indeed, one whose self is deluded, having grasped his mother Vedavatī or a daughter of a twice-born man,
becomes Vairocana himself through meditation on the purification of delusion. (10.1.7)
"Even though the mother of supreme knowledge was previously enjoyed by the father, it is nevertheless through her alone that accomplishment occurs; thus spoke Mahāsukha. (10.1.8)
One whose nature is aversion, having taken hold of either the daughter of a caṇḍāla woman or a yakṣa maiden,
attains the state of Akṣobhya in person by meditating on the purification of aversion.
One whose nature is passion, having taken hold of a dancing girl, a sister, a serpent-woman, or an asura-woman,
becomes Amitābha in essence through meditation on the purification of passion. (10.10)
One whose nature is jealous, having taken hold of a skilled Apsaras or his own sister’s daughter,
becomes the heroic Amoghasiddhi through meditation on the purification of jealousy. 10.1.11
One who possesses a proud nature, having taken as his bride a king’s daughter or a daughter of the Vidyādharas,
becomes one born of the Maṇi family by means of the purification of pride while remaining absorbed in meditation.
Together with Locanā, the Buddha Akṣobhya is accomplished; together with Pāṇḍarā and Tārā, Padmapāṇi Amoghasiddhi is accomplished. (10.13)
This principle has been stated: "Together with Ratnolkā, one succeeds as a Ratnī.
By this [method], other wrathful deities and the goddesses who are the offspring of the Jinas also attain accomplishment. 10.14.14.

Those who are wrathful are pacified and brought to accomplishment through the fierce rite; those who are passionate are accomplished through the peaceful rite alone; and those who are arrogant are accomplished through the rite of nourishment.
Thus has this method, which requires no arduous effort, been described by the omniscient ones who are exceedingly compassionate;
it is a means to happiness that is utterly effortless and free from the vows of difficult ascetic practices.
But having thus obtained the essence of immortality for the destruction of the afflictions, how can one who makes no effort achieve Buddhahood through difficult disciplines and observances? (10.17)
That foolish person who, having obtained the means for his own happiness, does not act for his own welfare— once he has passed away from here, no one knows where he will go again. (10.18)
Having understood this, the virtuous person should always regard all action as being like a dream or an illusion.
Therefore, one who knows the Buddha’s Dharma must perform [virtuous deeds] until they reach the further shore of the ocean of saṃsāra. 10.19.19.
Thus ends the first section of the tenth [chapter], concerning the empowerment of the seal of the teacher (ācāryamudrādhiṣṭhāna).

There, the perfected ones (*siddhas*) who dwell in the sky offer words of encouragement and cries of "Well done!"; the gods who abide in Tuṣita, the most excellent of deities, and the sons of the Suras and Asuras who rule over the higher and lower realms, as well as the *vidyādharas*, having arrived, bow down—all the way up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven. (10.29)

With supreme devotion, they create heaps of various flowers, a rain of fragrance with various scents, and various excellent incenses. What is the use of further elaboration? By means of the merit to be accomplished, these beings worship with all those offerings that exist throughout the three realms.
Thus ends the second section of the tenth [chapter], titled "The Worship and Honor for the Attainment of Great Bliss."
Part 3, Chapter 10.31:
"Where has the perfected Vidyāpuruṣa gone? Where does he abide? This is my doubt; tell me, O Mahāsukha. 10.3.1
The Blessed One said:

The perfected person of knowledge has gone nowhere, nor does he abide anywhere; devoid of beginning, middle, and end, free from duality, he is the light of the three worlds. All-pervading, all-knowing, universal, and the purpose of all, he dwells within the minds of all sentient beings and is utterly liberated from all states of woe. Adorned with every virtue, belonging to all, auspicious, peerless, eternally risen, the Lord and Protector whose conceptual constructions have been shaken off—he is the King, the sphere of the Victor, though devoid of shape and color. (10.32)

He is a vajra because he cannot be pierced; he is the moon because he is free from the scorching heat of the afflictions; he is a lion because he is fearless; he is the ocean because he is difficult to fathom. (10.33)
Thus, by means of various analogies, he alone is compared by yogins; he alone accomplishes the welfare of all sentient beings. 10.3.4

Though free from conceptual construction, he displays his supreme birth, his renunciation, and his childhood play; his own entry into the state of a monk, his transition to the site of the Vajra-throne, his destruction of Māra, and his peerless perfect enlightenment. He demonstrates the turning of the wheel of Dharma, the delightful and most wondrous miracle of descending among the gods, the taming of the elephant Dhana-pāla, and the pure guidance of worthy beings. He performs the faultless act of collecting alms and the subduing of the wheel of the three worlds, as well as the Bodhisattva’s status as crown prince. Finally, he manifests the great purpose of his final nirvāṇa and his sovereignty over the Dharma throughout the triple realm. (10.3.5)

Thus it is, O sons of noble family: in this way, that perfected one displays through the form of an illusion a divine Buddha-play called "the dream," characterized by manifold distinctions, for the sake of the entire world. (10.35)
Thus ends the third section of the tenth chapter, titled "The Magical Manifestation of the Buddha."

"O Lord, you have previously described the offering of feces, urine, blood, fish, and meat."
How indeed can there be no sin when filling the mouth with impurity among those who possess knowledge? If one is sinful, how can there be no fruit [of that action]? (10.4.2)
The Blessed One said:
"But those beings who are deluded by ignorance and deprived of the means to knowledge,"
Those who are indeed attached to external objects and rendered dull by the web of conceptual constructions—
for them, there is both sin and merit, based on the conceptualization of two heaps.
These phenomena are pure by nature, unarisen, and without abode. 10.4.4
The Buddhas have shown this means for the increase of wisdom in sentient beings:
merit should be relinquished from the perspective of ultimate truth; what need is there to mention the grasping of non-merit? (10.41)
Just as a being intent on reaching the far shore, having gathered wood and grass, makes a raft for floating across a river filled with water. (10.42)
Having become attached there, one should emerge, cast it off, and proceed with ease; thus,
having descended from both dharma and adharma, one reaches the further shore of saṃsāra.
Awakening, which is free from both dharma and non-dharma, is attained with ease;
therefore, having abandoned the web of conceptual construction, one should increase in the profundity of the Dharma. 10.44.8
The knower of mantras should not conceptualize the path proclaimed by the Tathāgata;
for conceptualization is great delusion, which casts one into the ocean of saṃsāra.
Established in non-conceptual samādhi, one shines like the stainless sky through the union of the two organs and the integration of body, speech, and mind.
One should conceive of the form of the Jina as devoid of all formal characteristics;
